Compared with a UNet diffusion baseline, our method improves both spatial accuracy and motion smoothness while reducing inference latency from 21.66 ms to 6.74 ms. Furthermore, unlike deterministic MLP baselines that catastrophically diverge under out-of-distribution deployment, MimicIK remains stable near singular configurations and enables robust 20 Hz real-time control on deployment hardware.

AI.tldr: MimicIK is a real-time generative inverse kinematics framework using conditional flow matching to learn smooth, robust joint-space motion priors from teleoperation demonstrations. It achieves low error (4.65 mm position error, 92.01% 10mm success rate), low trajectory spike rate (7.99%), and fast inference (6.74 ms) while remaining stable near singularities, outperforming UNet diffusion and deterministic MLP baselines.
AI.motivation: Inverse kinematics remains a bottleneck for real-time robot manipulation: classical solvers suffer from discontinuous branch switching and instability near singularities, while learned IK approaches struggle to balance accuracy, smoothness, and real-time efficiency, especially when trained on noisy human teleoperation data.
AI.method: MimicIK uses conditional flow matching with a Minimal Iterative Policy (MIP) backbone to predict continuous delta-joint commands via a two-step iterative refinement process. It incorporates an FK consistency loss — a differentiable forward-kinematics regularization that penalizes task-space deviations from the target pose during training.
AI.result: On a real-world 6-DOF robot dataset (8,848 demonstrations), MimicIK achieved mean position error of 4.65 mm, 10 mm success rate of 92.01%, trajectory spike rate of 7.99%, and inference latency reduced from 21.66 ms (UNet diffusion) to 6.74 ms. It remained stable near singularities under out-of-distribution deployment, enabling robust 20 Hz real-time control.
AI.conclusion: MimicIK demonstrates that generative flow-based IK with FK consistency regularization can simultaneously achieve high spatial accuracy, motion smoothness, and real-time efficiency, outperforming both diffusion-based and deterministic MLP baselines while maintaining robustness to singular configurations and out-of-distribution scenarios.

title: VGPT-RSI for RH-Adjacent Formal Progress: Boundary Certificates, Verified Finite Lagarias Inequalities, and Explicit Failure Localization
summary: The Riemann Hypothesis remains one of the central unsolved problems in mathematics. Rather than claiming proof, we investigate whether a verifiable AI-assisted reasoning system can produce reliable, formally checked partial progress while explicitly identifying the remaining mathematical obstructions. We apply the Verifiable Growing Physical Transformer with Recursive Self-Improvement (VGPT-RSI) to two RH-adjacent certification tasks. First, we construct and verify a finite RH-boundary certificate for inequality on a parameterized safe lower curve over a region. The numerical boundary curve is converted into a certificate-backed lower curve, audited using outward-rounded interval arithmetic and Arb/FLINT ball arithmetic, and then checked in Rocq/CoqInterval for the parameterized theorem. Second, we initiate a formal Lagarias-route certificate. Lagarias criterion states that RH is equivalent to the global inequality. We formalize the finite quantity and produce a Coq-checked finite certificate. The final system identifies the exact unresolved mathematical bottlenecks: formalizing the Lagarias equivalence, proving the global tail theorem beyond any finite cutoff, and potentially reducing counterexamples to colossally abundant or related extremal integers. These results demonstrate that VGPT-RSI can produce certified RH-adjacent formal progress, organize proof dependencies, and avoid overclaiming when the remaining obstruction is genuinely mathematical.

AI.tldr: This paper applies the VGPT-RSI system to produce formally verified, finite certificates for two Riemann Hypothesis-adjacent problems (a boundary inequality and a Lagarias criterion finite check) without claiming to prove RH itself, explicitly identifying the remaining mathematical obstructions that prevent a full proof.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that AI-assisted reasoning systems can produce reliable, formally checked partial progress on the Riemann Hypothesis while honestly delineating where the remaining unsolved mathematical challenges lie, rather than making false claims of a full proof.
AI.method: VGPT-RSI framework is applied to two RH-adjacent certification tasks: (1) a finite RH-boundary certificate using outward-rounded interval arithmetic, Arb/FLINT ball arithmetic, and Rocq/CoqInterval verification; (2) a formal Lagarias-route certificate implemented as a Coq-checked finite certificate.
AI.result: Successfully produced and formally verified finite certificates for both tasks; identified unresolved bottlenecks: formalizing the Lagarias equivalence, proving the global tail theorem beyond finite cutoff, and addressing colossally abundant counterexample reduction.
AI.conclusion: VGPT-RSI can generate certified partial progress on hard mathematical problems, organize proof dependencies, and avoid overclaiming when the remaining obstruction is genuinely mathematical rather than computational or formal.

title: Task-Aware Environment Augmentation for Reliable Navigation via Shielded Conditional Diffusion
summary:
Reliable trajectory planning under partial observability depends not only on computing a feasible geometric path, but also on whether the robot receives informative observations while executing that trajectory. Existing approaches usually keep the environment fixed and adapt the robot through belief-space planning, active localization, or added sensing, often incurring costly uncertainty propagation and brittle behavior in observation-poor regions. We flip this perspective and address the largely open problem of \emph{task-aware environment augmentation}: given a mapped environment, a planned task trajectory, and a small budget of visual fiducial markers, where should the environment be augmented so that the planned trajectory can be executed reliably under uncertainty? Our key observation is that useful marker layouts are defined by the localization support they provide along the task trajectory: a small number of well-timed observations can be sufficient to prevent uncertainty from accumulating in regions where state-estimation error would otherwise compromise control. Building on this observation, we present \tbp{SCoDA}, $\textbf{S}$hielded $\textbf{Co}$nditional $\textbf{D}$iffusion for Environment $\textbf{A}$ugmentation. \tbp{SCoDA} learns a conditional distribution over high-performing fiducial layouts from data, using the environment, planned trajectory, disturbance context, and desired execution profile as conditioning. Its shielded sampler reasons over where along the planned execution pose corrections should occur, and steers this distribution toward task-relevant, finite-budget augmentations. Across simulated benchmarks and hardware deployments, we show that \tbp{SCoDA} improves trajectory execution reliability and completion time over strong baselines.
  Code, models and dataset available at: \hyperlink{scoda-diffusion.github.io}{https://scoda-diffusion.github.io/}

AI.tldr: SCoDA uses conditional diffusion to augment environments with visual fiducial markers, improving trajectory execution reliability under partial observability by placing markers where they best support localization along a planned path.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches adapt the robot (belief-space planning, active localization) but keep the environment fixed, leading to costly uncertainty propagation and brittle behavior in observation-poor regions. The authors flip this by augmenting the environment itself with visual fiducial markers to support reliable execution.
AI.method: SCoDA (Shielded Conditional Diffusion for Environment Augmentation) learns a conditional distribution over fiducial marker layouts using the environment map, planned trajectory, disturbance context, and desired execution profile as conditioning. A shielded sampler reasons about where pose corrections should occur and steers the distribution toward task-relevant, finite-budget augmentations.
AI.result: Across simulated benchmarks and hardware deployments, SCoDA improves trajectory execution reliability and completion time over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware environment augmentation with a small number of well-placed visual fiducial markers can effectively prevent uncertainty accumulation in critical regions, enabling more reliable trajectory execution under partial observability without modifying the robot's planning or sensing pipeline.

title: Towards Verifiable Agentic Data Science: Solving Irregular TSQA Via Tool-Grounded Reasoning
summary: Time series data in real-world deployments is overwhelmingly irregular. Observations are asynchronous, missing values are informative rather than random, and sampling frequencies vary across sensors and operational windows. However, existing Time Series Question Answering (TSQA) benchmarks mostly assume regularly sampled inputs, leaving a fundamental gap in understanding how large language models (LLMs) and AI agents perform under irregular conditions. To bridge this gap, we introduce IRTS-ToolBench, a benchmark of 1,700 questions spanning 10 task types across 13 domains. IRTS-ToolBench is designed to be used independently by any researcher working on LLM-based irregular time series analysis, providing standardized inputs and a reproducible evaluation protocol. Code can be found in https://github.com/SanhornC/IRTS-ToolBench.

AI.tldr: IRTS-ToolBench is a benchmark of 1,700 questions across 10 task types and 13 domains designed to evaluate LLMs and AI agents on irregular time series data (asynchronous, missing values, varying sampling frequencies), addressing the gap in existing TSQA benchmarks that assume regular sampling.
AI.motivation: Real-world time series data is overwhelmingly irregular (asynchronous, informative missing values, varying sampling frequencies), yet existing TSQA benchmarks assume regularly sampled inputs, creating a fundamental gap in understanding LLM performance under realistic irregular conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct IRTS-ToolBench, a benchmark containing 1,700 questions spanning 10 task types across 13 domains, designed with standardized inputs and a reproducible evaluation protocol for assessing LLM-based irregular time series analysis.
AI.result: The benchmark provides 1,700 questions across 10 task types and 13 domains, with standardized inputs and reproducible evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: IRTS-ToolBench bridges the gap between regular-sampling TSQA benchmarks and real-world irregular time series, enabling researchers to independently evaluate LLM and AI agent performance on irregular time series analysis.

title: Seam-to-Graph Reconstruction for Garment Configuration Alignment
summary: Seams encode rich structural information about garments but are frequently partially observable in robotic manipulation scenarios. To robustly leverage seam information, we propose a Seam-to-Graph network based on graph neural networks and attention mechanisms. This network maps unstructured seam observations to a topology-encoded structural skeleton graph for real-time garment state estimation. Using this skeleton-graph-based state estimation, we design a deformation-aware, hierarchical visual servoing controller for garment configuration alignment. We implement this controller on a bimanual robot system to load a garment onto a screen printing platen and to align it to the desired configuration precisely. Real-robot experiments demonstrate that the robot using the proposed method not only achieves human-level alignment accuracy with reduced variance in alignment error but is also robust to different garments. These results demonstrate that the use of seam information is effective for garment manipulation.

AI.tldr: A Seam-to-Graph network using GNNs and attention mechanisms maps partial seam observations to a structural skeleton graph for real-time garment state estimation, enabling a deformation-aware hierarchical visual servoing controller that achieves human-level precision in bimanual garment loading onto a screen printing platen.
AI.motivation: Seams encode rich structural information about garments but are frequently partially observable in robotic manipulation, limiting their effective use.
AI.method: Seam-to-Graph network (GNN + attention) maps unstructured partial seam observations to topology-encoded skeleton graphs for state estimation; a deformation-aware, hierarchical visual servoing controller uses this for garment configuration alignment on a bimanual robot.
AI.result: The robot achieves human-level alignment accuracy with reduced variance in alignment error, and demonstrates robustness across different garments in real-robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: Seam information is effective for garment manipulation, enabling precise and robust robotic alignment.

title: CONCORD: Asynchronous Sparse Aggregation for Device-Cloud RAG under Document Isolation
comment: to be published in IEEE ICWS 2026
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a pivotal technique for improving language models by incorporating external knowledge at inference time. As device-cloud collaborative inference makes it feasible to deploy small language models on edge devices, a new setting arises in which private documents remain on the device and public knowledge resides in the cloud. Privacy and policy constraints often forbid raw document exchange, creating a document-isolated dual-end RAG setting. However, existing methods rely on frequent remote synchronization and dense evidence transfer, limiting throughput under realistic latency and bandwidth conditions. To address this issue, we propose CONCORD, an asynchronous sparse aggregation framework for dual-end RAG under document isolation. CONCORD treats the cloud as an asynchronously arriving evidence source rather than a continuously synchronized co-generator. Specifically, we introduce waiting debt control to decide whether each decoding step should continue waiting for remote participation based on the observed return of waiting. We also design a certificate-guided minimal supplementation mechanism that requests only the remote evidence needed to determine the current greedy decision. Steps that consult the cloud preserve the same greedy token as dense dual-end aggregation, while the remaining steps commit locally without remote evidence. Experiments on Natural Questions and WikiText-2 show that CONCORD improves end-to-end throughput over baselines by $1.66\times$ and $2.15\times$, respectively, while reducing per-token communication by over two orders of magnitude and maintaining comparable answer quality and perplexity.

AI.tldr: CONCORD is an asynchronous sparse aggregation framework for dual-end RAG under document isolation that improves throughput by 1.66×–2.15× and reduces communication by over two orders of magnitude while maintaining answer quality.
AI.motivation: Existing dual-end RAG methods rely on frequent remote synchronization and dense evidence transfer, limiting throughput under realistic latency and bandwidth conditions due to document isolation constraints.
AI.method: CONCORD treats the cloud as an asynchronously arriving evidence source using (1) waiting debt control to decide whether to wait for remote participation and (2) a certificate-guided minimal supplementation mechanism that requests only the remote evidence needed for the current greedy decision.
AI.result: On Natural Questions and WikiText-2, CONCORD improves end-to-end throughput by 1.66× and 2.15× respectively, reduces per-token communication by over two orders of magnitude, and maintains comparable answer quality and perplexity.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous sparse aggregation with selective waiting and minimal evidence supplementation is effective for achieving efficient dual-end RAG under document isolation constraints.

title: Rethinking Implicit Spatial Representation in Visuomotor Policy Learning
summary: Generative model-based imitation learning has become a widely adopted paradigm for robotic manipulation, where policy performance depends critically on the conditioned visual representations. Although spatial softmax-based representations have been adopted in prior visuomotor policies, their effectiveness and underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. This work rethinks the use of spatial softmax pooling: do such implicit spatial representations provide effective and stable visual features for robotic manipulation? Through systematic studies of different pooling methods in visual encoders, we find that this pooling operation produces compact and stable spatial representations, which outperform feature-value representations, despite using substantially fewer dimensions. Complementary saliency analysis further suggests that these spatial representations guide the encoder to focus more consistently on task-relevant regions. However, this advantage is limited by a representation bottleneck in current visual encoders: repeated downsampling operations weaken fine-grained spatial information before the action-generation module can use it, especially under low-resolution observations. Motivated by these findings, we propose PRISM, a visual encoder that preserves multiscale implicit spatial information through top-down cross-attention fusion. Experiments across multiple tasks and policy backbones show consistent improvements. In particular, on the low-resolution, high-precision ToolHang task, PRISM shows clear gains, improving the average success rate from 5.0% to 13.4% while increasing parameters by only 15.4%. These results support the use of multiscale implicit spatial representations as an effective and efficient design principle for robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates spatial softmax pooling in robotic imitation learning, identifying its effectiveness in producing compact, stable spatial representations that focus on task-relevant regions. However, a representation bottleneck arises from repeated downsampling that weakens fine-grained spatial info. The authors propose PRISM, a visual encoder using top-down cross-attention fusion to preserve multiscale implicit spatial information, achieving consistent improvements across tasks (e.g., ToolHang from 5.0% to 13.4% success rate with only 15.4% parameter increase).
AI.motivation: To systematically understand why spatial softmax-based representations work well in visuomotor policies and identify their limitations, in order to design more effective visual representations for robotic manipulation.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of pooling methods in visual encoders; saliency analysis to examine encoder focus; proposal of PRISM (a visual encoder that uses top-down cross-attention fusion to preserve multiscale implicit spatial information).
AI.result: Spatial softmax outperforms feature-value representations with fewer dimensions; but a representation bottleneck due to repeated downsampling limits fine-grained spatial information. PRISM improves success rate on low-resolution ToolHang from 5.0% to 13.4% with only 15.4% more parameters.
AI.conclusion: Multiscale implicit spatial representations are an effective and efficient design principle for robotic manipulation visuomotor policies.

title: CogGuard: Cognitive and Operational Profiling for Proactive Warning in Edge Intelligent Services
summary: Proactive warning is an important capability for edge intelligent services, where the system predicts whether a subject will successfully complete an incoming task under strict latency and privacy constraints. Such prediction depends on both long-term static attributes and short-term dynamic states derived from historical interaction logs. Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong long-context reasoning for constructing structured profiles from these logs, but existing solutions face two challenges for edge deployment: (1) profiling methods are typically domain-specific and lack a reusable abstraction across service scenarios, and (2) fine-tuning alignment models on heterogeneous edge clusters incurs high synchronization overhead due to the variance in input sequence lengths. To address these challenges, we propose CogGuard, a proactive-warning framework for edge intelligent services. CogGuard decouples offline LLM-based profile construction from online Small Language Model (SLM)-based score prediction through a shared static-dynamic profile-to-score pipeline, and instantiates it in two representative scenarios: educational performance warning and operational task outcome warning. For efficient profile construction, we design scenario-specific profiling methods with prefix-aligned KV-cache reuse to reduce repeated encoding overhead. For edge-side model alignment, we propose a length-aware distributed fine-tuning strategy with contrastive regularization to mitigate workload imbalance on heterogeneous clusters. Experiments on education and operation datasets show that CogGuard reduces profile construction time by up to 48% and distributed fine-tuning time by 19%, while achieving MAEs of 13.4 and 5.9, respectively, on 100-point-scale warning tasks. In the largest educational setting, CogGuard reduces prediction error by 15.4% compared with the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: CogGuard is a proactive-warning framework for edge intelligent services that decouples offline LLM-based profile construction from online SLM-based score prediction using a shared static-dynamic profile-to-score pipeline. It reduces profile construction time by 48% and distributed fine-tuning time by 19% while achieving MAEs of 13.4 and 5.9 on 100-point-scale warning tasks.
AI.motivation: Proactive warning for edge intelligent services requires predicting task outcomes under strict latency and privacy constraints, relying on both static attributes and dynamic states from historical logs. Existing LLM-based profiling methods are domain-specific and lack reusable abstractions, while fine-tuning alignment models on heterogeneous edge clusters suffers from high synchronization overhead due to varying input sequence lengths.
AI.method: CogGuard decouples offline LLM-based profile construction from online SLM-based score prediction via a shared static-dynamic profile-to-score pipeline. It uses scenario-specific profiling with prefix-aligned KV-cache reuse to reduce encoding overhead, and a length-aware distributed fine-tuning strategy with contrastive regularization to mitigate workload imbalance on heterogeneous clusters.
AI.result: On education and operation datasets, CogGuard reduces profile construction time by up to 48% and distributed fine-tuning time by 19%, achieving MAEs of 13.4 and 5.9 on 100-point-scale warning tasks. In the largest educational setting, it reduces prediction error by 15.4% compared to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: CogGuard provides an efficient and reusable framework for proactive warning on edge devices, leveraging LLMs for offline profiling while using lightweight SLMs for online prediction, with optimized fine-tuning strategies for heterogeneous edge clusters.

title: Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students
comment: Accepted for 18th International Conference on Social Robotics (ICSR + ART 2026), London, UK | 1-4 July 2026
summary: Open-source social robots offer accessibility, repairability, and student empowerment, yet the build itself often presents a barrier. Existing platforms either ship pre-assembled, foreclosing hands-on learning, or expose students to unfamiliar fasteners, opaque wiring, and inaccessible service points that erode engagement. Whether targeted mechanical redesign can lower this barrier whilst maintaining structural integrity remains untested. Here we show that Design for Assembly (DfA) and Design for Disassembly (DfD) interventions reshape how a build feels before they shorten how long it takes. Working with university students in Guyana and Estonia, we applied the Double Diamond framework to co-create the Robot Study Companion (RSC) v4.1: mapping pain points, then redesigning its chassis around twist-lock fasteners, snap-fit joints, and tool-free service latches. Across two studies with developers and first-time builders, system usability climbed from Poor to Excellent (SUS 59.4 to 89.4), perceived workload trended downward (NASA-TLX 4.29 to 4.00), and mean assembly time trended downward (21.4 to 13.7 minutes, with juniors' learning effect), whilst orientation cues and navigation continuity for first-time builders emerged as the next documentation frontier. Perceived workload, not completion time, appears to govern whether students take up open hardware.

AI.tldr: Design for Assembly/Disassembly interventions on the Robot Study Companion v4.1 improved system usability from Poor to Excellent (SUS 59.4→89.4), reduced perceived workload (NASA-TLX 4.29→4.00), and trended assembly time down (21.4→13.7 min), demonstrating that build feel matters more than speed for student adoption of open-source social robots.
AI.motivation: Open-source social robots are inaccessible because building them is a barrier—pre-assembled platforms prevent hands-on learning, while DIY kits use unfamiliar fasteners, opaque wiring, and inaccessible service points that erode student engagement. It was untested whether targeted mechanical redesign could lower this barrier without sacrificing structural integrity.
AI.method: Applied the Double Diamond co-creation framework with university students in Guyana and Estonia to redesign the Robot Study Companion (RSC) v4.1 chassis using twist-lock fasteners, snap-fit joints, and tool-free service latches. Evaluated via two studies with developers and first-time builders using SUS, NASA-TLX, and assembly time metrics.
AI.result: SUS improved from 59.4 (Poor) to 89.4 (Excellent); NASA-TLX trended downward (4.29→4.00); mean assembly time trended downward (21.4→13.7 min, with a learning effect in juniors); orientation cues and navigation continuity for first-time builders emerged as the next documentation challenge.
AI.conclusion: Perceived workload—not completion time—governs whether students engage with open hardware; DfA/DfD redesigns reshape how a build feels before they shorten how long it takes.

title: Attribute Inference from Interactive Targeted Ads
summary:
Targeted advertising systems can pair audiences selected by advertisers with ad units that expose visible user actions. When an interaction remains linked to the campaign that elicited it, the advertiser may receive an observation tied to a user rather than only an aggregate report. We model that channel as a noisy oracle for attribute inference. The model separates targeting predicates, exposure, interaction, and disclosure. These boundaries capture the gap between eligibility and delivery, and the gap between interaction and advertiser visibility.
  We build a reproducible benchmark using synthetic populations calibrated with public data, each with known sensitive labels. A generated campaign semantics layer provides topic variants and response priors. The simulator generates the ground truth, event traces, disclosed observations, and metrics. The evaluation compares Bayesian, supervised, positive and unlabeled, and adaptive attacks under common campaign and disclosure definitions.
  The final evaluation uses four topic variants, seven simulator seeds, and two interaction settings. Repeated campaigns with identity exposure produce measurable but bounded inference signal. At $160$ campaigns, Bayesian and supervised attacks reach about $0.64$ AUC in the main setting and about $0.65$ AUC in the higher interaction setting. Disclosure policy is the strongest control. Aggregate reporting removes the evaluated oracle input tied to users. Type filtering and randomized disclosure reduce the released signal. The result is a model, artifact, and defense evaluation method for privacy in interactive targeted advertising. The code is available at https://github.com/P-HOW/Interactive-Ad-Oracle.

AI.tldr: This paper models how targeted advertising systems can leak user attribute information through visible interaction signals (oracles). Using synthetic populations and simulated campaigns, the authors evaluate Bayesian, supervised, PU, and adaptive attacks, finding that disclosure policy (e.g., aggregate reporting, type filtering, randomized disclosure) is the strongest control, with Bayesian/supervised attacks reaching ~0.64-0.65 AUC after 160 campaigns.
AI.motivation: Targeted advertising systems expose visible user actions (e.g., clicks, conversions) linked to specific campaigns, creating a channel where advertisers can infer user attributes beyond aggregate reports. The authors aim to model, measure, and defend against this inference risk.
AI.method: The authors model the inference channel as a noisy oracle, separating targeting predicates, exposure, interaction, and disclosure. They build a reproducible benchmark with synthetic populations calibrated to public data, a campaign semantics layer for topic variants/response priors, and a simulator generating ground truth, event traces, disclosed observations, and metrics. Attacks include Bayesian, supervised, positive and unlabeled (PU), and adaptive methods under common campaign/disclosure definitions.
AI.result: After 160 campaigns, Bayesian and supervised attacks achieve ~0.64 AUC (main setting) and ~0.65 AUC (higher interaction setting). Disclosure policy is the strongest control: aggregate reporting removes the oracle input, while type filtering and randomized disclosure reduce the released signal.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a model, benchmark artifact, and defense evaluation method for privacy in interactive targeted advertising, demonstrating measurable but bounded inference signal that can be controlled via disclosure policy.

title: Driving, Fast or Slow? Neuro-Symbolic Guidance for Motion Prediction in Multi-Modal Ground Mobility
summary: Accurate and interpretable motion prediction for heterogeneous traffic spaces, including pedestrians, bicycles, cars, and trucks, is essential for safe autonomous navigation. Nevertheless, state-of-the-art approaches remain predominantly black-box, lacking explicit encoding of the regulatory and behavioral constraints of real-world mobility. We propose Trajectory Compliance-Shaping (TraCS), a neuro-symbolic framework that augments existing black-box motion prediction backbones with interpretable and probabilistic first-order logic. To do so, TraCS employs an agentic code-generation pipeline to bridge the gap between natural-language descriptions of traffic regulations and probabilistic motion prediction. Furthermore, TraCS employs a reactive data-streaming inference engine that maintains and efficiently updates compliance landscapes as scenes evolve. To prevent TraCS from overconfidently steering the backbone's predictions in the wrong direction, we propose a neural confidence rating learned as a context-aware attenuation of the compliance signal. We demonstrate on the Argoverse 2 benchmark how TraCS consistently improves state-of-the-art prediction backbones, showing that probabilistic and symbolic compliance reasoning is a broadly applicable and computationally efficient complement to purely neural motion predictors.

AI.tldr: TraCS is a neuro-symbolic framework that augments black-box motion prediction models with probabilistic first-order logic to enforce traffic rule compliance, using code generation from natural language, a reactive inference engine, and learned confidence ratings. It consistently improves SOTA backbones on Argoverse 2.
AI.motivation: Existing motion prediction methods for heterogeneous traffic are black-box and lack explicit encoding of regulatory and behavioral constraints, which is unsafe for autonomous navigation.
AI.method: TraCS combines an agentic code-generation pipeline that translates natural-language traffic regulations into probabilistic first-order logic, a reactive data-streaming inference engine for efficient compliance landscape updates, and a learned neural confidence rating to contextually attenuate compliance signals.
AI.result: On the Argoverse 2 benchmark, TraCS consistently improves state-of-the-art prediction backbones, demonstrating broad applicability and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic and symbolic compliance reasoning is a broadly applicable and computationally efficient complement to purely neural motion predictors for autonomous navigation.

title: Visual-Seeker: Towards Visual-Native Multimodal Agentic Search via Active Visual Reasoning
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in many visual tasks, but they often struggle with factual grounding when confronted with complex, open-world scenarios. While recent multimodal deep search agents attempt to address this issue by utilizing external tools, the visual-native search paradigm remains underexplored. Existing methods primarily rely on simple images with explicit semantics and text-only evidence trajectories, limiting the agent's ability to perform multi-hop, cross-modal reasoning and search. To address these limitations, we propose Visual-Seeker, a visual-native multimodal deep search agent via active visual reasoning. Rather than treating vision as a static input, our agent actively attends to fine-grained visual details, dynamically harvests visual evidence throughout the search process. To unlock its visual-native potential, we design an active visual reasoning data pipeline and synthesize 5K high-quality multimodal trajectories for model training. Extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance across five challenging multimodal search benchmarks, even surpassing several proprietary models, validating robust visual-native reasoning and search in real-world web environments. The code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/ZhengboZhang/Visual-Seeker.

AI.tldr: Visual-Seeker is a visual-native multimodal deep search agent that actively reasons with fine-grained visual details rather than treating vision as static input, achieving SOTA across five challenging multimodal search benchmarks via an active visual reasoning data pipeline with 5K high-quality trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs struggle with factual grounding in complex open-world scenarios. Current multimodal deep search agents rely on simple images with explicit semantics and text-only evidence trajectories, limiting multi-hop cross-modal reasoning and search capabilities. The visual-native search paradigm remains underexplored.
AI.method: Visual-Seeker actively attends to fine-grained visual details and dynamically harvests visual evidence throughout the search process. An active visual reasoning data pipeline is designed to synthesize 5K high-quality multimodal trajectories for model training.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance across five challenging multimodal search benchmarks, surpassing several proprietary models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed visual-native approach validates robust visual-native reasoning and search in real-world web environments, demonstrating that active visual reasoning is key to overcoming limitations of existing MLLM-based search agents.

title: OSDAG: Online Scheduling for Efficient Multi-Robot Collaboration
summary: Coordinating heterogeneous multi-robot systems (MRS) for complex, long-horizon tasks requires both flexible high-level reasoning and efficient low-level scheduling. Existing LLM-based approaches address the reasoning side but introduce two critical bottlenecks: (1) repeated LLM inference during execution, which inflates latency with agent count, and (2) offline, pre-committed scheduling, which forces robots to idle while waiting for sequentially ordered predecessors even when independent work is available. This paper presents OSDAG, a novel framework that integrates LLM-based task reasoning with Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representation and constraint-aware online scheduling. The LLM is invoked once to decompose a natural-language instruction into a dependency-annotated task graph, and a lightweight online scheduler then allocates ready tasks to idle agents in real time. The DAG representation encodes both precedence and resource constraints, ensuring correctness while exposing all available parallelism. Experiments across five benchmark scenarios demonstrate that OSDAG achieves 5-15x faster reasoning time compared to dialogue-based methods, reduces makespan by up to 38% over sequential baselines, and maintains competitive success rates. Both simulation and real-world experiments on dual-arm manipulation tasks validate the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed approach for efficient multi-robot coordination. The website and resources are available at http://thanhnguyencanh.github.io/LLM_DAG4MultiRobot

AI.tldr: OSDAG integrates LLM-based task reasoning with DAG representation and constraint-aware online scheduling to coordinate heterogeneous multi-robot systems, reducing latency and makespan by eliminating repeated LLM inference and enabling real-time task allocation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-robot coordination methods suffer from two bottlenecks: repeated LLM inference during execution causing high latency, and offline pre-committed scheduling causing idle robots waiting for predecessors.
AI.method: OSDAG uses a single LLM call to decompose a natural-language instruction into a dependency-annotated DAG, then employs a lightweight online scheduler to allocate ready tasks to idle agents in real time, respecting precedence and resource constraints.
AI.result: 5-15x faster reasoning time vs. dialogue-based methods, up to 38% makespan reduction vs. sequential baselines, competitive success rates; validated in simulation and real-world dual-arm manipulation.
AI.conclusion: OSDAG effectively combines LLM reasoning with DAG-based online scheduling for efficient, practical multi-robot coordination, eliminating key bottlenecks of prior approaches.

title: Mask-Proof: An LLM-based Automated Data Curation Pipeline on Mathematical Proofs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of mathematical problem solving and can even assist with research-level proofs, yet we still lack a scalable and reproducible way to measure step-level reasoning in long proofs across diverse sources. This evaluation gap limits trustworthy AI assistance in proof-certified scientific progress. Existing evaluations often emphasize final answers or rely on costly expert grading, while end-to-end proof generation remains open-ended and hard to verify automatically. We introduce Mask-Proof, a pipeline that turns real proofs into automatically checkable masked-step tasks. It masks key formula steps, provides the necessary surrounding context, and evaluates model reconstructions with an LLM-based equivalence judge using repeated votes for stability. The resulting Mask-ProofBench contains 292 curated problems across diverse research areas. Experiments with 17 models show that reasoning-enhanced models outperform standard models by 12% to 27%. Our evaluator achieves 96.8% agreement with expert annotators, enabling faithful, reproducible, and comparable measurement of step-level mathematical reasoning. Benchmark, annotations, and code are available at https://github.com/weating/Mask-Proof.

AI.tldr: Mask-Proof is a pipeline that converts real mathematical proofs into automatically checkable masked-step tasks, producing Mask-ProofBench (292 problems), where LLMs must reconstruct masked key formula steps. An LLM-based equivalence judge with repeated voting achieves 96.8% expert agreement, enabling scalable, reproducible step-level reasoning evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations for LLM mathematical reasoning focus on final answers or rely on costly expert grading; end-to-end proof generation remains open-ended and hard to verify automatically, creating a gap for scalable, reproducible measurement of step-level reasoning in long proofs.
AI.method: Mask-Proof pipeline: (1) mask key formula steps from real proofs, (2) provide surrounding context, (3) ask LLMs to reconstruct masked steps, (4) evaluate using an LLM-based equivalence judge with repeated votes for stability. Created Mask-ProofBench (292 problems) from diverse research areas.
AI.result: Reasoning-enhanced models outperform standard models by 12-27% on Mask-ProofBench. The LLM-based evaluator achieves 96.8% agreement with expert annotators.
AI.conclusion: Mask-Proof enables faithful, reproducible, and comparable measurement of step-level mathematical reasoning, bridging the evaluation gap for trustworthy AI-assisted proof-certified scientific progress.

title: Acting While Understanding: Asynchronous Semantic-Action Decoupling for Real-Time Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have demonstrated strong task understanding and generalization in robotic manipulation, yet the high computational cost of full-model inference limits their deployment in low-latency, high-frequency closed-loop control. We propose an asynchronous semantic-action decoupling framework that separates semantic understanding from action generation along the internal semantic-action interface of existing VLAs, without redesigning the vision-language backbone or introducing an external planner. A low-frequency understanding module asynchronously updates reusable semantic conditions, while a high-frequency action module continuously outputs control actions without repeatedly invoking the full model. To mitigate the temporal mismatch between stale semantics and the current execution state, we further introduce historical action conditioning and time-misalignment training, which provide short-horizon execution context and improve feedback control robustness under stale semantic conditions. Experiments on LIBERO with $π_{0.5}$ and UniVLA, together with real-robot deployment using UniVLA, show that the proposed framework achieves up to 35.6 Hz server-side action-module inference throughput and offers a low-intrusion path to high-frequency closed-loop control without running full VLA inference at control rate.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an asynchronous semantic-action decoupling framework for VLAs that separates semantic understanding (low-frequency) from action generation (high-frequency) to enable low-latency, high-frequency closed-loop robotic control without full VLA inference at control rate.
AI.motivation: Full-model inference of Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) is computationally expensive, limiting their deployment in low-latency, high-frequency closed-loop robotic control tasks.
AI.method: The framework decouples semantic understanding from action generation along the internal semantic-action interface of existing VLAs. A low-frequency module asynchronously updates reusable semantic conditions, while a high-frequency action module outputs control actions continuously. Historical action conditioning and time-misalignment training are introduced to mitigate temporal mismatch between stale semantics and current execution state.
AI.result: Achieves up to 35.6 Hz server-side action-module inference throughput on LIBERO with π0.5 and UniVLA. Real-robot deployment using UniVLA demonstrates effective high-frequency closed-loop control.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a low-intrusion path to high-frequency closed-loop control without requiring full VLA inference at control rate, enabling practical deployment of VLAs in latency-sensitive robotic tasks.

title: Feature Attribution in Directed Acyclic Graphs Using Edge Intervention
summary: Shapley value-based feature attribution methods face challenges in scenarios involving complex feature interactions and causal relationships, even when a causal structure is provided. Existing methods typically adopt a node-centric view, attributing importance solely to individual features. Consequently, they often fail to simultaneously capture the externality and exogenous influence of features, leading to unreasonable interpretations. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel feature attribution method called DAG-SHAP, which is based on edge intervention. DAG-SHAP treats each feature edge as an individual attribution object, ensuring that both externality and exogenous contributions of features are appropriately captured. Additionally, we introduce an approximation method for efficiently computing DAG-SHAP. Extensive experiments on both real and synthetic datasets validate the effectiveness of DAG-SHAP. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-DIVER/DAG-SHAP.

AI.tldr: DAG-SHAP is a new feature attribution method that treats feature edges (rather than nodes) as attribution objects in causal graphs, enabling better capture of both externality and exogenous feature contributions, with efficient approximation and strong empirical validation.
AI.motivation: Existing Shapley-based feature attribution methods adopt a node-centric view, attributing importance solely to individual features, which fails to simultaneously capture the externality and exogenous influence of features in scenarios with complex feature interactions and causal relationships.
AI.method: DAG-SHAP is a feature attribution method based on edge intervention rather than node intervention; it treats each feature edge as an individual attribution object in a causal DAG. An approximation method is introduced to compute DAG-SHAP efficiently.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on both real and synthetic datasets validate the effectiveness of DAG-SHAP in capturing both externality and exogenous contributions of features.
AI.conclusion: DAG-SHAP overcomes the limitations of node-centric causal Shapley methods by adopting an edge-based attribution perspective, offering more reasonable interpretations for complex causal feature interactions.

title: Covariance-Regulated Recursive Koopman Learning for Nonlinear Systems with Uncertain Time-Varying Dynamics
summary: Offline models for autonomous robots often fail under time-varying dynamics outside their training distribution. Koopman operator theory offers a linear representation of nonlinear dynamics via lifting, but its transition to real-time recursive estimation may suffer numerical vulnerabilities: covariance windup under low excitation when using exponential forgetting, and vanishing gain without forgetting. This paper introduces a Covariance-Regulated Recursive Koopman Learning (CR-RKL) framework with two complementary strategies--error dead-zone gating and constant-trace normalization--each independently capable of preventing covariance explosion and parameter freezing, with the latter additionally preserving the geometric structure of uncertainty. Validated on a non-holonomic differential-drive robot with wheel slip and Stribeck friction and on a 26-gram butterfly-inspired flapping-wing micro aerial vehicle, CR-RKL achieves numerically stable and accurate online modeling, and when embedded in model predictive control, it maintains reliable tracking performance under uncertain, time-varying dynamics.

AI.tldr: CR-RKL framework prevents covariance windup and parameter freezing in recursive Koopman learning for robots under time-varying dynamics, using error dead-zone gating and constant-trace normalization, validated on ground and aerial robots.
AI.motivation: Offline models for autonomous robots fail under time-varying dynamics outside training distribution; Koopman-based online learning suffers from numerical issues like covariance windup (low excitation with forgetting) and vanishing gain (without forgetting).
AI.method: Covariance-Regulated Recursive Koopman Learning (CR-RKL) with two strategies: error dead-zone gating and constant-trace normalization, the latter preserving geometric uncertainty structure.
AI.result: Validated on a differential-drive robot with wheel slip/Stribeck friction and on a 26-gram flapping-wing micro aerial vehicle; achieves stable/accurate online modeling and maintains reliable MPC tracking under uncertain time-varying dynamics.
AI.conclusion: CR-RKL provides numerically stable and accurate online Koopman learning for robots under time-varying dynamics, enabling reliable model-predictive control.

title: A Formal Framework for Declarative Agentic AI in Business Process Analysis
summary: Agentic AI opens new opportunities for automating Business Process (BP), enabling autonomous decision-making and dynamic adaptation. However, realising this potential requires BP entities and their interactions to be defined with formal precision. This paper presents a formal framework for Agentic BP analysis through the AGO methodology. AGO captures the modelling perspective in terms of who is acting (Agents), why it is carried out (Goals), and what the relevant entities are (Objects). Grounded in set theory and mathematical logic, we formally define the AGO entity types and their interactions, organising all definitions into a BP Knowledge Base (BPKB). The resulting BPKB supports structured querying, incremental updates, and automatic generation of BP workflows, while ensuring soundness and completeness of the derived paths.

AI.tldr: The paper presents AGO, a formal framework for Agentic Business Process analysis using Agents, Goals, and Objects, grounded in set theory and mathematical logic to create a BP Knowledge Base supporting structured querying, updates, and automatic workflow generation with soundness and completeness guarantees.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI enables autonomous decision-making and dynamic adaptation in Business Processes, but realizing this potential requires formal precision in defining BP entities and their interactions, which existing approaches lack.
AI.method: The AGO methodology captures the modeling perspective via three entity types: Agents (who acts), Goals (why), and Objects (what entities are relevant). The framework is formally grounded in set theory and mathematical logic, organizing all definitions into a Business Process Knowledge Base (BPKB).
AI.result: The BPKB supports structured querying, incremental updates, and automatic generation of BP workflows, while ensuring soundness and completeness of the derived paths.
AI.conclusion: The formal AGO framework provides a rigorous foundation for Agentic BP analysis, enabling reliable automation of business processes with formal guarantees.

title: SimWeaver: Zero-Shot RGB Sim-to-Real for Deformable Manipulation
summary: RGB sim-to-real for deformable manipulation has remained largely unsolved without real-world fine-tuning. We present SimWeaver, which trains zero-shot RGB VLA policies on 200 simulated demonstrations per task, reaching above 80% per-task and 91% average real-world success across 5 diverse deformable tasks including plastic-bag manipulation, without teleoperation or per-task calibration. SimWeaver combines a reliable measurement-backed simulator (SimWeaver-Sim) with an extensible asset framework supporting single-image generation(SimWeaver-Asset), a deterministic topology-aware trajectory synthesizer (SimWeaver-Syn), and a sim-to-real protocol with ISP-aware photometric augmentation (SimWeaver-Real). On silk grasping, the sim-trained policy reaches 100% under visual distribution shifts where real-data baselines drop to 9-70%, at two orders of magnitude lower per-trajectory cost. We will release SimWeaver and a representative asset subset. Project page: https://simweaver.github.io/

AI.tldr: SimWeaver trains zero-shot RGB VLA policies on 200 simulated demonstrations per task, achieving >80% per-task and 91% average real-world success across 5 deformable tasks without real-world fine-tuning, teleoperation, or per-task calibration.
AI.motivation: RGB sim-to-real for deformable manipulation remains unsolved without real-world fine-tuning; the goal is to enable zero-shot transfer of vision-language-action policies for deformable objects using only simulation data.
AI.method: SimWeaver combines four components: (1) SimWeaver-Sim (measurement-backed simulator), (2) SimWeaver-Asset (extensible asset framework with single-image generation), (3) SimWeaver-Syn (deterministic topology-aware trajectory synthesizer), and (4) SimWeaver-Real (sim-to-real protocol with ISP-aware photometric augmentation).
AI.result: Achieves >80% per-task and 91% average success across 5 deformable tasks; on silk grasping, 100% success under visual distribution shifts where real-data baselines drop to 9-70%, at two orders of magnitude lower per-trajectory cost.
AI.conclusion: SimWeaver demonstrates that zero-shot RGB VLA policies for deformable manipulation are feasible without real-world fine-tuning, significantly outperforming real-data baselines under distribution shift at drastically lower cost.

title: CODA-BENCH: Can Code Agents Handle Data-Intensive Tasks?
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026. 37 pages, 11 figures. Project page: https://coda-bench.github.io/ Code: https://github.com/ruc-datalab/CoDA-Bench Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/RUC-DataLab/CoDA-Bench
summary: Advanced agents are increasingly demonstrating the potential to operate as autonomous engineers, creating a growing demand for evaluation benchmarks that capture the complexity of real-world development. Such environments typically involve both complex code and large-scale data (i.e., file system). However, existing benchmarks usually evaluate code-centric or data-centric capabilities in isolation, leaving a clear gap with real development scenarios. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing CODA-BENCH, the first benchmark to jointly evaluate code and data intelligence in a data-intensive environment. We construct a data-intensive Linux sandbox based on the Kaggle ecosystem (containing hundreds of datasets), where agents must actively explore complex file hierarchies to identify relevant resources and generate code for data-driven analytical tasks. CODA-BENCH comprises 1,009 tasks spanning 31 communities, with each task environment containing an average of 980 files, simulating realistic data scale and noise. Evaluations of advanced agents reveal that even top-performing systems struggle to effectively integrate data discovery with code execution, achieving a success rate of only 61.1%. These results highlight a substantial gap in current agentic capabilities for data-intensive tasks and point to promising directions for future research.

AI.tldr: CODA-BENCH is the first benchmark jointly evaluating code and data intelligence in data-intensive environments, revealing that even top agents achieve only 61.1% success rate, highlighting a significant gap in autonomous engineering capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate code-centric or data-centric capabilities in isolation, leaving a gap with real-world development scenarios that involve both complex code and large-scale data (file systems).
AI.method: Constructed a data-intensive Linux sandbox based on the Kaggle ecosystem with hundreds of datasets. Created 1,009 tasks across 31 communities, each environment averaging 980 files. Agents must explore complex file hierarchies to find relevant resources and generate code for data-driven analytical tasks.
AI.result: Top-performing agents achieved only 61.1% success rate, indicating substantial difficulty in effectively integrating data discovery with code execution.
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial gap in current agentic capabilities for data-intensive tasks, pointing to promising directions for future research in developing agents that can jointly handle code and data intelligence.

title: A Hybrid Model-Based and Model-Free Framework for Active Multi-View Viewpoint Optimization in Sonar Target Recognition
summary: This paper presents a hybrid model-based and model-free framework for active multi-view target recognition using forward-looking sonar. A convolutional neural network (CNN) provides data-driven observation likelihoods, while Radon-based orientation estimation enables viewpoint-aware sensing without requiring angle annotations. During training, an information-gain-based reward guides a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent to learn a belief-aware viewpoint selection policy offline. At deployment, the learned policy performs real-time viewpoint selection using only CNN-based belief updates, eliminating the need for computationally expensive online POMDP tree search. Experiments on a marine-debris forward-looking sonar dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive recognition accuracy while reducing sensing steps and motion cost compared to model-based baselines.

AI.tldr: A hybrid model-based and model-free framework for active multi-view target recognition using forward-looking sonar, combining CNN-based observation likelihoods with PPO-learned viewpoint selection policy, achieving competitive accuracy with reduced sensing steps and motion cost.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient active multi-view target recognition with forward-looking sonar by combining the strengths of model-based and model-free approaches, eliminating the need for computationally expensive online POMDP tree search while still achieving viewpoint-aware sensing without requiring angle annotations.
AI.method: (1) CNN provides data-driven observation likelihoods; (2) Radon-based orientation estimation enables viewpoint-aware sensing without angle annotations; (3) Information-gain-based reward guides PPO agent to learn belief-aware viewpoint selection policy offline during training; (4) At deployment, learned policy performs real-time viewpoint selection using only CNN-based belief updates.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves competitive recognition accuracy while reducing sensing steps and motion cost compared to model-based baselines on a marine-debris forward-looking sonar dataset.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid framework successfully balances model-based and model-free paradigms for active perception, offering a practical solution for real-time multi-view target recognition with forward-looking sonar in resource-constrained underwater scenarios.

title: Forced Deferral: Manipulating Routing Decisions in Multimodal LLM Cascades
summary: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong visual reasoning abilities, serving a large model for every query is computationally expensive. MLLM cascades mitigate this cost by first querying a weak but cheaper model and deferring to a strong model when the weak model's output is unconfident. However, since the weak model's confidence directly controls compute allocation, these systems expose a new attack surface: an adversary can manipulate confidence so that their queries are consistently deferred to the strong model. Motivated by this vulnerability, we introduce the Forced Deferral Attack (FDA), an adversarial image attack that lowers the weak model's confidence and causes cascades to route queries to the strong model. FDA learns a universal border trigger by optimizing a temperature-flattened objective. This objective pushes the weak model's token distribution on triggered inputs toward less concentrated targets constructed from its clean responses. Across datasets, model families, and deferral metrics, FDA consistently increases strong-model routing while outperforming image-perturbation and prompt-injection baselines. These results show that MLLM cascades are vulnerable to attacks that manipulate compute allocation, forcing unintended strong-model usage without directly targeting answer correctness.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Forced Deferral Attack (FDA), an adversarial attack that manipulates confidence in MLLM cascades to force queries to be routed to the expensive strong model, demonstrating a new security vulnerability in compute allocation mechanisms.
AI.motivation: MLLM cascades expose a new attack surface where adversaries can manipulate the weak model's confidence to consistently defer queries to the strong model, incurring higher computational cost.
AI.method: FDA learns a universal border trigger by optimizing a temperature-flattened objective that pushes the weak model's token distribution on triggered inputs toward less concentrated targets constructed from its clean responses.
AI.result: Across datasets, model families, and deferral metrics, FDA consistently increases strong-model routing while outperforming image-perturbation and prompt-injection baselines.
AI.conclusion: MLLM cascades are vulnerable to attacks that manipulate compute allocation, forcing unintended strong-model usage without directly targeting answer correctness.

title: A Corridor-Scale CARLA-VISSIM Co-Simulation Framework for Multi-Intersection Urban Traffic
summary: This paper presents an implemented CARLA-VISSIM co-simulation framework for an urban corridor comprising approximately fifteen connected intersections centered on Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard in Chattanooga, Tennessee. The system integrates CARLA 0.10.0 Unreal Engine 5 with PTV VISSIM 2026 through a bidirectional, step-synchronized interface that couples VISSIM's microscopic vehicle, pedestrian, and signal-controller logic with CARLA's high-fidelity 3D rendering. A LiDAR-derived elevation model and RoadRunner-based High Definition (HD) map provide terrain-accurate road geometry deployed consistently across both simulators. The framework incorporates explicit actor ownership, mirrored lifecycle management, coordinate reconciliation, and a latest-state-per-actor update policy, enabling stable interaction between VISSIM-controlled traffic and a CARLA-controlled ego vehicle. A corridor-scale case study demonstrates consistent traffic-signal mirroring, synchronized vehicle-pedestrian interactions, and stable mixed-authority operation under peak loads of approximately 100 vehicles and 100 pedestrians. The deployment captures the interaction of the five signalized intersections along MLK Street and their connecting upstream and downstream intersections, revealing synchronization challenges unique to multi-intersection corridors. Results indicate that this MLK-centered corridor provides an effective testbed for verifying cross-simulator consistency and that the proposed architecture supports reliable, perception-ready co-simulation for corridor-level traffic studies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a CARLA-VISSIM co-simulation framework for a 15-intersection urban corridor in Chattanooga, TN, integrating VISSIM's traffic logic with CARLA's high-fidelity 3D rendering via a bidirectional, step-synchronized interface. A case study demonstrates stable mixed-authority operation with ~100 vehicles and ~100 pedestrians, supporting perception-ready corridor-level traffic studies.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable, perception-ready co-simulation for multi-intersection corridor-level traffic studies by integrating microscopic traffic simulation with high-fidelity 3D rendering.
AI.method: A bidirectional, step-synchronized interface coupling CARLA 0.10.0 (Unreal Engine 5) with PTV VISSIM 2026, featuring explicit actor ownership, mirrored lifecycle management, coordinate reconciliation, LiDAR-derived elevation model, and RoadRunner-based HD map deployed consistently across both simulators.
AI.result: Consistent traffic-signal mirroring, synchronized vehicle-pedestrian interactions, and stable mixed-authority operation under peak loads of ~100 vehicles and ~100 pedestrians across five signalized intersections plus connecting upstream/downstream intersections.
AI.conclusion: The MLK-centered corridor provides an effective testbed for verifying cross-simulator consistency, and the proposed architecture supports reliable, perception-ready co-simulation for corridor-level traffic studies.

title: ChatPlanner: A Large Language Model Framework for Personalized Public Transit Routing
comment: Under Review at Transportation Research Part C
summary: Personalized public transit routing in public transit systems remains challenging due to the difficulty of capturing and integrating diverse user preferences into routing algorithms. This paper presents ChatPlanner, a novel framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to enable preference aware public transit routing. Our approach employs fine-tuned LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to extract routing parameters and interpret nuanced user preferences from natural language queries, subsequently integrating these preferences into the objective function of a public transit routing algorithm. This study designs preference aware datasets incorporating eight personas and five contexts to establish scoring standards for both fine-tuning and RAG. This work conducted three experiments to validate the solutions' feasibility, extraction of routing information and preferences, and solution set quality and completeness. Results demonstrate that ChatPlanner generates feasible solutions reliably. Fine-tuning enforces the required output structure and learns general preference patterns, while RAG provides query-specific context to resolve imprecise or conversational expressions and calibrate continuous scores. The combination of both achieves the highest accuracy in routing information extraction and user preference interpretation. Results based on selected case studies show that by capturing user preferences, ChatPlanner identifies valuable solutions across different dimensions that existing route planners overlook, generating more valuable route alternatives. This research establishes a new paradigm for integrating natural language understanding into transportation optimization.

AI.tldr: ChatPlanner is a framework that combines fine-tuned LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to extract user preferences from natural language queries and integrate them into public transit routing algorithms, outperforming existing planners by generating more valuable, preference-aware route alternatives.
AI.motivation: Personalized public transit routing is challenging because capturing and integrating diverse user preferences into routing algorithms is difficult; existing route planners overlook valuable solutions across different preference dimensions.
AI.method: The framework employs fine-tuned LLMs with RAG to extract routing parameters and interpret nuanced user preferences from natural language queries, integrating them into the objective function of a public transit routing algorithm. Preference-aware datasets with eight personas and five contexts were designed for fine-tuning and RAG scoring standards.
AI.result: ChatPlanner generates feasible solutions reliably. Fine-tuning enforces output structure and learns general preference patterns, while RAG provides query-specific context to resolve imprecise expressions and calibrate scores. Combining both achieves highest accuracy in routing information extraction and preference interpretation. Case studies show it identifies valuable solutions that existing route planners overlook.
AI.conclusion: This research establishes a new paradigm for integrating natural language understanding into transportation optimization, demonstrating that LLM-based preference capture significantly improves personalized public transit routing quality.

title: A Bilateral Teleoperation Framework for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Dexterous teleoperation requires precise arm-hand coordination, low-latency feedback, and robust interaction in real-world contact-rich environments. This paper presents a modular bilateral teleoperation framework that integrates operator-side input interfaces with a robot-side dexterous hand and compliant robotic arm in a unified control architecture. The system supports position-based hand retargeting, differential arm control, multi-scale haptic feedback, and shared control for stable manipulation. We validate the framework through a real-world dexterous manipulation task, highlighting coordinated arm-hand control and contact-aware interaction. Beyond feasibility, we identify key design insights related to cross-embodiment mismatch, haptic feedback granularity, and shared control. The proposed platform provides a practical teleoperation system and a foundation for collecting high-quality demonstrations for future learning-from-demonstration research.

AI.tldr: A modular bilateral teleoperation framework integrating arm-hand coordination, haptic feedback, and shared control for dexterous manipulation, validated in real-world contact-rich tasks.
AI.motivation: To enable precise arm-hand coordination, low-latency feedback, and robust interaction in contact-rich teleoperation environments, supporting both practical use and data collection for learning from demonstration.
AI.method: A bilateral teleoperation framework with position-based hand retargeting, differential arm control, multi-scale haptic feedback, and shared control, integrating operator-side interfaces with a robot-side dexterous hand and compliant arm.
AI.result: Validation through a real-world dexterous manipulation task demonstrating coordinated arm-hand control and contact-aware interaction; identified design insights on cross-embodiment mismatch, haptic feedback granularity, and shared control.
AI.conclusion: The platform serves as a practical teleoperation system and a foundation for collecting high-quality demonstrations for future learning-from-demonstration research.

title: APEX: Adaptive Principle EXtraction A Three-Layer Self-Evolution Framework for Production AI Agents
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Evaluated on a production 15-node compute fleet with 114 real task traces. Code available at https://aispark.airlive.com/joe-hackathon/
summary: Self-improvement in AI agents has emerged as a key research frontier: systems that modify their own prompts, workflows, and decision rules based on accumulated operational experience. The state-of-the-art Self-Harness framework [1] achieves 14--21% improvement on Terminal-Bench-2.0 by mining failure clusters and patching the agent harness. However, Self-Harness optimises only one dimension -- the prompt harness -- leaving behavioural principles and workflow topology unchanged. We propose APEX (Adaptive Principle EXtraction), a three-layer co-evolution framework that simultaneously evolves: (L1) the harness via failure-mode patching, (L2) behavioural principles via success-trace distillation [2], and (L3) the agent workflow topology via structural fitness-based selection [6]. We implement APEX on Joe [13], a production-grade super AI Agent built on NVIDIA Nemotron and designed as an Edge AI Agent Factory for the NVIDIA Agent Challenge 2026, managing a 15-node compute fleet using 114 real task traces collected over 18 days. APEX achieves an APEX Health Score of 0.570 (+90% vs. baseline 0.300) in a single evolutionary run, distilling 6 novel reusable principles and selecting a research-first workflow topology scoring 0.900 (+20%). Our results demonstrate that multi-dimensional co-evolution substantially outperforms single-axis harness optimisation, at a cost of only 4 LLM calls (~270 s) on a local qwen2.5-coder:32b instance.

AI.tldr: APEX is a three-layer co-evolution framework for AI agent self-improvement that simultaneously evolves the prompt harness, behavioural principles, and workflow topology, achieving +90% health score improvement over baseline and outperforming single-axis optimization methods like Self-Harness, with minimal computational cost (4 LLM calls ~270s).
AI.motivation: Existing self-improvement frameworks (e.g., Self-Harness) only optimize the prompt harness (single dimension), leaving behavioural principles and workflow topology unchanged. The authors aim to demonstrate that multi-dimensional co-evolution substantially outperforms single-axis harness optimization.
AI.method: APEX co-evolves three layers: (L1) harness via failure-mode patching, (L2) behavioural principles via success-trace distillation, and (L3) agent workflow topology via structural fitness-based selection. Implemented on Joe, a production-grade super AI Agent built on NVIDIA Nemotron, managing a 15-node compute fleet with 114 real task traces over 18 days.
AI.result: APEX achieves APEX Health Score of 0.570 (+90% vs. baseline 0.300) in a single evolutionary run, distills 6 novel reusable principles, and selects a research-first workflow topology scoring 0.900 (+20%), at cost of only 4 LLM calls (~270s) on a local qwen2.5-coder:32b instance.
AI.conclusion: Multi-dimensional co-evolution substantially outperforms single-axis harness optimisation with minimal computational overhead, validated on a production-grade AI agent system.

title: Learning Context-Aware Neural ODE Dynamics for Adaptive Robotic Control
summary: Robotic systems deployed in uncertain and dynamically changing environments often face variations in contact conditions, aerodynamic effects, and external disturbances that challenge reliable control. To remain effective under model-based control, these systems require dynamics models that can adapt to such changes, especially when direct access to complete environmental information is limited. To enable adaptability and facilitate integration with model predictive control, we propose a context-aware dynamics model based on neural ordinary differential equations, which infers environmental factors from state-action histories using a two-phase training procedure. We validate the approach across diverse robotic platforms, including a quadrotor in simulation, as well as a Sphero BOLT robot and a Fanuc manipulator in real-world experiments. The results demonstrate that our method effectively adapts to temporally and spatially varying environmental changes across different tasks. Videos are available at https://youtu.be/PY0sNyF2rqE , and the source code is available at https://github.com/syyu410-yu/context-aware-neural-ode-control.git .

AI.tldr: A context-aware dynamics model using neural ODEs is proposed to adapt robotic control to changing environments, validated across simulation and real-world platforms.
AI.motivation: Robotic systems in uncertain environments face variations (contact conditions, aerodynamic effects, external disturbances) that challenge model-based control; direct access to complete environmental information is often limited.
AI.method: A context-aware dynamics model based on neural ordinary differential equations (Neural ODEs) that infers environmental factors from state-action histories using a two-phase training procedure, integrated with model predictive control.
AI.result: Validated on a simulated quadrotor, a Sphero BOLT robot, and a Fanuc manipulator in real-world experiments; the method effectively adapts to temporally and spatially varying environmental changes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed context-aware Neural ODE approach enables reliable adaptive control under varying environmental conditions across diverse robotic platforms.

title: S1-DeepResearch: Beyond Search, Toward Real-World Long-Horizon Research Agents
summary: Deep research agents aim to solve complex knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon planning, evidence gathering, reasoning, and report generation. While recent progress in search agents has demonstrated strong capabilities in information retrieval and answer verification, most existing training datasets remain search-centric, focusing primarily on closed-ended question answering and information localization. As a result, they mainly train information-seeking behavior while providing limited coverage of key deep research capabilities, including evidence integration, knowledge synthesis, planning, file understanding, and structured report generation. In this work, we propose a unified trajectory construction paradigm for deep research agents that combines closed-ended QA and open-ended exploration. The proposed framework consists of graph-grounded task formulation, agentic trajectory rollout, and multi-dimensional trajectory verification, enabling scalable synthesis of high-quality agentic trajectories spanning long-chain complex reasoning, deep research instruction following, report writing, file understanding and generation, and skills usage. Compared with existing search-oriented datasets, our synthesized trajectories place greater emphasis on knowledge synthesis, complex reasoning, and planning. S1-DeepResearch-32B achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models of comparable scale across 20 benchmarks spanning five capability dimensions, including complex reasoning, instruction following, report generation, file understanding, and skills usage. On several challenging deep research benchmarks, it approaches the performance of leading proprietary frontier models. These results highlight the importance of jointly modeling information acquisition, knowledge synthesis, and planning-oriented agent behaviors for building effective deep research agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified trajectory construction framework for deep research agents that combines closed-ended QA and open-ended exploration, enabling scalable synthesis of high-quality agentic trajectories. Their model, S1-DeepResearch-32B, achieves SOTA among comparable open-source models across 20 benchmarks spanning complex reasoning, instruction following, report generation, file understanding, and skills usage, approaching proprietary frontier models on challenging deep research benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing training datasets for search agents are search-centric, focusing primarily on closed-ended QA and information localization. They provide limited coverage of key deep research capabilities such as evidence integration, knowledge synthesis, planning, file understanding, and structured report generation.
AI.method: A unified trajectory construction paradigm consisting of three components: (1) graph-grounded task formulation, (2) agentic trajectory rollout, and (3) multi-dimensional trajectory verification. This framework combines closed-ended QA with open-ended exploration to synthesize high-quality agentic trajectories covering long-chain reasoning, instruction following, report writing, file handling, and skills usage.
AI.result: S1-DeepResearch-32B achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models of comparable scale across 20 benchmarks spanning five capability dimensions, and approaches the performance of leading proprietary frontier models on several challenging deep research benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling information acquisition, knowledge synthesis, and planning-oriented agent behaviors is critical for building effective deep research agents.

title: FARM: Find Anything using Relational Spatial Memory
summary: Robots operating in homes, warehouses, and other object-rich environments need memory systems that can find specific object instances on demand. Object-level memory alone is often insufficient: scenes contain many plausibly matching objects, and users refer to the target through relations to landmarks and surrounding objects (e.g. ``the tall lamp below the dartboard and to the left of the poster''), demanding a relational spatial memory that supports retrieval through semantic, appearance, and spatial predicates over objects.
