AI.method: Proposes XEPV encoding (Explore, Execute, Plan, Verify) to convert agent traces into symbolic sequences; applies n-gram pattern mining, Markov transition matrices, and point-biserial correlation to 347 execution traces from a production ReAct system; designs Governor—a three-layer runtime intervention with rule engine, statistical accumulator, and chi-square-based threshold adaptor.
AI.result: (1) P-X-P trigram lowers success rate by 10.4%; (2) P-ratio is the strongest negative predictor (r=-0.256, p<0.0001); (3) E->V transition probability is only 2.1%; Governor achieves +6.2% success increase and 44% token reduction; cross-system validation on 2,000 SWE-agent trajectories confirms pattern replication.
AI.conclusion: The XEPV framework effectively captures behavioral patterns of LLM agents and enables data-driven runtime interventions. Six future directions are outlined including base sequence language models, cross-agent behavioral fingerprinting, and reward shaping. An open-source toolkit is released.

title: Can Causal Models Enhance Robot Navigation? Online Causal Adaptation for Real-Robot Navigation
comment: Accepted for publication at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN)
summary: Causality in robotics aims to produce more interpretable and flexible robot behaviours by enabling robots to predict the consequences of their actions; however, deploying causal models with existing systems (e.g., navigation) operating in real environments remains understudied. This paper addresses the challenging problem of transferring causal models in real-robot experiments for a navigation scenario. We study this problem in two ways: (i) using the causal model as an offline evaluation module that predicts the competence of recorded real-robot navigation trajectories and relates it to quantitative navigation performance, and (ii) using the causal model as an online adaptation module that intervenes when the predicted competence of the default navigation is low. We validate our approach in a physical service robot that patrols around corridors. We show that the predicted competence correlates positively with path efficiency, and negatively with path irregularities (suboptimal behaviour). The model predictions also show strong agreement with human annotations (Cohen's kappa value of 0.88). In online experiments, the proposed method improves navigation performance in complex scenarios such as cornering and obstacle avoidance, yielding higher predicted competence and better navigation metrics than the default navigation baseline. In simpler scenarios, where the baseline already performs near-optimally, the causal adaptation provides limited benefit. These results indicate that causal models are particularly effective in enhancing navigation under increased task complexity. Overall, our results demonstrate that causal models developed for behavioural interpretation can be successfully integrated into real-robot navigation systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies transferring causal models to real-robot navigation, using them both for offline evaluation (predicting competence of trajectories, correlating with navigation performance) and online adaptation (intervening when competence is low). Validated on a physical service robot, the approach shows positive correlation between predicted competence and path efficiency, high agreement with human annotations (Cohen's κ=0.88), and improved navigation in complex scenarios (cornering, obstacle avoidance), with limited benefit in simple scenarios.
AI.motivation: Causality in robotics promises interpretable and flexible behaviours by enabling robots to predict action consequences, but deploying causal models in existing real-world navigation systems remains understudied.
AI.method: The authors study two modes: (i) offline evaluation—predicting competence of recorded real-robot navigation trajectories and correlating it with quantitative navigation metrics; (ii) online adaptation—intervening when the predicted competence of the default navigation is low. Validation is done on a physical service robot patrolling corridors.
AI.result: Predicted competence positively correlates with path efficiency and negatively with path irregularities. High agreement with human annotations (Cohen's κ=0.88). In online experiments, the method improves navigation in complex scenarios (cornering, obstacle avoidance) but provides limited benefit in simpler near-optimal scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Causal models developed for behavioural interpretation can be successfully integrated into real-robot navigation systems, being particularly effective under increased task complexity.

title: Agentic Retrieval and Reinforcement Learned Equation Chains: A Controlled Generation Framework for Complex and Novel Physics Word Problems
summary: Generating high-quality Physics Word Problems (PWPs) that are novel, complex, and solvable remains a challenging and underexplored problem in educational content generation. Existing approaches, many adapted from Math Word Problem (MWP) generation, often produce ambiguous, unsolvable, or structurally simple questions with limited linguistic diversity. We introduce ARVRE (Agentic Retrieval Value Reinforced Equation-chain), a two-stage framework for generating diverse and mathematically valid PWPs. In the first stage, a form of offline temporal-difference learning is used to construct valid chains of physics equations, while an agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework dynamically selects topic-specific concepts and vocabulary. This design enables explicit control over problem structure and difficulty. In the second stage, a Large Language Model (LLM) converts the equation chain and retrieved concepts into a natural-language physics question. By grounding generation in valid equation chains, our method preserves mathematical correctness while promoting linguistic diversity and contextual richness. Human and automated evaluations demonstrate that ARVRE generates PWPs that are more complex, novel, and solvable than those produced by existing approaches. These results highlight the potential of combining reinforcement learning, retrieval, and LLMs for reliable generation of educational physics content.

AI.tldr: ARVRE is a two-stage framework that generates high-quality, solvable Physics Word Problems by first constructing valid equation chains using offline temporal-difference learning and agentic retrieval-augmented generation, then converting them into natural-language questions via LLMs, outperforming existing methods in complexity, novelty, and solvability.
AI.motivation: Generating novel, complex, and solvable Physics Word Problems (PWPs) remains challenging and underexplored; existing methods adapted from Math Word Problem generation often yield ambiguous, unsolvable, or structurally simple questions with limited linguistic diversity.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: Stage 1 uses offline temporal-difference learning to construct valid equation chains and an agentic RAG framework to select topic-specific concepts/vocabulary; Stage 2 uses an LLM to convert the equation chain and retrieved concepts into a natural-language physics question.
AI.result: ARVRE generates PWPs that are more complex, novel, and solvable than those produced by existing approaches, as demonstrated by human and automated evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Combining reinforcement learning, retrieval, and LLMs offers reliable generation of educational physics content, with ARVRE preserving mathematical correctness while enhancing linguistic diversity and contextual richness.

title: LaWAM: Latent World Action Models for Efficient Dynamics-Aware Robot Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) leverage large-scale vision-language pretraining for semantic robot control, but often lack explicit foresight into how robot actions change the scene. World-Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by conditioning policies on predicted futures, yet existing approaches typically rely on computationally expensive video generation with substantial pixel-level redundancy. We present LaWAM, a Latent World Action Model that exposes predictive dynamics to robot policies through compact latent visual subgoals instead of reconstructed future video. At the core of LaWAM is a latent-action-conditioned Latent World Model (LaWM). We obtain LaWM by training a latent action model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model and repurposing its forward decoder to predict future observation features for scene evolution. LaWAM then conditions action generation on these predicted latent visual subgoals to enable dynamics-aware robot control. LaWAM achieves state-of-the-art or competitive success rates (SRs) across LIBERO (98.6% SR), RoboTwin (91.22% SR), and real-world manipulation tasks while retaining low-latency inference. LaWAM runs in 187 ms per action-chunk prediction and achieves up to 24x lower wall-clock latency than pixel-space WAMs.

AI.tldr: LaWAM introduces a Latent World Action Model that uses compact latent visual subgoals from a Latent World Model (LaWM) instead of expensive pixel-level video prediction to enable efficient, dynamics-aware robot control, achieving state-of-the-art success rates on LIBERO (98.6%), RoboTwin (91.22%), and real-world tasks with 24x lower latency than pixel-space WAMs.
AI.motivation: Existing VLAs lack foresight into how actions change the scene, and pixel-space World-Action Models (WAMs) address this but suffer from computationally expensive video generation with significant pixel-level redundancy, motivating a more efficient approach.
AI.method: LaWAM trains a latent action model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model, repurposes its forward decoder to predict future observation features, and conditions action generation on these compact latent visual subgoals for dynamics-aware control.
AI.result: LaWAM achieves 98.6% SR on LIBERO, 91.22% SR on RoboTwin, strong real-world performance, 187 ms per action-chunk prediction, and up to 24x lower latency than pixel-space WAMs.
AI.conclusion: Operating predictive dynamics in latent space rather than pixel space achieves both high success rates and low-latency inference for robot control.

title: Integrating Reasoning and Generalization in Text-to-SQL via Self-Enhanced Fine-Tuning
summary: Text-to-SQL aims to translate natural language questions into executable SQL queries over structured databases, enabling non-expert users to access data intuitively. While recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in this task, existing LLM-based approaches often struggle to strike a balance between strong reasoning capabilities and robust generalization. To address these limitations, we propose CoTE-SQL to enhance the LLM-based text-to-SQL generation with three key innovations: (i) self-enhanced reasoning traces distilled from LLMs without human annotation, (ii) structured chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting with modular decomposition and examples retrieval, and (iii) error-aware revision based on SQL execution feedback. Extensive experiments on the Spider and Bird benchmarks demonstrate that CoTE-SQL achieves new state-of-the-art performance among methods built on open-source LLMs with comparable model sizes on Bird (53.39% EX / 59.02 VES) and strong results on Spider (79.60% EX / 77.19 VES), with especially significant gains on complex queries. Results highlight the effectiveness of combining self-enhancement, structured reasoning, and execution-time feedback within an LLM-based framework for text-to-SQL design.

AI.tldr: CoTE-SQL enhances LLM-based text-to-SQL generation via self-enhanced reasoning traces, structured chain-of-thought prompting, and error-aware revision, achieving state-of-the-art results on Spider and Bird benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based text-to-SQL approaches struggle to balance strong reasoning capabilities and robust generalization, particularly for complex queries.
AI.method: Three key innovations: (i) self-enhanced reasoning traces distilled from LLMs without human annotation, (ii) structured chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting with modular decomposition and examples retrieval, and (iii) error-aware revision based on SQL execution feedback.
AI.result: New state-of-the-art on Bird (53.39% EX / 59.02 VES) and strong results on Spider (79.60% EX / 77.19 VES) among open-source LLMs of comparable size, with significant gains on complex queries.
AI.conclusion: Combining self-enhancement, structured reasoning, and execution-time feedback is effective for improving LLM-based text-to-SQL generation.

title: FlashNav: Ultra-Fast Policy Training for Robot Navigation within 20 Seconds
summary: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for robot navigation, but its practical deployment is still limited by the long wall-clock cost of policy training. This paper presents FlashNav, a GPU-first framework for ultra-fast range-based robot navigation training. To the best of our knowledge, FlashNav is the first DRL-based robot navigation framework that reaches seconds-level policy training, with the fastest deployable policy trained in less than 20 seconds. The key idea is to align simulation with the navigation MDP: FlashNav preserves the essential components for velocity-level navigation, including occupancy geometry, range sensing, goal-conditioned control, robot motion dynamics, collision handling, termination, and reset, while removing unnecessary rendering and high-fidelity physical details from the training loop. Built on a batched bitmap simulator and a fully GPU-resident training pipeline with our FastDSAC learner, FlashNav generates massive parallel navigation transitions entirely on GPU. Experiments on TurtleBot2 and Unitree Go2 show that FlashNav achieves a 100\% success-rate below 20 seconds on an RTX 5090 and remains within tens of seconds across desktop GPUs. The learned policies further transfer to physical wheeled and legged robots in static and dynamic indoor scenes, demonstrating that DRL-based navigation can be trained at seconds-level speed while preserving deployable obstacle-avoidance behavior.

AI.tldr: FlashNav is a GPU-first DRL framework that achieves seconds-level robot navigation policy training (fastest in <20s) by stripping simulation to essential MDP components and using batched bitmap simulation with fully GPU-resident training.
AI.motivation: Deep RL for robot navigation suffers from long wall-clock training times, hindering practical deployment. The goal is to drastically reduce training time from hours/days to seconds while preserving deployable policy quality.
AI.method: FlashNav aligns simulation with the navigation MDP by keeping only essential components (occupancy geometry, range sensing, goal-conditioned control, dynamics, collision, termination, reset) and removing rendering/physics overhead. It uses a batched bitmap simulator and a fully GPU-resident training pipeline with the FastDSAC learner, generating massive parallel transitions entirely on GPU.
AI.result: 100% success-rate training in under 20 seconds on an RTX 5090, tens of seconds across desktop GPUs. Policies transfer to physical TurtleBot2 and Unitree Go2 robots in both static and dynamic indoor scenes.
AI.conclusion: DRL-based navigation can be trained at seconds-level speed while retaining deployable obstacle-avoidance behavior, demonstrating that the key bottleneck was unnecessary simulation fidelity, not the learning algorithm itself.

title: NeuroSymbolic AI for Legal AI-TRISM: Trustworthy, Reliable, Interpretable, Safe Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, but their lack of interpretable reasoning and tendency to hallucinate pose significant challenges for legal applications. While LLMs show promise for legal text analysis and generation, they struggle with accurate citation attribution and precedent verification. For example, in legal contexts, a single incorrect precedent can jeopardize a case. Current approaches to improve LLM reliability in legal domains suffer from two key limitations: inadequate integration of structured legal knowledge during training or fine-tuning, and insufficient verification mechanisms for generated legal content. To address these challenges, we propose the TRISM (Trustworthy, Reliable, Interpretable, Safe Models) framework, which integrates NeuroSymbolic AI principles with LLMs to leverage both neural learning capabilities and symbolic reasoning over structured legal knowledge. The TRISM approach addresses the above limitations while maintaining interpretable decision pathways. Our framework formalizes the extraction of symbolic knowledge from legal textual documents and incorporates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a core component for grounding LLM outputs in verified legal sources. In this position paper, we make the following contributions: (1) An analysis of the limitations of AI in law; (2) Introduce RASOR RAG which creates foundations for neurosymbolic RAG by generating explicit interpretable rationales that could be formalized into symbolic representations; (3) A formalized methodology for creating symbolic legal knowledge bases that support both interpretable reasoning and output verification in LLMs; and (4) The TRISM framework for integrating symbolic legal knowledge with LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the TRISM framework, which integrates NeuroSymbolic AI principles with LLMs to improve interpretability, reliability, and citation accuracy in legal applications, addressing limitations in structured legal knowledge integration and output verification.
AI.motivation: LLMs lack interpretable reasoning and hallucinate in legal contexts, where accurate citation attribution and precedent verification are critical. Current approaches fail to adequately integrate structured legal knowledge during training and lack sufficient verification mechanisms for generated legal content.
AI.method: The TRISM framework combines NeuroSymbolic AI with LLMs by formalizing symbolic knowledge extraction from legal texts, incorporating RASOR RAG (a neurosymbolic RAG approach that generates explicit interpretable rationales), creating symbolic legal knowledge bases, and integrating them with LLMs for interpretable reasoning and output verification.
AI.result: The paper is a position paper; it presents a formalized methodology and framework design rather than empirical results. Key contributions include: analysis of AI limitations in law, RASOR RAG for neurosymbolic RAG, a methodology for symbolic legal knowledge bases, and the TRISM framework.
AI.conclusion: The TRISM framework addresses key limitations of LLMs in legal domains by integrating symbolic reasoning with neural learning, leveraging RAG for grounded outputs and interpretable decision pathways, potentially improving trustworthiness and reliability in legal AI applications.

title: LoComposition: Terrain-Adaptive Energy-Efficient Quadruped Locomotion without Gait Priors
summary: Learning-based quadrupedal locomotion typically relies on complex reward formulations that entangle task specification, operational limits, gait preference, and terrain adaptation within a single optimization objective. We instead treat these functions through distinct mechanisms: rewards for task specification, constraints for operational limits, energy minimization for gait preference, and exteroceptive perception for adapting energy use to terrain difficulty. We show that these components jointly enable efficient, terrain-adaptive locomotion, and that removing each component exposes a distinct failure mode. Our formulation removes explicit gait priors (including air-time, contact-count, and foot-clearance targets) in favor of emergent behavior. Compared to a conventional complex-reward baseline, our formulation achieves comparable terrain traversal while reducing cost of transport by 56% and operational-limit violations by 96%. The resulting policies transfer zero-shot to a physical Unitree Go2 using LiDAR-based elevation mapping. Project website with videos: https://tinyurl.com/locomposition.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a decomposed locomotion framework that separates rewards (task), constraints (limits), energy minimization (gait), and exteroception (terrain adaptation), achieving comparable terrain traversal with 56% lower cost of transport and 96% fewer limit violations compared to complex-reward baselines, with zero-shot transfer to a real Unitree Go2 robot.
AI.motivation: Current learning-based quadrupedal locomotion relies on complex reward formulations that entangle task specification, operational limits, gait preference, and terrain adaptation into a single objective, making design and tuning difficult.
AI.method: The method decomposes locomotion control into distinct components: rewards for task specification, constraints for operational limits, energy minimization for gait preference, and exteroceptive perception for terrain-adaptive energy use, removing explicit gait priors like air-time or foot-clearance targets.
AI.result: Compared to a conventional complex-reward baseline, the formulation achieves comparable terrain traversal while reducing cost of transport by 56% and operational-limit violations by 96%. Policies transfer zero-shot to a physical Unitree Go2 with LiDAR-based elevation mapping.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling reward, constraints, energy minimization, and perception yields efficient, terrain-adaptive locomotion without explicit gait priors, with each component addressing a distinct failure mode.

title: Towards Next-Generation Healthcare: A Survey of Medical Embodied AI for Perception, Decision-Making, and Action
summary: Foundation models have demonstrated impressive performance in enhancing healthcare efficiency across a wide range of medical applications. Nevertheless, their limited ability to perceive, understand, and interact with the physical world significantly constrains their effectiveness in real-world clinical workflows, where safety-critical decision-making and physical execution are tightly coupled. Recently, embodied artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising physical-interactive paradigm for intelligent healthcare, enabling agents to operate in complex medical environments. As research in this area rapidly expands, understanding how intelligent agents function as integrated, end-to-end systems in clinical environments becomes increasingly critical. However, existing surveys on medical embodied AI largely emphasize individual aspects or functional components, lacking a unified system-level organization of the field. To support and consolidate recent advances, we systematically survey the core components of medical embodied AI, with a particular emphasis on the coordinated integration of perception, decision-making, and action. We further review representative medical applications and relevant datasets, and we analyze the major challenges encountered in real-world clinical practice. Finally, we discuss key directions for future research in this rapidly evolving field. The associated project can be found at https://github.com/VMVLab/Medical_Embodied_AI_Paper_List.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys medical embodied AI, focusing on the integrated system-level coordination of perception, decision-making, and action for clinical workflows, reviewing applications, datasets, challenges, and future directions.
AI.motivation: Foundation models lack the ability to perceive, understand, and interact with the physical world, limiting their effectiveness in safety-critical clinical workflows where decision-making and physical execution are tightly coupled.
AI.method: The authors systematically survey the core components of medical embodied AI, emphasizing coordinated integration of perception, decision-making, and action, and review representative medical applications and datasets.
AI.result: A unified system-level organization of medical embodied AI is presented, covering perception, decision-making, and action components, along with reviewed applications, datasets, and identified challenges in real-world clinical practice.
AI.conclusion: Medical embodied AI is a promising paradigm for intelligent healthcare, but faces significant challenges in real-world clinical deployment; key future research directions are discussed.

title: VL2Spike: Spike-driven Distillation from VLMs for Low-Power Visual Perception in Embodied AI
summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are brain-inspired, event-driven models that compute with sparse spikes, which enables highly efficient visual perception in resource-constrained embodied AI models. The emergence of Spiking-Transformer models with spike self-attention has substantially improved the learning capacity of pure SNNs. Although SNNs are energy efficient, their performance is still limited by the spike-based architecture and optimization challenges, as standard gradient descent rules cannot be directly applied. Recently, vision-language models (VLMs) have shown rich multi-modal knowledge representation capabilities for visual perception. Thus, it is promising to leverage VLMs for better Spikformer training. To this end, we present VL2Spike, a novel spike-based knowledge distillation (KD) framework that bridges multi-modal knowledge from VLMs with compact Spikformer models. This design enhances the learning capacity of Spikformer models while preserving their energy-efficiency merits, thereby offering a practical pathway toward low-power robotic perception. Our VL2Spike brings two key technical contributions. To align with spiking dynamics, we first propose spatial-temporal visual spike (SVS) distillation, which achieves (1) shared manifold alignment between VLM image features and spike tokens, and (2) warm-started temporal consistency on membrane potentials and spike rates. We then design a novel spike prototype-guided linguistic (SPL) distillation strategy that aligns Spikformer's class prototypes and logits with promptable VLM text embeddings. Extensive experiments show that VL2Spike achieves 6.81% gain across three static datasets with only 15.7% energy consumption. It also exhibits strong generalization capacity on robotic visual place recognition (VPR) with a gain of 6.63%, highlighting its potential for low-power perception in embodied AI.

AI.tldr: VL2Spike is a novel spike-based knowledge distillation framework that transfers multi-modal knowledge from vision-language models (VLMs) to Spikformer models, enhancing their learning capacity while maintaining energy efficiency. It introduces spatial-temporal visual spike (SVS) distillation and spike prototype-guided linguistic (SPL) distillation, achieving ~6.8% gains on static datasets and robotic visual place recognition with only 15.7% energy consumption.
AI.motivation: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) like Spikformer are energy-efficient but limited in performance due to spike-based architecture and optimization challenges. Meanwhile, vision-language models (VLMs) possess rich multi-modal knowledge. The authors aim to bridge this gap by transferring VLM knowledge to compact Spikformer models to boost learning capacity while preserving energy efficiency for low-power embodied AI applications.
AI.method: VL2Spike employs two distillation strategies: (1) Spatial-temporal visual spike (SVS) distillation — aligns VLM image features with spike tokens via shared manifold alignment, and applies warm-started temporal consistency on membrane potentials and spike rates. (2) Spike prototype-guided linguistic (SPL) distillation — aligns Spikformer's class prototypes and logits with promptable VLM text embeddings.
AI.result: VL2Spike achieves a 6.81% performance gain across three static datasets with only 15.7% energy consumption. It also shows strong generalization on robotic visual place recognition (VPR) with a 6.63% gain, demonstrating its potential for low-power embodied AI perception.
AI.conclusion: Bridging VLMs with Spikformer via knowledge distillation is a promising pathway to enhance SNN learning capacity without sacrificing energy efficiency, offering practical solutions for low-power perception in resource-constrained embodied AI systems.

title: Advanced Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques for Enhanced Cattle Identification and Detection: A Comprehensive Review
comment: Published in the journal of Annals of Emerging Technologies in Computing (AETiC), 34 pages, 5 Figures. The Article is available here: http://aetic.theiaer.org/archive/v10/v10n2/p1.html
summary: The need for effective cattle identification technology is now more acutely felt than ever in maintaining biosecurity, food safety, and supply chain efficacy in livestock management. This paper presents a systematic review of recent research in cattle identification using machine learning and deep learning techniques. The present systematic review measures the effectiveness of traditional and modern cattle identification techniques using studies from major academic databases, where articles were subjected to full-text review. Among these techniques, classical Machine Learning Techniques such as K-Nearest Neighbors and Support Vector Machines have demonstrated good results in cattle identification; however, Deep Learning Techniques, such as Convolutional Neural Networks, Residual Networks, and You Only Look Once, are better in cognition, detection, and identification tasks. Feature extraction relies on common techniques like Local Binary Pattern (LBP), Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF), and Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), while key features commonly used in these studies include muzzle prints and coat patterns. The review highlights key hurdles involving cattle identification, such as the limited number of publicly accessible datasets, issues with data quality susceptible to environmental changes and animal mobility, and high demand for real-time processing ability. The paper aims to inform researchers, policymakers, and stakeholders about implementing scalable, humane, and effective cattle identification systems to achieve sustainable livestock management.

AI.tldr: This systematic review evaluates cattle identification techniques using machine learning and deep learning, finding that DL methods (CNNs, ResNet, YOLO) outperform traditional ML methods (KNN, SVM), with key features including muzzle prints and coat patterns, while noting challenges like limited datasets, data quality issues, and real-time processing demands.
AI.motivation: The growing need for effective cattle identification technology to maintain biosecurity, food safety, and supply chain efficacy in livestock management motivates this systematic review.
AI.method: A systematic review was conducted using studies from major academic databases, with articles subjected to full-text review, comparing traditional and modern cattle identification techniques including classical ML (KNN, SVM) and deep learning (CNNs, ResNet, YOLO) methods, with feature extraction techniques like LBP, SURF, and SIFT.
AI.result: Deep learning techniques (CNNs, ResNet, YOLO) outperform classical machine learning techniques (KNN, SVM) in cattle identification tasks. Common features used include muzzle prints and coat patterns. Key challenges identified: limited public datasets, data quality issues from environmental changes and animal mobility, and high real-time processing demands.
AI.conclusion: The paper aims to inform researchers, policymakers, and stakeholders about implementing scalable, humane, and effective cattle identification systems to achieve sustainable livestock management.

title: GeoTLM: Geometry-aware Tactile-Language Models for Contact Motion Orientation Reasoning of Dynamic Objects
summary: Modern tactile-language models (TLMs) have shown potential for robot learning tasks, such as material and texture recognition. However, for contact-rich scenarios, these TLMs struggle to understand the physical properties of dynamic objects, such as rotation and sliding directions. For instance, our preliminary experiments reveal that popular TLMs, such as Sparsh and AnyTouch2, exhibit weak performance on basic rotation direction reasoning from GelSight Mini tactile data. This surprising gap inspires us to explore a novel research question: Can we inject physically grounded geometric priors into TLMs to enable reliable contact orientation reasoning of dynamic object properties? To this end, we propose GeoTLM, a novel geometric representation-guided TLM for the perception of dynamic contact events. Our key idea is to preserve and structure tactile shear-field geometry before language-level reasoning, rather than forcing low-resolution tactile tokens into fragile closed-form physics operators. To achieve this, we propose a lightweight (only 14k parameters) yet novel Differentiable Geometric Representation (DGR). Specifically, DGR learns a contact-mask-guided representation in the shear field and aggregates it through an antisymmetric seven-region pooling design, motivated by the physical intuition that rotational contact produces antisymmetric deformation patterns. We conduct experiments on two representative tasks: rotation direction and sliding direction reasoning. Extensive experiments show that GeoTLM improves novel-object rotation accuracy by +14.6% and real-sensor sliding accuracy by +16.2% over the same backbone without the geometric encoder. Overall, our work paves a new way for physically grounded tactile-language reasoning, with strong potential for dynamic object understanding and contact-rich robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: GeoTLM introduces a lightweight Differentiable Geometric Representation (DGR) that preserves shear-field geometry in tactile data, achieving +14.6% rotation and +16.2% sliding reasoning accuracy over existing TLMs by using antisymmetric pooling guided by physical priors.
AI.motivation: Existing tactile-language models (e.g., Sparsh, AnyTouch2) perform poorly on dynamic contact reasoning tasks like rotation direction detection from GelSight Mini data, revealing a fundamental gap in understanding physical properties of dynamic objects.
AI.method: GeoTLM uses a Differentiable Geometric Representation (DGR, only 14k parameters) that learns a contact-mask-guided representation in the shear field, aggregated via an antisymmetric seven-region pooling design inspired by the physical intuition that rotational contact produces antisymmetric deformation patterns.
AI.result: GeoTLM improves novel-object rotation accuracy by +14.6% and real-sensor sliding accuracy by +16.2% over the same backbone without the geometric encoder.
AI.conclusion: This work paves a new way for physically grounded tactile-language reasoning, showing strong potential for dynamic object understanding and contact-rich robotic manipulation.

title: Overcoming the Impedance Mismatch: A Theoretical Roadmap for Fusing Foundation Models and Knowledge Graphs
comment: 12 pages. Accepted at the ACL 2026 4th Workshop on Towards Knowledgeable Foundation Models (https://openreview.net/forum?id=hXDYsNAq8m)
summary: Modern artificial intelligence remains fundamentally divided between the continuous, probabilistic spaces of Foundation Models and the discrete, deterministic structures of Knowledge Graphs. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) attempts to connect them by serializing graph data into text, we argue this lexical bridging is merely a superficial patch. In this paper, we formalize the underlying structural and geometric friction as the \textit{Impedance Mismatch}. By categorizing current neuro-symbolic integration strategies into a three-tiered hierarchy, we demonstrate that neither surface-level prompt injection nor continuous representation alignment can preserve the strict logical motifs required for reliable multi-hop reasoning. We define the specific mathematical limits, such as the Lexical Bottleneck and Topological Collapse, that show current architectures will eventually hallucinate or conflate semantic nodes. To achieve true semantic fusion, we propose a rigorous theoretical roadmap. We advocate for natively internalizing discrete symbolic structures through Structured Residual Streams, utilizing Vector Symbolic Architectures for latent sub-graph injection, and performing model updates via Orthogonal Subspace Editing. This actionable framework paves the way for models that seamlessly fuse the precision of symbolic logic with the expressivity of parametric memory.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies the fundamental structural and geometric friction between continuous Foundation Models and discrete Knowledge Graphs, termed Impedance Mismatch, and proposes a theoretical roadmap for true semantic fusion through Structured Residual Streams, Vector Symbolic Architectures, and Orthogonal Subspace Editing.
AI.motivation: Current RAG-based approaches to connect Foundation Models with Knowledge Graphs rely on lexical bridging (serializing graph data into text), which is merely a superficial patch. The underlying structural and geometric friction between continuous probabilistic spaces and discrete deterministic structures remains unresolved, leading to hallucinations and semantic conflations in multi-hop reasoning.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the Impedance Mismatch problem, categorizes neuro-symbolic integration strategies into a three-tiered hierarchy, and identifies mathematical limits (Lexical Bottleneck, Topological Collapse). It then proposes a theoretical roadmap featuring: (1) Structured Residual Streams for natively internalizing discrete symbolic structures, (2) Vector Symbolic Architectures for latent sub-graph injection, and (3) Orthogonal Subspace Editing for model updates.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that neither surface-level prompt injection nor continuous representation alignment can preserve strict logical motifs needed for reliable multi-hop reasoning, and provides formal mathematical limits showing current architectures will eventually hallucinate or conflate semantic nodes.
AI.conclusion: True semantic fusion requires natively internalizing discrete symbolic structures rather than superficial lexical bridging. The proposed framework paves the way for models that seamlessly fuse the precision of symbolic logic with the expressivity of parametric memory.

title: Identification of a Physics-Based Electrical Power Consumption Model for the Unitree G1 Humanoid Arm
summary: Accurate prediction of electrical power consumption is essential for energy-aware motion planning, battery management, and thermal monitoring in battery-powered humanoid robots. This letter presents a physics-based, linear-in-parameters model for the electrical power consumption of the seven-degree-of-freedom left arm of the Unitree~G1 humanoid robot. The proposed formulation combines actuator loss terms with a baseline-torque correction that captures changes in gravity-compensation load and enables accurate prediction of negative net power trajectories. Pairwise interaction terms are introduced to model power coupling during simultaneous multi-joint motion. Model parameters are identified from experimental data collected on a physical Unitree~G1 using onboard power measurements as the regression target. Across 897 trajectories covering single-joint and coordinated arm motions at multiple speed levels, the identified model achieves $R^2 = 0.933$ with an RMSE of 1.07 (W). Validation on 46 trajectories executed at previously unseen speeds yields $R^2 = 0.965$, demonstrating strong generalisation beyond the identification dataset. Analysis of the identified parameters reveals distinct power-consumption characteristics across the arm, with viscous friction dominating most joints (shoulder pitch and all three wrist joints), copper losses dominating shoulder yaw and the elbow, and shoulder roll uniquely dominated by Coulomb friction.

AI.tldr: A physics-based linear model for predicting electrical power consumption of a humanoid robot arm achieves high accuracy (R²=0.933 training, 0.965 validation) by combining actuator losses, baseline-torque correction, and pairwise interaction terms, revealing joint-specific dominant loss mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Accurate power consumption prediction is crucial for energy-aware motion planning, battery management, and thermal monitoring in battery-powered humanoid robots.
AI.method: A physics-based linear-in-parameters model combining actuator loss terms, baseline-torque correction for gravity-compensation changes, and pairwise interaction terms for multi-joint coupling. Parameters identified via regression on physical Unitree G1 arm measurements across 897 trajectories.
AI.result: Training: R²=0.933, RMSE=1.07W (897 trajectories). Validation: R²=0.965 (46 unseen-speed trajectories). Joint-specific analysis revealed viscous friction dominates shoulder pitch and wrist joints, copper losses dominate shoulder yaw and elbow, Coulomb friction dominates shoulder roll.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model provides accurate, generalizable power consumption prediction for humanoid robot arms, with interpretable parameters that identify dominant loss mechanisms per joint.

title: Where Did It Go Wrong? Process-Level Evaluation of Web Agents with Semantic State Tracking
summary: Web agents act through long interaction sequences, yet existing benchmarks evaluate only terminal success, discarding all process information and offering little guidance on improvement. In this work, we conduct a process-level analysis of web agents. We introduce WebStep, a benchmark of 1,800 task instances with controlled difficulty and automatic semantic state tracking. Each website exposes a deterministic semantic MDP alongside the GUI: the agent operates on the interface, while the environment records high-level states and transitions in the background, enabling fine-grained analysis without manual annotation. Based on the semantic trajectory, we first show that process metrics reveal differences invisible to outcome evaluation: three agents whose success rates cluster within 31-33% diverge in exploration reach versus execution accuracy. Then, decomposing by skill characterizes the nature of these differences, exposing opposite per-skill rankings hidden within the same website: e.g., on Housing, OpenAI CUA outperforms Qwen3.5 by 23.7% on commit actions yet underperforms it by 15.6% on filtering, pinpointing a concrete skill to improve even within a domain. Bifurcation analysis further localizes the decisive error that loses the task and shows that this error is agent-specific rather than shared. Finally, these differences widen as tasks grow harder: success rate is similar on easy tasks but separates sharply as exploration becomes more demanding. Our process-level analysis opens a new avenue in web agent evaluation, providing fine-grained and actionable insight into where and how each agent should be improved.

AI.tldr: WebStep is a benchmark of 1,800 task instances with controlled difficulty and automatic semantic state tracking, enabling process-level analysis of web agents. It reveals that process metrics expose differences invisible to outcome evaluation, skill-level decompositions pinpoint concrete improvement directions, bifurcation analysis localizes agent-specific decisive errors, and these differences widen as task difficulty increases.
AI.motivation: Existing web agent benchmarks evaluate only terminal success, discarding all process information and offering little guidance on improvement. The authors aim to provide fine-grained, actionable insights into where and how each agent should be improved through process-level analysis.
AI.method: The authors introduce WebStep, a benchmark of 1,800 task instances with controlled difficulty and automatic semantic state tracking. Each website exposes a deterministic semantic MDP alongside the GUI; agents operate on the interface while the environment records high-level states and transitions in the background, enabling fine-grained analysis without manual annotation. They conduct process-level analysis including process metrics comparison, skill decomposition, and bifurcation analysis.
AI.result: Three agents with similar success rates (31-33%) diverge in exploration reach vs. execution accuracy. Skill decomposition reveals opposite per-skill rankings within the same website: e.g., on Housing, OpenAI CUA outperforms Qwen3.5 by 23.7% on commit actions yet underperforms by 15.6% on filtering. Bifurcation analysis shows decisive errors are agent-specific. Differences widen as tasks grow harder.
AI.conclusion: Process-level analysis opens a new avenue in web agent evaluation, providing fine-grained and actionable insight into where and how each agent should be improved.

title: Energy-Efficient Arm Reaching for a Humanoid Robot via Deep Reinforcement Learning with Identified Power Models
summary: Humanoid robots performing in-field manipulation tasks, such as robotic apple harvesting, face severe energy constraints that directly limit the number of reaching motions that can be executed per battery charge. This paper presents an end-to-end, energy-aware reinforcement learning framework for the 7-degree-of-freedom left arm of the Unitree~G1 humanoid robot, combining a physics-based, experimentally identified electrical power model with a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) policy trained in a Pinocchio-based rigid-body dynamics simulator. The RL policy operates on an incremental joint-position action space and is trained with a Hybrid Constellation Reward that combines a four-point end-effector constellation distance with a torque-norm energy proxy; after % $5\times10^6$ training it reaches a $69.9\%$ success rate over $1\,000$ random targets in kinematic simulation, at a mean energy of \SI{98.16}{\joule} on successful episodes. Finally, on the physical Unitree~G1, the policy is validated over three independent 10-target batches, achieving a mean energy of $71.5 \pm 48.3$\,J, an end-effector position error of $2.64 \pm 1.04$\,cm, and an orientation error of $6.92 \pm 1.33^\circ$ -- within the \SI{4}{\centi\metre}/$8.6^\circ$ training tolerance. These results constitute a first step toward energy-aware reinforcement-learning-based arm reaching for humanoid robots.

AI.tldr: An energy-aware reinforcement learning framework using SAC is developed for the Unitree G1 humanoid arm to minimize energy consumption during reaching tasks, achieving ~70% success rate in simulation and validated on physical hardware with ~71 J mean energy and ~2.6 cm position error.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots performing in-field manipulation (e.g., apple harvesting) face severe energy constraints limiting the number of reaching motions per battery charge, motivating the need for energy-aware control.
AI.method: Combines a physics-based experimentally identified electrical power model with a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) policy trained in a Pinocchio-based simulator; uses incremental joint-position action space and a Hybrid Constellation Reward (four-point end-effector constellation distance + torque-norm energy proxy).
AI.result: After 5e6 training steps, 69.9% success rate over 1,000 random targets at mean 98.16 J in simulation; on physical hardware: 71.5 ± 48.3 J mean energy, 2.64 ± 1.04 cm position error, 6.92 ± 1.33° orientation error.
AI.conclusion: These results constitute a first step toward energy-aware reinforcement-learning-based arm reaching for humanoid robots.

title: Multi-agent Framework for Time-Sensitive Complementary Collaboration in Minecraft
summary: We present TickingCollabBench, a Minecraft-based multi-agent benchmark for a novel class of time-sensitive complementary collaboration tasks. Our benchmark reflects four core characteristics of real-world collaboration: agent heterogeneity, mandatory collaboration, dynamic environments, and strict real-time constraints with failure risks. To enable this, we develop the TickingCollab framework, which supports the generation of diverse dynamic environments and abstracts Minecraft's primitive APIs to enable declarative YAML task specifications for composing these events. Building on this, we design a feasibility-aware automated benchmark generation pipeline, where an LLM drafts structurally diverse task configurations and feasibility verifier filters out invalid ones using approximate constraints. Evaluations demonstrate that lang latency and inherent difficulty of coordinating under partial observability and agent heterogeneity cause LLMs to frequently fail under dynamic environments and fall significantly short of a global-knowledge oracle.

AI.tldr: TickingCollabBench is a Minecraft-based multi-agent benchmark testing time-sensitive complementary collaboration with heterogeneous agents, mandatory cooperation, dynamic environments, and real-time constraints. The TickingCollab framework generates diverse tasks using YAML specifications, and an LLM-based pipeline with feasibility verification creates valid configurations. Results show LLMs fail under dynamic conditions due to latency and coordination challenges, performing far below global-knowledge oracles.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent benchmarks lack realistic time-sensitive collaboration features such as agent heterogeneity, mandatory cooperation, dynamic environments, and strict real-time constraints with failure risks—key aspects of real-world teamwork that need evaluation.
AI.method: The TickingCollab framework abstracts Minecraft APIs for declarative YAML task specifications, enabling dynamic environment generation. A feasibility-aware automated pipeline uses LLMs to draft structurally diverse configurations and a verifier filters invalid ones via approximate constraints.
AI.result: LLM-based agents frequently fail under dynamic environments due to language latency and coordination difficulties arising from partial observability and agent heterogeneity, significantly underperforming compared to a global-knowledge oracle baseline.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals critical gaps in current LLM agents' ability to handle time-sensitive complementary collaboration in dynamic, partially observable settings, highlighting the need for improved real-time multi-agent coordination methods.

title: ControlMap: Controllable High-Definition Map Generation for Traffic Scenario Simulation
summary:
Simulation is central to validating autonomous driving systems, yet current pipelines are limited by insufficient scenario diversity due to costly High Definition (HD) map creation. Scaling HD maps requires expensive data collection and manual processing. Moreover, existing generative models lack the fine-grained control necessary to target specific road topologies during generation.
  This paper presents a data-driven pipeline for controllable HD map generation using latent diffusion and ControlNet for spatial conditioning. To our knowledge, we are the first to inject spatial guidance signals into a diffusion model for HD map synthesis. Furthermore, our model supports adjustable conditioning strength through classifier-free guidance and city-level style transfer via city label conditioning. To complement existing metrics, we introduce two novel metrics to evaluate adherence to the control signal and similarity to ground-truth maps. Experiments demonstrate that our model generates realistic HD maps that faithfully follow input road topologies while accurately preserving city-specific details.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a controllable HD map generation pipeline using latent diffusion and ControlNet, enabling realistic map synthesis that follows specific road topologies and preserves city-specific details.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous driving simulation pipelines suffer from insufficient scenario diversity due to costly and labor-intensive HD map creation. Existing generative models lack fine-grained control over road topologies during generation.
AI.method: The approach uses latent diffusion models with ControlNet for spatial conditioning, injects spatial guidance signals into the diffusion process, supports adjustable conditioning strength via classifier-free guidance, and enables city-level style transfer through city label conditioning.
AI.result: The model generates realistic HD maps that faithfully follow input road topologies while preserving city-specific details. Two novel metrics were introduced to evaluate control signal adherence and ground-truth similarity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed data-driven pipeline addresses the scalability and controllability limitations in HD map generation for autonomous driving simulation, offering fine-grained topological control and style transfer capabilities.

title: Recurrent Reasoning on Symbolic Puzzles with Sequence Models
summary: Large language models often appear strong on symbolic and algorithmic tasks, yet this apparent strength can hide brittle behaviour when problems become longer, harder, or slightly out of distribution. A major limitation of current reasoning benchmarks is that many primarily test whether a model can produce a valid answer, while paying less attention to whether the solution is minimal, robust, and stable under controlled difficulty scaling. We introduce RecurrReason, a difficulty-controlled benchmark of four recurrent logic puzzles (Tower of Hanoi, River Crossing, Block World, and Checkers Jumping) with BFS-optimal trajectories and a single interpretable difficulty parameter $N \in \{1,\dots,10\}$, totalling 10{,}817 unique puzzles and 285{,}933 moves. We benchmark two Transformer families, an encoder-decoder model (T5-style) and a decoder-only model (GPT-2-style), under consistent data splits and evaluation criteria, training on $N{=}1$ to $7$ and evaluating on both held-out in-distribution instances and harder out-of-distribution instances at $N{=}8$ to $10$. Fine-tuned pre-trained T5 achieves 97.27\% validation and 81.00\% OOD accuracy on Block World; all models score 0.00\% on River Crossing under all conditions. Failure mode analysis reveals that architecture is a stronger determinant of success than scale. Pre-training transfers only to puzzles with locally structured transition functions. Our code and dataset will be open-sourced upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RecurrReason, a difficulty-controlled benchmark of four recurrent logic puzzles with BFS-optimal trajectories, and evaluates Transformer models (T5-style and GPT-2-style) on in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, showing architecture matters more than scale and pre-training only helps for locally structured puzzles.
AI.motivation: Current reasoning benchmarks focus on answer validity but neglect solution minimality, robustness, and stability under controlled difficulty scaling; the paper aims to address this gap.
AI.method: They introduce RecurrReason, a benchmark of four recurrent logic puzzles (Tower of Hanoi, River Crossing, Block World, Checkers Jumping) with BFS-optimal trajectories and a single difficulty parameter N (1–10), totaling 10,817 puzzles and 285,933 moves. They benchmark T5-style (encoder-decoder) and GPT-2-style (decoder-only) Transformers, training on N=1–7 and evaluating on held-out in-distribution (N=1–7) and out-of-distribution (N=8–10).
AI.result: Fine-tuned T5 achieves 97.27% validation and 81.00% OOD accuracy on Block World; all models score 0.00% on River Crossing under all conditions. Architecture is a stronger determinant of success than scale; pre-training transfers only to puzzles with locally structured transition functions.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals brittle reasoning in Transformers, particularly on certain puzzles, and highlights that architectural choice and local structure matter more than model scale for out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Friction Characterization of a Cable-Driven Differential Actuation System for Lower-Limb Exoskeletons
comment: Accepted for presentation IEEE RAS/EMBS 11th International Conference on Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronics
summary: Lower-limb exoskeletons require actuation systems that can provide accurate joint torque control while preserving low mass and encumbrance. Conventional architectures often rely on independently actuated joints and joint-level torque sensors, increasing system complexity and weight. This paper presents a novel differential actuation architecture for hip-knee flexion/extension, enabling cooperative torque sharing between two motors via a linear differential mapping between motor and joint. To compensate for transmission losses, a model-based friction estimation strategy is developed and experimentally implemented, allowing accurate joint torque estimation without the need for torque sensors. The proposed solution is validated on a physical prototype, demonstrating the feasibility of sensorless torque estimation in a differentially actuated hip-knee module of a lower-limb exoskeleton.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel differential actuation architecture for hip-knee exoskeletons that enables cooperative torque sharing between two motors and uses model-based friction estimation for sensorless joint torque control, validated on a physical prototype.
AI.motivation: Lower-limb exoskeletons need accurate joint torque control with low mass and encumbrance, but conventional architectures using independently actuated joints and torque sensors increase system complexity and weight.
AI.method: A differential actuation architecture with linear differential mapping between motors and joints for cooperative torque sharing, plus a model-based friction estimation strategy to compensate for transmission losses and enable sensorless torque estimation.
AI.result: The proposed approach was validated on a physical prototype, demonstrating feasible sensorless torque estimation in a differentially actuated hip-knee module.
AI.conclusion: Sensorless torque estimation is feasible in differentially actuated lower-limb exoskeleton modules, reducing system complexity and weight while maintaining accurate torque control.

title: Do LLMs Reliably Identify Correct Information Units in Aphasic Discourse?
summary: Correct Information Units (CIUs) are central to discourse assessment in aphasia because they quantify communicative informativeness rather than linguistic form alone. However, CIU scoring is time intensive and requires trained raters. This study examined whether instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) can reliably perform token-level CIU classification from aphasic discourse transcripts. Sixteen picture-description transcripts elicited with the Cat Rescue stimulus were annotated for CIU status according to Nicholas and Brookshire (1993). The sample spanned four severity strata: control, mild, moderate, and severe aphasia. Four publicly available instruction-tuned LLMs were benchmarked under zero-shot and two few-shot prompting conditions across five stratified random seeds. Performance was evaluated against consensus human labels using accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and Cohen's kappa. Zero-shot prompting was insufficient across models. In contrast, few-shot prompting yielded substantial gains and produced competitive performance for three viable models. Mean few-shot F1 scores ranged from 0.776 to 0.817 across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B, with no significant differences between fixed global and per-chunk local example selection. Phi-3-mini was unstable and did not yield reliable performance. Viable models showed high recall but lower precision, suggesting systematic over-classification of tokens as CIUs. Performance also varied by discourse severity, with the weakest results in more severe aphasia. Few-shot LLM prompting can support automated CIU identification without gradient-based task training, but agreement with human annotation remains insufficient for fully autonomous use. These findings support LLM-based CIU scoring as a promising human-in-the-loop component of discourse assessment systems.

AI.tldr: This study evaluated whether instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3-mini) can perform token-level CIU classification from aphasic discourse transcripts. Zero-shot prompting failed, but few-shot prompting yielded competitive F1 scores (0.776–0.817) for three models, though agreement remains insufficient for full automation. Performance degraded with more severe aphasia, and models tended to over-classify tokens as CIUs.
AI.motivation: CIUs are essential for quantifying communicative informativeness in aphasia discourse assessment, but manual CIU scoring is time-intensive and requires trained raters. Automating this process could significantly reduce clinical burden.
AI.method: Sixteen picture-description transcripts (Cat Rescue stimulus) were annotated for CIU status across four severity strata. Four instruction-tuned LLMs were benchmarked under zero-shot and two few-shot prompting conditions across five stratified random seeds. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and Cohen's kappa against human consensus labels.
AI.result: Zero-shot prompting was insufficient. Few-shot prompting produced substantial gains; three models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) achieved mean F1 scores of 0.776–0.817 with no significant difference between global and per-chunk example selection. Phi-3-mini was unstable. Models showed high recall but lower precision (over-classification). Performance was weakest for severe aphasia.
AI.conclusion: Few-shot LLM prompting can support automated CIU identification without task-specific training, but agreement with human annotation is not yet sufficient for fully autonomous deployment. LLM-based CIU scoring is promising as a human-in-the-loop component for discourse assessment systems.

title: $λ$-Reachability: Geometric-Horizon Safety Bellman Equations for Humanoid Safety
summary: We introduce $λ$-Reachability, a scalable approach to Hamilton--Jacobi safety analysis for high-dimensional robotic systems. Unlike prior discounted formulations that rely on fixed one-step Bellman updates, $λ$-Reachability employs a stochastic multi-step estimator of the safety value, using a geometrically distributed rollout horizon together with a randomly absorbed terminal. Conceptually analogous to TD($λ$), $λ$-Reachability interpolates between local self-consistency updates and long-horizon max-over-trajectory safety targets via an interpretable horizon-control parameter. Unlike TD($λ$), where the terminal value is always incorporated in learning targets, the terminal safety value in $λ$-Reachability is only used at a probability controlled by parameter $δ$. We formally show that for $δ<1$, the update induces a contraction mapping that allows temporal-difference learning; as $λ\to 1$, the estimator recovers the undiscounted reachability objective. We apply $λ$-Reachability to high-dimensional safety learning problems with both simulated and real humanoid robots under balance and collision avoidance constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that $λ$-Reachability significantly improves both safe-set boundary classification and safety margin estimation compared to single-step temporal-difference baselines.

AI.tldr: λ-Reachability is a scalable method for Hamilton-Jacobi safety analysis in high-dimensional robotics that uses stochastic multi-step rollout estimation with a controllable terminal absorption parameter, interpolating between local updates and long-horizon safety targets, and significantly improves safe-set classification and margin estimation over TD baselines on humanoid robots.
AI.motivation: Existing discounted formulations for Hamilton-Jacobi safety analysis rely on fixed one-step Bellman updates, which are insufficient for high-dimensional robotic systems with long-horizon safety constraints like balance and collision avoidance.
AI.method: λ-Reachability employs a stochastic multi-step estimator of the safety value using a geometrically distributed rollout horizon with randomly absorbed terminal. It uses a parameter δ controlling the probability of incorporating terminal safety values, and λ controlling interpolation between local self-consistency and long-horizon max-over-trajectory safety targets. The method is formally shown to induce a contraction mapping for δ<1, enabling TD learning.
AI.result: Applied to high-dimensional humanoid robots under balance and collision avoidance constraints in both simulation and real hardware. λ-Reachability significantly improves safe-set boundary classification and safety margin estimation compared to single-step temporal-difference baselines.
AI.conclusion: λ-Reachability provides a principled, scalable, and interpretable framework for safety analysis in high-dimensional robotics, recovering the undiscounted reachability objective as λ→1 while maintaining tractable TD learning.

title: Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2026
summary: Welcome to the ninth edition of the AI Index report. As AI continues to advance rapidly, the question becomes whether the systems built around it can keep up. Governance frameworks, evaluation methods, education systems, and the data infrastructure needed to track AI's impact are struggling to match the pace of the technology itself. That gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it runs through every chapter of this year's report. New in this edition, the report tracks how AI is being tested more ambitiously across reasoning, safety, and real-world task execution, and why those measurements are increasingly difficult to rely on. It also features new estimates of generative AI's economic value alongside emerging evidence of its labor market effects, an analytical framework on AI sovereignty, and a science chapter developed in collaboration with Schmidt Sciences. For the first time, the report features standalone chapters on AI in science and AI in medicine, reflecting AI's growing impact across these two domains.

AI.tldr: The 9th AI Index report examines the growing gap between rapid AI advancement and the preparedness of governance, evaluation, education, and data infrastructure to manage it. It covers new areas: ambitious AI testing (reasoning, safety, real-world tasks), generative AI's economic value and labor market effects, AI sovereignty, and features first-time standalone chapters on AI in science and medicine.
AI.motivation: To track and analyze the accelerating pace of AI development against the readiness of governance frameworks, evaluation methods, education systems, and data infrastructure to manage AI's impact responsibly.
AI.method: A comprehensive report tracking AI testing across reasoning, safety, and real-world task execution; estimating generative AI's economic value and labor market effects; developing an analytical framework on AI sovereignty; and collaborating with Schmidt Sciences on a science chapter.
AI.result: The report finds a widening gap between AI capabilities and society's preparedness to manage them, with evaluation measurements becoming increasingly difficult to rely on. New estimates of generative AI's economic impact and labor market effects are provided, alongside new standalone analyses of AI in science and medicine.
AI.conclusion: AI is advancing faster than the systems designed to govern, evaluate, and track it, necessitating improved frameworks and infrastructure to bridge this preparedness gap.

title: Leveraging Deep Learning for Object and Position Recognition of Load Carriers for Autonomous Logistics Vehicles
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, IFAC World Congress2026, \c{opyright} 2026 the authors. This work has been accepted to IFAC for publication under a Creative Commons Licence CC-BY-NC-ND
summary:
This work explores the use of artificial intelligence in mobile robotics to achieve autonomous detection and pose estimation of load carriers for automated pickup. A deep neural network is designed to recognize predefined landmarks on the carrier from RGBD data; these landmarks are then used to compute the carrier's pose. The network operates directly on RGBD images to estimate landmark positions, which form the basis for determining the carrier's location. The approach is validated in extensive experiments and comprises both software and hardware implementations.
  A deep learning-based framework is presented to detect load carriers and estimate their pose for use with autonomous logistics vehicles. Our method uses a convolutional neural network to identify characteristic reference points on the carrier from RGBD input and computes its pose by combining these inferred landmarks with prior geometric knowledge. Experiments show that the resulting accuracy is sufficient for reliable load carrier detection in industrial environments, confirming the suitability of the method for autonomous intralogistics applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a deep learning framework using a CNN to detect predefined landmarks on load carriers from RGBD data, enabling pose estimation for autonomous pickup by mobile robots in industrial logistics. The method is validated through software and hardware experiments, demonstrating sufficient accuracy for reliable intralogistics applications.
AI.motivation: To enable autonomous mobile robots to detect and estimate the pose of load carriers for automated pickup in industrial intralogistics, replacing manual or less robust approaches.
AI.method: A deep neural network (CNN) takes RGBD images as input to detect predefined landmarks on load carriers; these detected 2D/3D landmark positions are then combined with prior geometric knowledge of the carrier to compute its 6-DOF pose.
AI.result: Extensive experiments (both software and hardware) demonstrate that the method achieves accuracy sufficient for reliable load carrier detection in industrial environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed deep learning-based approach is suitable for autonomous intralogistics applications, enabling reliable automated pickup of load carriers.

title: AI-Driven Framework for Adaptive Water Network Management with Proof-of-Concept Implementation: Addressing Non-Revenue Water in Jordan
summary: Jordan faces severe water scarcity with 50\% of water produced is lost to leakage, theft and metering issues also known as non-revenue water (NRW). Traditional reactive approaches have proven insufficient for sustained NRW reduction. This paper proposes an intelligent framework integrating EPANET hydraulic modeling, digital twin technology, SCADA systems, and large language model (LLM)-based AI agents for continuous network monitoring and adaptive decision-making. The system combines real-time data streams with physics-based simulation to detect anomalies, employing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for policy interpretation and function calling for network control. A proof-of-concept implementation validates technical feasibility using EPYT with offline LLMs (llama3.1:8b via Ollama) on a 1,164-junction Amman district network. The system demonstrates automated hydraulic simulation, flow-based anomaly detection aligned with water distribution zone (DZ) practice, and AI-generated health reports with response times under 2 minutes and zero API costs. Burst detection relies on local flow anomaly analysis: a 30.1~L/s simulated leak produces measurable flow redistribution in 15 pipes, flagging a 15-junction cluster that localises the burst -- confirming alignment with water distribution zone (DZ) monitoring practice. The framework accommodates Jordan's intermittent supply patterns and limited automation through phased implementation, offering a scalable pathway for water-scarce regions to leverage intelligent automation for NRW reduction and operational efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an intelligent framework combining EPANET hydraulic modeling, digital twin technology, SCADA systems, and LLM-based AI agents to detect and manage non-revenue water (NRW) in Jordan's water networks. A proof-of-concept on a 1,164-junction Amman district shows automated anomaly detection, AI-generated health reports under 2 minutes with zero API cost, and burst localization via flow redistribution analysis.
AI.motivation: Jordan faces severe water scarcity where 50% of produced water is lost to leakage, theft, and metering issues (NRW). Traditional reactive approaches have proven insufficient for sustained NRW reduction, motivating the need for an intelligent, automated monitoring and decision-making framework.
AI.method: The framework integrates EPANET hydraulic modeling, digital twin technology, SCADA systems, and LLM-based AI agents. It combines real-time data streams with physics-based simulation, uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for policy interpretation and function calling for network control. A proof-of-concept uses EPYT with offline LLMs (llama3.1:8b via Ollama) on a 1,164-junction Amman district network. Burst detection is performed via local flow anomaly analysis.
AI.result: The system demonstrates automated hydraulic simulation, flow-based anomaly detection aligned with water distribution zone (DZ) practice, and AI-generated health reports with response times under 2 minutes and zero API costs. A simulated 30.1 L/s leak produces measurable flow redistribution in 15 pipes, flagging a 15-junction cluster that localizes the burst, confirming alignment with DZ monitoring practice.
AI.conclusion: The framework accommodates Jordan's intermittent supply patterns and limited automation through phased implementation, offering a scalable pathway for water-scarce regions to leverage intelligent automation for NRW reduction and operational efficiency.

title: A Smart-Scheduled Hybrid (SSH) EKF-FGO State Estimation
comment: This work has been accepted for presentation/publication at the 2026 IEEE Canadian Conference on Electrical and Computer Engineering (CCECE). The final published version will appear in IEEE Xplore
summary: Reliable state estimation in robotics and control re quires balancing estimation accuracy against computational cost. While filtering-based methods such as the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) provide efficient real-time updates, and optimisation based formulations using factor graphs improve global consistency, the role of optimisation scheduling is often treated implicitly rather than examined as an explicit design variable. This paper presents an experimental study that explicitly isolates optimisation scheduling using a Smart Scheduled Hybrid (SSH) EKF-FGO framework as a controlled testbed. By combining EKF-based state propagation with periodically invoked batch optimisation and holding solver structure and effort fixed, the main contribution of this work is the experimental characterisation of optimisation scheduling as an independent design variable governing the trade-off between intermediate estimation accuracy and computational cost. Simulation results in a planar SLAM environment show that scheduling strongly influences pre optimisation drift, transient error behaviour, and runtime. In particular, the results identify operating regimes in which most of the benefit of global optimisation can be retained at a fraction of the computational cost, highlighting optimisation scheduling as an under-explored yet critical consideration in hybrid state estimation systems.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally characterizes optimization scheduling as an explicit design variable in hybrid EKF-FGO state estimation, showing that periodic batch optimization scheduling governs the trade-off between estimation accuracy and computational cost in SLAM.
AI.motivation: Optimization scheduling in hybrid filtering-graph optimization frameworks is often treated implicitly rather than examined as an explicit design variable governing the accuracy-cost trade-off.
AI.method: The authors propose a Smart Scheduled Hybrid (SSH) EKF-FGO framework combining EKF-based state propagation with periodically invoked batch optimization, holding solver structure and effort fixed to isolate scheduling as an independent variable.
AI.result: Simulation results in planar SLAM show scheduling strongly influences pre-optimization drift, transient error behavior, and runtime; most of the benefit of global optimization can be retained at a fraction of the computational cost under specific operating regimes.
AI.conclusion: Optimization scheduling is an under-explored yet critical consideration in hybrid state estimation systems, serving as a key design variable for balancing accuracy and computational cost.

title: RoboPIN: Grounded Embodied Reasoning via Pinned Chain-of-Thought
summary: Embodied reasoning requires models to perceive task-relevant objects and spaces in physical environments and maintain consistent visual grounding throughout multi-step reasoning. However, current vision-language models rely on text-only or coordinate-augmented chain-of-thought, where entity references remain implicit and ambiguous. This may cause the reasoning process to decouple from visual evidence, entity references to drift across steps, and a causal disconnection between the reasoning trajectory and the final answer, with these problems further amplified in multi-view scenarios due to cross-view appearance changes. To address these issues, we propose Pinned Chain-of-Thought (\pincot{}), a structured reasoning paradigm that pins every reasoning step to visual evidence. \pincot{} introduces the concept of \reasoninganchor{}, which binds each task-relevant entity to a structured visual anchor with entity name, unique identity, view index, and spatial grounding, enabling consistent entity tracking across reasoning steps and views. We build a fully automated data generation pipeline to construct \dataset{}, a high-quality \pincot{}-formatted reasoning dataset. We then train \method{} through three-stage post-training that progressively injects embodied knowledge, structured reasoning ability, and process-supervised alignment, with rewards that directly constrain both anchor localization and identity consistency during reasoning. On 14 benchmarks covering embodied spatial reasoning, multi-view reasoning, and pointing, \method{} with only 4B parameters consistently outperforms 7B level open-source embodied models, achieving a 12\% average improvement over the strongest 7B baseline, Mimo-Embodied. Further analysis shows that \pincot{} improves grounding accuracy and cross-step identity consistency, validating the effectiveness of process supervision.

AI.tldr: Pinned Chain-of-Thought (PinCoT) introduces visual-anchored reasoning steps to improve embodied reasoning, achieving 12% average improvement over 7B baselines with only 4B parameters.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs rely on text-only or coordinate-augmented CoT, causing entity references to be implicit/ambiguous, leading to decoupling from visual evidence, cross-step entity drift, causal disconnection between reasoning and answers, and amplified issues in multi-view scenarios.
AI.method: Proposes PinCoT with reasoning anchors (entity name, unique ID, view index, spatial grounding) for consistent visual grounding across steps/views. Builds automated data pipeline for PinCoT-formatted dataset. Trains model via three-stage post-training: embodied knowledge injection, structured reasoning, process-supervised alignment with rewards constraining anchor localization and identity consistency.
AI.result: On 14 benchmarks, 4B PinCoT model outperforms 7B open-source embodied models with 12% average improvement over strongest baseline (Mimo-Embodied).
