AI.method: Measured exploit rates on SWE-bench Verified and R2E-Gym; conducted random-effects meta-analysis on 134 models; proposed a hardening procedure using an LLM judge with a Docker gold-sanity gate and diversity-biased retry.
AI.result: 28.5% of SWE-bench Verified tasks accept incorrect patches; 25% on R2E-Gym; models score +14.14 pp higher on hackable tasks; the gate detects 61.9% defective LLM-generated tests; loop converges 9/11 tasks to gated upgrades.
AI.conclusion: Code RL benchmarks have significant test suite weaknesses that inflate model scores, but a gated hardening procedure can mitigate these issues.

title: HATS: A Human-Agent Teleoperation System for Multi-Arm Data Collection
summary: Many real-world manipulation scenarios, such as handling complex collaborative tasks and dealing with large workspaces, require coordination of more than two robotic arms. Consequently, an effective multi-arm teleoperation system is required to collect demonstrations for training coordinated multi-arm manipulation policies. However, existing teleoperation frameworks mainly focus on single-operator or multi-operator setups, facing a practical trade-off between the cognitive load placed on a single operator and the coordination cost incurred by multiple operators. To address this problem, we introduce HATS, a human-agent teleoperation system that enables a single human operator, assisted by an MLLM-based agent, to collect data for multi-arm manipulation tasks. Our system decouples the control space: two primary arms are directly teleoperated by the human, while two assistive arms are controlled by a training-free agent that handles sub-tasks. In addition, the human operator can use voice commands to prevent collisions and correct assistive arm behaviors during execution. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that HATS achieves data collection efficiency and success rates comparable to expert dual-human teams. Moreover, downstream policy evaluations demonstrate the efficacy and quality of the data collected through HATS.

AI.tldr: HATS is a human-agent teleoperation system that enables a single operator, assisted by an MLLM-based agent, to efficiently collect demonstrations for multi-arm manipulation tasks by decoupling control between human-driven primary arms and agent-controlled assistive arms.
AI.motivation: Existing teleoperation frameworks face a trade-off between high cognitive load on a single operator and high coordination cost when using multiple operators for multi-arm manipulation tasks. A more efficient data collection system is needed for training coordinated multi-arm policies.
AI.method: HATS decouples control: a human directly teleoperates two primary arms while a training-free MLLM-based agent controls two assistive arms for sub-tasks. The human can also use voice commands to prevent collisions and correct assistive arm behaviors in real time.
AI.result: HATS achieves data collection efficiency and success rates comparable to expert dual-human teams, and downstream policy evaluations confirm the quality of collected data.
AI.conclusion: HATS effectively balances cognitive load and coordination cost, providing a practical single-operator solution for collecting high-quality multi-arm manipulation demonstrations.

title: Mind-Studio: Executable World Models with Lookahead Evaluation for Partially Observable Games
summary: World-model synthesis aims to turn interaction experience into an internal model of environment dynamics. Existing symbolic approaches often fit observed transitions or mixtures of local rules, but they do not produce a complete executable program that can run independently of the real environment. We present Mind-Studio, a framework that synthesizes executable pygame-style world models from state-action-next-state trajectories using large language models. Mind-Studio combines entropy-selected traces with a lightweight game skill file containing object, action, and static scene information extracted from screenshots. We evaluate synthesis quality with a K-step lookahead fidelity protocol that compares generated world-model rollouts against Real-ALE rollouts from the same state. On Montezuma's Revenge, Mind-Studio improves chosen-action next-state prediction from 0.3% for PoE-World to 48.7% while verifying 5 of 8 subgoals; across Alien, Assault, and Skiing, it achieves stronger branch-level fidelity than prior learned lookahead sources.

AI.tldr: Mind-Studio is a framework using LLMs to synthesize executable pygame-style world models from interaction trajectories, achieving significantly better next-state prediction (48.7% vs 0.3%) and subgoal verification than prior symbolic approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing symbolic world-model synthesis approaches fit observed transitions or local rule mixtures but fail to produce complete executable programs that can run independently of the real environment.
AI.method: Mind-Studio combines entropy-selected traces with a lightweight game skill file (object, action, static scene info from screenshots) using LLMs to synthesize executable pygame-style world models from state-action-next-state trajectories.
AI.result: On Montezuma's Revenge: next-state prediction improved from 0.3% (PoE-World) to 48.7%, verified 5 of 8 subgoals; across Alien, Assault, Skiing: achieved stronger branch-level fidelity than prior learned lookahead sources.
AI.conclusion: Mind-Studio demonstrates that LLM-based synthesis of executable world models from trajectories is feasible and significantly outperforms prior symbolic approaches in fidelity and subgoal verification.

title: APEX: Adaptive Policy Execution for Precise Manipulation
summary: Modern imitation learning methods, including visuomotor and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, typically output high-level action references that are executed by low-level controllers. However, the absence of higher-order reference signals, together with the policy's lack of awareness of the underlying low-level control dynamics during training, inevitably induces an execution gap. As a result, realized actions deviate systematically from policy-commanded ones, with a critical impact on precision-sensitive manipulation. Prior work either modifies the policy architecture or the low-level controller, both requiring intrusive changes to the pretrained policy or packaged controller. This raises a natural question: when the policy and controller are both treated as inaccessible black boxes, can we bridge the execution gap? We propose Adaptive Policy Execution (APEX), a plug-and-play framework inserted between the policy and the controller that reconstructs a dynamically feasible reference from policy outputs and adapts at test-time according to low-level state feedback, with a provable convergence guarantee. Extensive empirical studies show that APEX reduces controller-induced tracking error by 41.2% on demonstration replay and improves manipulation success by 4.8--25.8 percentage points across four visuomotor and VLA policy classes.

AI.tldr: APEX is a plug-and-play framework inserted between policy and controller to bridge the execution gap caused by discrepancies between high-level action references and low-level control dynamics, reducing tracking error by 41.2% and improving manipulation success by 4.8–25.8 percentage points across multiple policy classes.
AI.motivation: Modern imitation learning methods (visuomotor and VLA policies) suffer from an execution gap because they output high-level action references without awareness of low-level control dynamics, causing systematic deviations in precision-sensitive manipulation. Prior work requires intrusive modifications to either policy architecture or low-level controller, which is impractical when both are treated as inaccessible black boxes.
AI.method: APEX is a plug-and-play framework inserted between the policy and the controller that reconstructs a dynamically feasible reference from policy outputs and adapts at test-time according to low-level state feedback, with a provable convergence guarantee.
AI.result: APEX reduces controller-induced tracking error by 41.2% on demonstration replay and improves manipulation success by 4.8–25.8 percentage points across four visuomotor and VLA policy classes.
AI.conclusion: The execution gap between high-level policy outputs and low-level control can be bridged without modifying either the policy or the controller, using a plug-and-play adaptive framework that reconstructs dynamically feasible references from policy commands.

title: Rhythm of the Deep: A Computational-Linguistic Test of Duality of Patterning in Sperm Whale Codas
summary: Human language has often been described as combining structure at two levels: lower-level units combine into larger units, which then combine into larger sequences. We test for this design feature, duality of patterning, in sperm whale codas using 1,483 codas from the Dominica Sperm Whale Project. Because acoustic similarity can imitate symbolic structure, we treat the problem as computational-linguistic structure discovery from continuous audio rather than as a direct claim about language or meaning. We use a consensus of frozen audio encoders, held-out structural tests, per-statistic nulls, and acoustic-null recoverability gates. The evidence supports a narrow two-tier architecture. At the lower tier, clicks compose into codas not by a stable ordered rule, but by which clicks are present together with their inter-click rhythm. At the upper tier, coda tokens show bout-level sequential dependence, with an NSB second-order transfer-entropy lift of 0.132 bits (p = 0.002). Under tempo scaling, encoder-derived click identity is strongly rate-bound, while coda identity remains substantially more stable, yielding a measurable abstraction gradient across the click-to-coda step. Rhythm-only baselines recover substantial lower-tier structure but fail to reproduce the upper-tier sequential-dependence signal. We do not claim language, semantics, perception, or human-like phonemes. Instead, we report representation-level evidence for a duality-of-patterning-like architecture whose lower tier is rhythmic rather than segmental, and provide a portable null-controlled framework for testing combinatorial structure in induced acoustic token systems.

AI.tldr: This paper tests for duality of patterning (combinatorial structure at two levels) in sperm whale codas using computational-linguistic methods on 1,483 recordings. It finds evidence for a lower tier where clicks compose into codas based on presence and rhythm rather than fixed order, and an upper tier where codas show sequential dependence across bouts. The lower tier is rhythmic rather than segmental, differing from human language.
AI.motivation: To test whether sperm whale communication exhibits duality of patterning—a foundational design feature of human language where lower-level units combine into larger units, which themselves combine into sequences—using rigorous computational methods rather than making direct claims about language or meaning.
AI.method: Applied computational-linguistic structure discovery on 1,483 sperm whale codas from the Dominica Sperm Whale Project, using: (1) consensus of frozen audio encoders, (2) held-out structural tests, (3) per-statistic nulls, (4) acoustic-null recoverability gates, and (5) NSB second-order transfer-entropy analysis with tempo scaling and rhythm-only baselines.
AI.result: Found: (1) lower-tier clicks compose into codas by click presence and inter-click rhythm, not stable order; (2) upper-tier codas show bout-level sequential dependence (0.132 bits transfer-entropy lift, p=0.002); (3) click identity is rate-bound while coda identity is more stable under tempo scaling, showing an abstraction gradient; (4) rhythm-only baselines recover lower-tier structure but fail on upper-tier sequential dependence.
AI.conclusion: Sperm whale codas exhibit a duality-of-patterning-like architecture with a rhythmic (not segmental) lower tier. The study provides a portable null-controlled framework for testing combinatorial structure in animal acoustic communication systems without invoking claims about language, semantics, or perception.

title: Agile Fall Recovery for Quadrotors with Bidirectional Thrust via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Autonomous fall recovery is a critical capability for quadrotors operating in real-world environments, where collisions or failures may leave the vehicle resting on the ground in an arbitrary attitude. This problem is challenging because recovery must be achieved under limited onboard sensing, in constrained free space, with ground contact, and in the presence of unknown disturbances. In this letter, we present an RL-based framework for autonomous fall recovery of a quadrotor from arbitrary ground attitudes to stable hover using only lightweight onboard sensors. To address severe partial observability and intermittent sensor invalidity, we train a recurrent policy within an asymmetric actor--critic architecture, leveraging an Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI) controller to track the policy output. Combined with high-fidelity simulations of motor response and optical flow, the overall training framework significantly reduces the sim-to-real gap. Simulation ablation studies validate the importance of the main design choices, while real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot transfer and robust recovery under different initial attitudes, wind disturbances, and additional payloads. These results demonstrate that agile quadrotor fall recovery can be achieved without explicit state estimation using only limited and unreliable onboard sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an RL-based framework enabling quadrotors to autonomously recover from arbitrary ground attitudes to stable hover using only lightweight onboard sensors, with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer demonstrated in real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Quadrotors operating in real-world environments need autonomous fall recovery capability after collisions or failures, but this is challenging due to limited onboard sensing, constrained free space, ground contact, and unknown disturbances.
AI.method: The method uses a recurrent policy trained with asymmetric actor-critic architecture, combined with an Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI) controller for tracking policy outputs, and high-fidelity simulations of motor response and optical flow to reduce sim-to-real gap.
AI.result: Simulation ablation studies validate key design choices; real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot transfer and robust recovery under different initial attitudes, wind disturbances, and additional payloads.
AI.conclusion: Agile quadrotor fall recovery can be achieved without explicit state estimation using only limited and unreliable onboard sensing.

title: RecourseBench: A Modular Framework for Reproducible Algorithmic Recourse Evaluation
summary: Algorithmic recourse methods provide counterfactual explanations that inform individuals of the actions required to overturn an unfavorable model decision. Despite rapid methodological progress, principled comparison remains elusive; existing frameworks are often difficult to extend and lack both interoperability and systematic verification that integrated methods faithfully reproduce their originally reported results. We introduce \emph{RecourseBench}, a unified evaluation framework built around three commitments namely, modularity, reproducibility, and interactivity. The framework decomposes the pipeline into five fully decoupled layers -- Data, Preprocessing, Model, Recourse Method, and Evaluation -- governed by abstract interfaces and a dynamic registry. To address the reproducibility gap in prior benchmarks, we introduce a four-tier classification system in which every integrated method is validated by an automated test suite against its originally reported results. We further provide an interactive web interface for flexible, configuration-driven comparison across methods, datasets, and model architectures. Our framework currently integrates 28 state-of-the-art recourse methods and, to our knowledge, constitutes the first recourse benchmark to explicitly enforce method-level reproducibility through automated, quantitative testing.

AI.tldr: RecourseBench is a unified, modular, reproducible, and interactive evaluation framework for algorithmic recourse methods, integrating 28 state-of-the-art methods with automated reproducibility testing.
AI.motivation: Existing frameworks for evaluating algorithmic recourse methods are difficult to extend, lack interoperability, and fail to systematically verify that integrated methods faithfully reproduce their originally reported results, creating a reproducibility gap.
AI.method: The framework decomposes the recourse pipeline into five decoupled layers (Data, Preprocessing, Model, Recourse Method, Evaluation) governed by abstract interfaces and a dynamic registry. A four-tier classification system with automated test suites validates each method against its originally reported results. An interactive web interface enables configuration-driven comparison.
AI.result: Currently integrates 28 state-of-the-art recourse methods and constitutes the first recourse benchmark to explicitly enforce method-level reproducibility through automated, quantitative testing.
AI.conclusion: RecourseBench addresses the reproducibility gap in algorithmic recourse evaluation by providing a modular, verifiable, and interactive benchmarking framework that enables principled comparison across methods, datasets, and model architectures.

title: ADAPT: Analytical Disturbance-Aware Policy Training for Humanoid Locomotion
summary: Humanoids deployed in human-centered environments must handle force-interactive tasks, where external contacts introduce unexpected disturbances that disrupt locomotion accuracy and stability. Existing learning-based approaches rely on broad domain randomization, task-specific force objectives, or learning-based force estimators from motion history, each of which compromises accuracy, task transferability, or out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness. We present Analytical Disturbance-Aware Policy Training (ADAPT), a framework that equips humanoid policies with a physically grounded disturbance observer. The core of ADAPT is an analytical whole-body disturbance observer that estimates residual force/torque online with the accessible robot dynamics, without requiring force/torque sensors. Fed directly into the policy, the estimated disturbances give the humanoid an explicit, physics-derived sense of external force/torque that can generalize across diverse unseen scenes. Experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid show that ADAPT achieves accurate disturbance prediction and stronger robustness than a proprioception-only baseline under torso perturbations, standing pushes, and asymmetric hand payloads, with improved velocity tracking even on OOD disturbances. Moreover, ADAPT enables penalizing inferred disturbances at lower-body joints to encourage lighter locomotion.

AI.tldr: ADAPT is a framework that uses an analytical whole-body disturbance observer to estimate external forces/torques online without sensors, feeding these physics-derived estimates into humanoid locomotion policies to improve robustness across diverse disturbances and tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based methods for humanoid force-interactive tasks suffer from accuracy, task transferability, or out-of-distribution robustness issues due to reliance on domain randomization, task-specific objectives, or motion-history-based force estimators.
AI.method: ADAPT integrates an analytical whole-body disturbance observer that computes residual force/torque estimates from accessible robot dynamics in real-time, and feeds these estimates directly into the policy as explicit disturbance signals.
AI.result: On a Unitree G1 humanoid, ADAPT achieves accurate disturbance prediction and stronger robustness than proprioception-only baselines under torso perturbations, standing pushes, and asymmetric hand payloads, with improved velocity tracking even on OOD disturbances.
AI.conclusion: ADAPT provides a physically grounded, sensor-free disturbance awareness that generalizes across unseen scenes and also enables penalizing inferred disturbances at lower-body joints for lighter locomotion.

title: Know Your Limits : On the Faithfulness of LLMs as Solvers and Autoformalizers in Legal Reasoning
comment: 10 pages, submitted to COLM 2026 (under review, average score of 6.25 across 4 reviewers) and accepted by the AI4Law workshop at ICML. This is the version where we already addressed most of the reviews from the COLM reviewers
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on reasoning tasks, but whether this reflects faithful logical inference or heuristic approximation remains unclear. We study this question in legal entailment by comparing three paradigms, including pure LLM classification, LLM-based Formal Reasoning, and solver-based Formal Reasoning using the Z3 SMT solver, on a re-annotated subset of ContractNLI across five LLMs. Our re-annotation reveals a systematic and measurable gap between pragmatic legal interpretation and strict formal entailment, where a substantial proportion of legally sound inferences are not formally grounded without additional unstated assumptions. While introducing formal structure improves accuracy, with LLM-based Formal Reasoning achieving the highest benchmark performance, we show that this gain does not imply faithful reasoning. We identify three recurring failure modes: scope laundering, where LLMs report solver-inconsistent classifications without executing the underlying formal reasoning, producing conclusions that appear logically grounded but are not; implicit constraint blindness, where LLMs overlook logical constraints present in formal representations; and program synthesis failures, where LLMs generate incorrect Z3 code despite structured prompting. Critically, scope laundering persists across all models, raising serious concerns about the faithfulness of LLM-based formal reasoning as a proxy for symbolic execution. These results reveal a fundamental gap between benchmark accuracy and logical faithfulness.

AI.tldr: LLMs achieve high accuracy on legal reasoning benchmarks but do so through unfaithful heuristics rather than logical inference. The paper identifies three failure modes—scope laundering, implicit constraint blindness, and program synthesis failures—showing that accuracy gains from formal methods do not guarantee faithful reasoning.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs' strong performance on reasoning tasks reflects faithful logical inference or heuristic approximation, specifically in the context of legal entailment.
AI.method: Compared three paradigms (pure LLM classification, LLM-based Formal Reasoning, solver-based Formal Reasoning with Z3) on a re-annotated subset of ContractNLI across five LLMs, analyzing failure modes.
AI.result: LLM-based Formal Reasoning achieved highest benchmark performance, but accuracy gains do not imply faithfulness. Identified three failure modes: scope laundering, implicit constraint blindness, and program synthesis failures. Scope laundering persisted across all models.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental gap between benchmark accuracy and logical faithfulness; LLM-based formal reasoning cannot be trusted as a proxy for symbolic execution.

title: Elastic ODYN: Differentiable Optimization for Infeasible Control and Learning in Robotics
summary: Robotic systems routinely encounter conflicting objectives, modeling errors, and degenerate contact conditions that render quadratic programs (QPs) infeasible. Yet most optimization solvers and differentiable QP layers assume feasibility, leading to numerical failures, unstable gradients, or solver breakdown when constraints cannot be simultaneously satisfied. We present Elastic ODYN, a primal--dual non-interior-point QP solver that handles infeasibility through smooth squared-$\ell_2$ elastic relaxations. The resulting formulation remains well posed under ill-conditioning and degeneracy, supports warm starting, and converges to closest-to-feasible solutions when no feasible point exists. A lightweight refinement stage recovers physically meaningful dual variables from the elastic solution. Building on this framework, we develop Elastic OdynLayer, a differentiable QP layer with stable gradients under infeasibility, and Elastic OdynSQP, an infeasibility-aware SQP method that resolves inconsistent subproblems and intrinsically infeasible optimal control tasks through selective constraint relaxation. We evaluate the framework on benchmark QPs, singular contact mechanics, differentiable parameter identification, and quadrupedal and humanoid trajectory optimization. Across all settings, Elastic ODYN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art elastic QP solvers in robustness, warm-start performance, and convergence reliability, enabling optimization, simulation, control, and learning beyond the feasibility assumptions of existing methods.

AI.tldr: Elastic ODYN is a primal-dual QP solver that handles infeasibility via squared-ℓ2 elastic relaxations, with a differentiable layer (Elastic OdynLayer) and SQP extension (Elastic OdynSQP), outperforming state-of-the-art methods in robustness and convergence on benchmarks, contact mechanics, parameter identification, and trajectory optimization.
AI.motivation: Robotic systems face conflicting objectives, modeling errors, and degenerate contacts that make standard QP solvers infeasible, causing numerical failures and unstable gradients; existing differentiable QP layers assume feasibility, limiting their applicability in optimization, control, and learning.
AI.method: Elastic ODYN uses a primal-dual non-interior-point QP solver with smooth squared-ℓ2 elastic relaxations to maintain well-posedness under ill-conditioning and degeneracy. It includes a refinement stage for physically meaningful dual variables. Built on this, Elastic OdynLayer provides differentiable QP with stable gradients under infeasibility, and Elastic OdynSQP extends to infeasibility-aware sequential quadratic programming with selective constraint relaxation.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art elastic QP solvers in robustness, warm-start performance, and convergence reliability across benchmark QPs, singular contact mechanics, differentiable parameter identification, and quadrupedal/humanoid trajectory optimization.
AI.conclusion: Enables optimization, simulation, control, and learning beyond the feasibility assumptions of existing methods by handling infeasible QPs robustly with stable gradients and physically meaningful dual variables.

title: Thinking with Visual Grounding
summary: Visual thinking should not only sound right; it should show its evidence. While recent vision-language models (VLMs) can produce natural-language reasoning traces, these traces often leave the supporting image regions implicit, making them hard to verify and difficult to supervise. We introduce visually grounded thinking, a reasoning process in which models interleave natural-language thoughts with explicit point or box groundings of the visual evidence used at each step. This lets the model express intermediate reasoning in language while grounding key objects in the image regions they refer to. To train this behavior, we construct a scalable synthesis pipeline that distills correct visual reasoning traces, extracts the visual objects required by the traces, grounds them with a SAM3-based agent, and derives aligned point and box supervision from the resulting masks. We further propose grounding-aware reinforcement learning, which combines answer correctness rewards with dense grounding rewards that score whether generated object references match the correct image evidence. Across two counting benchmarks and four spatial reasoning benchmarks, adding visually grounded thinking to Gemma3-4B-IT consistently improves performance over the original model and the non-grounded thinking baseline. On spatial reasoning, the visually grounded thinking 4B models match, and in some cases surpass, Gemma3-27B-IT from the same model family. Our analysis shows that point grounding is well suited to counting, while box grounding benefits most from explicit grounding rewards on spatial tasks. Overall, our results show that VLMs think better when their intermediate thoughts are tied to the image regions that make them true.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces visually grounded thinking, where VLMs interleave natural-language reasoning with explicit point/box groundings to visual evidence. Using a scalable synthesis pipeline and grounding-aware reinforcement learning, the method improves performance on counting and spatial reasoning benchmarks, with 4B models matching or surpassing 27B baselines.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs produce natural-language reasoning traces that leave supporting image regions implicit, making verification difficult and supervision challenging. The authors aim to make visual reasoning both linguistically explicit and visually grounded for better verifiability and performance.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) visually grounded thinking where models produce interleaved language + point/box groundings; (2) a scalable synthesis pipeline that distills correct reasoning traces, extracts visual objects, grounds them via a SAM3-based agent, and derives aligned supervision; (3) grounding-aware reinforcement learning combining answer correctness rewards with dense grounding rewards.
AI.result: On two counting and four spatial reasoning benchmarks, visually grounded thinking consistently improves Gemma3-4B-IT over the base model and non-grounded thinking baseline. The 4B grounded model matches or surpasses Gemma3-27B-IT on spatial reasoning. Point grounding excels at counting; box grounding benefits most from explicit grounding rewards on spatial tasks.
AI.conclusion: VLMs reason better when intermediate thoughts are explicitly tied to the image regions that support them, demonstrating that grounded intermediate reasoning improves both verifiability and task performance.

title: Automated Digital Twin Construction for Highway Scenarios Using LiDAR Point Clouds and OpenStreetMap
summary: Accurate road environment modeling is fundamental to the simulation and validation of automated driving systems. However, constructing road maps in standardized formats such as ASAM OpenDRIVE from real-world sensor data remains a time-consuming and costly process. Mobile mapping LiDAR captures accurate lane-level geometry but is confined to the driven corridor, while OpenStreetMap (OSM) provides broad road network topology but lacks geometric precision at the lane level. To address this, an automated workflow is proposed to fuse LiDAR point clouds with OSM data to generate georeferenced ASAM OpenDRIVE maps of highway environments, requiring minimal manual intervention. The pipeline reconstructs mainline roads from LiDAR-derived measurements and infers ramp geometry and topology from the OSM road graph, enabling complete highway interchange modeling without full sensor coverage. Experiments demonstrate a mean lateral RMSE of 0.740 m, and the generated maps are directly usable in mainstream simulation platforms including IPG CarMaker and Esmini. These results validate the effectiveness of combining measurement-derived geometry with map-derived topology for automated OpenDRIVE digital twin generation. The project code is available at https://github.com/ftgTUGraz/opendrive-digital-twin-generator

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automated workflow that fuses LiDAR point cloud data with OpenStreetMap (OSM) to generate georeferenced ASAM OpenDRIVE maps for highway environments, achieving a mean lateral RMSE of 0.740 m and enabling direct use in simulation platforms like IPG CarMaker and Esmini.
AI.motivation: Constructing standardized ASAM OpenDRIVE road maps from real-world sensor data is time-consuming and costly. LiDAR provides accurate lane-level geometry but only covers the driven corridor, while OSM offers broad topology but lacks lane-level precision. A fusion approach is needed to automate map generation.
AI.method: The pipeline reconstructs mainline roads from LiDAR-derived measurements and infers ramp geometry and topology from the OSM road graph, enabling complete highway interchange modeling without full sensor coverage. The workflow fuses measurement-derived geometry with map-derived topology to generate ASAM OpenDRIVE maps.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate a mean lateral RMSE of 0.740 m. The generated maps are directly usable in mainstream simulation platforms including IPG CarMaker and Esmini.
AI.conclusion: The results validate the effectiveness of combining measurement-derived geometry with map-derived topology for automated OpenDRIVE digital twin generation, and the project code is open-sourced.

title: VibeThinker-3B: Exploring the Frontier of Verifiable Reasoning in Small Language Models
summary: This technical report introduces VibeThinker-3B, a compact dense model with 3B parameters developed to investigate how far verifiable reasoning can be pushed within a strictly small-model regime. Building upon the Spectrum-to-Signal post-training paradigm, we systematically enhance the model through an optimized pipeline that includes curriculum-based supervised fine-tuning, multi-domain reinforcement learning, and offline self-distillation. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that VibeThinker-3B achieves frontier-level performance on highly demanding verifiable tasks. Specifically, it attains a score of 94.3 on AIME26 (improving to 97.1 with claim-level test-time scaling), an 80.2 Pass@1 on LiveCodeBench v6, and exhibits strong out-of-distribution generalization with a 96.1\% acceptance rate on recent unseen LeetCode contests. This effectively places it in the performance band of first-tier reasoning systems, matching or exceeding flagship models that are orders of magnitude larger, such as DeepSeek V3.2, GLM-5, and Gemini 3 Pro. Furthermore, a score of 93.4 on IFEval confirms that this extreme reasoning enhancement does not compromise strict instruction controllability. Extending our previous 1.5B work, these findings motivate the Parametric Compression-Coverage Hypothesis, which views verifiable reasoning as compressible into compact reasoning cores, while open-domain knowledge and general-purpose competence require broad parameter coverage over facts, concepts, and long-tail scenarios. This perspective suggests that compact models are not merely deployment-efficient substitutes, but a complementary path toward frontier-level performance in parameter-dense capability regimes.

AI.tldr: VibeThinker-3B is a 3B-parameter model that achieves frontier-level verifiable reasoning performance through curriculum SFT, multi-domain RL, and offline self-distillation, matching or exceeding much larger models like DeepSeek V3.2 and Gemini 3 Pro on benchmarks (AIME26: 94.3, LiveCodeBench v6: 80.2, IFEval: 93.4), and motivates the Parametric Compression-Coverage Hypothesis.
AI.motivation: To investigate how far verifiable reasoning can be pushed within a strictly small-model regime (3B parameters), and to challenge the assumption that frontier reasoning capability requires massive model scales.
AI.method: Building on the Spectrum-to-Signal post-training paradigm with an optimized pipeline comprising: (1) curriculum-based supervised fine-tuning, (2) multi-domain reinforcement learning, and (3) offline self-distillation.
AI.result: AIME26: 94.3 (97.1 with claim-level test-time scaling); LiveCodeBench v6: 80.2 Pass@1; LeetCode unseen contests: 96.1% acceptance rate; IFEval: 93.4. Matches/exceeds DeepSeek V3.2, GLM-5, and Gemini 3 Pro.
AI.conclusion: The Parametric Compression-Coverage Hypothesis posits that verifiable reasoning is compressible into compact reasoning cores, while open-domain knowledge requires broad parameter coverage. Compact models are a complementary path toward frontier-level performance, not just deployment-efficient substitutes.

title: Steering Generative Reinforcement Learning into Stable Robotic Controller
summary: Diffusion and flow-based generative policies provide a powerful policy class for reinforcement learning by inducing rich stochastic exploration through iterative action generation. However, the stochasticity of diffusion policies is not suitable for stable and precise control in high-dimensional robotic systems, where small action variations can accumulate into inconsistent motion and reduced robustness. To address this issue, we propose SteerGenPO, a latent-space reinforcement learning framework that steers a trained generative policy into a robust deterministic robotic controller. The key idea is to replace stochastic latent sampling of the trained generative policy with a learned latent actor that predicts a state-dependent latent input for the generative policies. This separates exploration and control: stochastic generative sampling provides diverse action proposals during policy learning, while deterministic latent steering provides stable and adaptive control at deployment. We evaluate SteerGenPO on six Isaac Lab benchmarks and a Unitree G1 locomotion task. The results show SteerGenPO improves over both classical RL and generative RL baselines, while its deterministic latent steering produces more stable inference-time behaviors and more reliable command responses.

AI.tldr: SteerGenPO replaces stochastic latent sampling in diffusion/flow-based generative policies with a learned deterministic latent actor, creating a robust robotic controller that separates exploration (stochastic during training) from control (deterministic at deployment). It outperforms classical and generative RL baselines on six Isaac Lab benchmarks and a Unitree G1 locomotion task.
AI.motivation: Diffusion and flow-based generative policies enable rich stochastic exploration via iterative action generation, but their stochasticity is unsuitable for stable, precise control in high-dimensional robotic systems where small action variations cause inconsistent motion and reduced robustness.
AI.method: A latent-space RL framework (SteerGenPO) that replaces stochastic latent sampling of a trained generative policy with a learned latent actor predicting state-dependent deterministic latent inputs, thereby decoupling exploration (stochastic generative sampling during training) from control (deterministic latent steering at deployment).
AI.result: SteerGenPO improves over both classical RL and generative RL baselines on six Isaac Lab benchmarks and a Unitree G1 locomotion task, with more stable inference-time behaviors and more reliable command responses.
AI.conclusion: Separating exploration from control via deterministic latent steering of generative policies yields superior robustness and stability in robotic control compared to purely stochastic generative policies or classical RL methods.

title: LiteOdyssey: A Lightweight Reasoning AI Agent for Interpretable Rare-Disease Diagnosis
summary: Most medical AI systems improve by scaling additional machinery: more fine-tuning data, more agents, and/or larger retrieval databases. In rare-disease diagnosis, however, such scaling can produce systems that are difficult to deploy, audit, and maintain. We asked whether state-of-the-art diagnostic performance could instead be achieved by extending the reasoning chain of a single AI agent: guiding it with a diagnostic policy, developed through human-AI collaboration and augmenting with freely available biomedical tools. We introduce LiteOdyssey, a lightweight rare-disease diagnostic framework that guides reasoning language model through a clinical genetics workflow. This framework was developed through Policy Iteration with Human Feedback (PIHF) and uses dynamic access to public biomedical tools. On two challenging benchmarks that provide only patient clinical features, LiteOdyssey achieved state-of-the-art performance, with an overall disease Recall@1 of 59.3% over the combined 1,243 cases of LIRICAL (n = 370) and the PhenoPacket Store (n = 873). Both benchmarks have a high proportion of ultra-rare disease (a prevalence below 1 in 1,000,000, with ultra-rare shares of approximately 45% and 52.8%, respectively). On the more difficult PhenoPacket subset, where causal diseases were not mapped to Orphanet in our rarity-mapping pipeline, LiteOdyssey achieved 60.7% Recall@1, compared with 10.7% for the same baseline model (GPT-5.4) without tools. This performance was achieved without fine-tuning, multi-agent ensembles, or a large case-retrieval database. Gains were also observed in the following: on cases never seen during development, on a private cohort of real-world rare disease patients, and on a smaller open-weights model. LiteOdyssey suggests a path toward rare-disease AI systems that are accurate, easier to deploy, and more transparent for physician review.

AI.tldr: LiteOdyssey achieves state-of-the-art rare-disease diagnosis by extending a single AI agent's reasoning chain with a clinical genetics workflow and public biomedical tools, without requiring fine-tuning, multi-agent ensembles, or large retrieval databases.
AI.motivation: Scaling medical AI systems (more data, agents, retrieval) is difficult for rare-disease diagnosis due to deployment, audit, and maintenance challenges. The authors investigate whether extending a single agent's reasoning chain can achieve SOTA performance instead.
AI.method: LiteOdyssey is a lightweight framework that guides a reasoning language model through a clinical genetics workflow, developed via Policy Iteration with Human Feedback (PIHF), with dynamic access to public biomedical tools.
AI.result: Achieved 59.3% overall Recall@1 on 1,243 combined cases (LIRICAL + PhenoPacket Store). On the difficult PhenoPacket subset, 60.7% Recall@1 vs 10.7% for GPT-5.4 baseline without tools. Gains held on unseen cases, a private real-world cohort, and a smaller open-weights model.
AI.conclusion: LiteOdyssey demonstrates that focusing on reasoning chain extension via human-AI collaboration yields accurate, transparent, and deployable rare-disease AI without costly scaling of data or model ensembles.

title: WaveSync: Constrained Wavefront Optimization for Synchronized Co-Speech Gestures in Humanoid Robots
summary: Expressive co-speech gestures are crucial for natural human-robot interaction, but generating them on physical humanoid robots is difficult because gesture strokes must align with speech emphasis while satisfying strict kinematic and dynamic constraints. Unlike virtual avatars, humanoid robots cannot freely execute rapid or overlapping motions, making word-level synchronization and hardware-safe motion planning a coupled problem. We present \textbf{WaveSync}, a hybrid framework in which a Large Language Model decomposes dialogue responses into structured semantic schemas and assigns per-word importance weights, constructing a continuous Semantic Importance Wave. Gesture trajectories are shaped through Dynamic Movement Primitives, enforcing kinematic feasibility while enhancing expressiveness. A Wavefront Optimization stage aligns peak-to-peak gesture-speech synchronization and resolves residual kinematic violations through gesture-duration compression and forward propagation. Experimental evaluation based on five dialogue scenarios shows that our method achieves high synchronization accuracy and outperforms three baselines in both objective and subjective evaluations. Each component in WaveSync plays a necessary role in producing gestures that are expressive, semantically grounded, and kinematically compliant. The code, resources, and videos are available at \href{https://github.com/pairs-lab/WaveSync}{WaveSync}

AI.tldr: WaveSync is a hybrid framework that combines LLM-based semantic analysis with Dynamic Movement Primitives and wavefront optimization to generate expressive, kinematically feasible co-speech gestures for humanoid robots, achieving high synchronization accuracy and outperforming baselines in five dialogue scenarios.
AI.motivation: Generating expressive co-speech gestures on physical humanoid robots is challenging because gesture strokes must align with speech emphasis while satisfying strict kinematic and dynamic constraints, unlike virtual avatars which can freely execute rapid or overlapping motions.
AI.method: WaveSync uses an LLM to decompose dialogue into semantic schemas with per-word importance weights forming a Semantic Importance Wave, then shapes gesture trajectories via Dynamic Movement Primitives for kinematic feasibility, followed by Wavefront Optimization for peak-to-peak gesture-speech synchronization and residual kinematic violation resolution through duration compression and forward propagation.
AI.result: In five dialogue scenarios, WaveSync achieves high synchronization accuracy and outperforms three baselines in both objective and subjective evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Each component in WaveSync is necessary for producing gestures that are expressive, semantically grounded, and kinematically compliant, making it an effective solution for hardware-safe co-speech gesture generation on humanoid robots.

title: The Quality-Utility Paradox: Why High-Reward Data Impairs Small Model Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Knowledge distillation from powerful reasoning models is widely used to improve Small Language Models (SLMs) on mathematical reasoning, often assuming that traces with higher reward model scores provide more useful supervision. We identify a counterintuitive \textbf{Quality-Utility Paradox} in mathematical reasoning distillation. Data refined or synthesized by a stronger Oracle obtains higher perceived quality according to reward models, yet consistently underperforms traces generated by the SLM itself and selected through rejection sampling across Qwen2.5, LLaMA-3, and DeepSeek families. Our analysis shows that Oracle refinement couples logical repair with distributional drift away from the SLM's native reasoning distribution. This drift increases the learner's adaptation cost and can outweigh the benefit of improved reasoning logic. To test this mechanism, we introduce \textbf{Style-Aligned Refinement}, which preserves the native trajectory of the SLM while retaining logical repair from the Oracle. This intervention lowers adaptation cost and restores downstream utility. These findings suggest that effective mathematical reasoning distillation should jointly optimize perceived solution quality and learner-data compatibility, rather than relying solely on reward-model scores. The datasets and code are available at https://github.com/Dracoqhl/Quality-Utility-Paradox.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a Quality-Utility Paradox in mathematical reasoning distillation: data refined by stronger Oracles scores higher on reward models but underperforms when used to train SLMs compared to the SLM's own traces selected via rejection sampling. The cause is distributional drift from Oracle refinement, which increases the learner's adaptation cost. Style-Aligned Refinement, which preserves the SLM's native trajectory while fixing logic, restores utility.
AI.motivation: To challenge the common assumption that higher reward model scores necessarily lead to better supervision signals in mathematical reasoning distillation, and to understand why Oracle-refined data underperforms despite higher perceived quality.
AI.method: The authors conduct systematic experiments across Qwen2.5, LLaMA-3, and DeepSeek families, comparing Oracle-refined traces against SLM's own traces selected via rejection sampling. They introduce Style-Aligned Refinement to isolate the effect of logical repair from distributional drift.
AI.result: Oracle refinement couples logical repair with distributional drift away from the SLM's native reasoning distribution. This drift increases adaptation cost and outweighs improved logic. Style-Aligned Refinement, which preserves native trajectory while applying logical repair, lowers adaptation cost and restores downstream utility.
AI.conclusion: Effective mathematical reasoning distillation should jointly optimize perceived solution quality and learner-data compatibility, not rely solely on reward-model scores.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Inner-loop Dynamics Estimator for Aerial Manipulation under Uncertainty
summary: Aerial manipulators enable physical interaction in hard-to-reach environments; however, the combined problem of direct whole-body aerial manipulation under rapid arm motion, payload changes, and related unknown dynamic uncertainty remains a largely unsolved problem. We present a hierarchical control framework that combines Reinforcement Learning (RL) with an inner-loop dynamics estimator to address this problem. The RL outer loop maps desired 6-degrees-of-freedom (DOF) end-effector targets to coordinated whole-body commands, enabling direct task-driven control without relying on a fully accurate coupled dynamic model in the policy layer. An inner loop then tracks these commands while compensating for transient inertial shifts and uncertainty during execution via a dynamics estimator scheme without requiring system model knowledge. We validate the proposed approach on a custom quadrotor equipped with a 3-DoF manipulator through hardware experiments under varying payload conditions. Compared with RL+PID and RL+INDI+PID baselines, the proposed method reduces end-effector tracking error and improves task success rate across the tested hardware conditions. These results show that combining learned whole-body coordination with estimator-based low-level compensation improves the precision and robustness of aerial manipulation under changing operating conditions.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical control framework combining Reinforcement Learning (outer loop) with a dynamics estimator (inner loop) for whole-body aerial manipulation, validated on a quadrotor+3-DoF arm, reducing tracking error and improving robustness under payload changes.
AI.motivation: Aerial manipulators face unsolved challenges in whole-body control under rapid arm motion, payload changes, and unknown dynamic uncertainty; existing methods lack a combined solution for direct task-driven control without full coupled dynamic models.
AI.method: A two-layer hierarchical framework: (1) RL outer loop maps 6-DOF end-effector targets to whole-body commands without a fully accurate coupled model; (2) inner-loop dynamics estimator tracks commands and compensates for inertial shifts and uncertainty without system model knowledge. Validated on a quadrotor with a 3-DoF manipulator in hardware experiments under varying payloads.
AI.result: Compared to RL+PID and RL+INDI+PID baselines, the proposed method reduces end-effector tracking error and improves task success rate across varying payload conditions in real hardware experiments.
AI.conclusion: Combining learned whole-body coordination (RL) with estimator-based low-level compensation improves precision and robustness of aerial manipulation under changing operating conditions.

title: AI Pluralism and the Worlds It Misses
comment: To be presented at the ICML Pluralistic Alignment Workshop
summary: AI pluralism is often framed as a problem of representing diverse values, preferences, users, or outputs. This paper argues that this framing is incomplete because AI systems also impose ontologies: they define what counts as an entity, relation, feature, harm, benefit, and valid form of evidence. We define ontological flattening as the conversion of situated, contested, and historically specific meanings into a restricted technical category, proxy, aggregation rule, or benchmark target that is treated as neutral and difficult to contest. The paper develops a bounded conceptual and qualitative synthesis across value pluralism, pluralistic alignment, participatory and democratic AI, procedural justice, science and technology studies, accountability research, aggregate themes from 11 expert interviews, and three urban AI companion cases. The cases illustrate how pluralistic methods can improve or structure model behavior while still compressing categories, proxies, aggregation rules, and revision rights before affected actors have procedural standing. We introduce Pluralistic Lifecycle Governance (PLG) as a preliminary qualitative audit scaffold for documenting ontological openness, epistemic inclusion, procedural authority, evaluation pluralism, and lifecycle accountability. PLG is not presented as a validated scoring instrument; it is a framework for making the evidence and governance conditions of pluralistic AI explicit.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that AI pluralism must address not just diverse values but also how AI systems impose ontologies—defining what counts as entities, harms, and evidence. It introduces ontological flattening and proposes Pluralistic Lifecycle Governance (PLG), a qualitative audit framework for documenting ontological openness, epistemic inclusion, procedural authority, evaluation pluralism, and lifecycle accountability.
AI.motivation: Current AI pluralism framings focus on representing diverse values, preferences, or outputs but overlook how AI systems impose ontologies—defining what counts as entities, relations, features, harms, benefits, and valid evidence. This incompleteness can lead to ontological flattening, where situated, contested meanings are converted into restricted, seemingly neutral technical categories that are difficult to contest.
AI.method: The paper develops a bounded conceptual and qualitative synthesis across value pluralism, pluralistic alignment, participatory/democratic AI, procedural justice, STS, accountability research, aggregate themes from 11 expert interviews, and three urban AI companion cases.
AI.result: Cases show pluralistic methods can improve model behavior while still compressing categories, proxies, aggregation rules, and revision rights before affected actors have procedural standing. The paper introduces Pluralistic Lifecycle Governance (PLG) as a preliminary qualitative audit scaffold for documenting ontological openness, epistemic inclusion, procedural authority, evaluation pluralism, and lifecycle accountability.
AI.conclusion: PLG is not a validated scoring instrument but a framework for making the evidence and governance conditions of pluralistic AI explicit.

title: PATCH: Action-Chunk-Conditioned Latent Patch Innovation Monitoring for Robot Manipulation
summary: Learning-based manipulation policies have made substantial progress in real-world robot manipulation, particularly for short-horizon action generation. However, deployment in open workspaces remains fragile under unexpected local scene dynamics, such as moving objects, transient occlusions, or disturbances near the intended motion. Existing runtime monitors often rely on global observation anomalies, policy uncertainty, or frame-level visual changes, and struggle to distinguish task-relevant execution risk from benign visual variation. We introduce PATCH, an action-chunk-conditioned latent patch innovation monitor for deployment-time intervention. Given the active action chunk, PATCH defines a projected execution corridor, predicts latent patch evolution inside it, and accumulates persistent residuals unexplained by the robot's own motion. These residuals form a localized intervention signal that allows PATCH-Router to pause execution, select an available recovery source, and resume the original policy once localized innovation subsides. Experiments on real robot rollout data show that PATCH produces more stable and context-relevant triggers than competing runtime monitors. Real-robot deployment further demonstrates monitor-driven intervention and policy resumption for disturbance-aware manipulation. Project Page: https://yananzhou5555.github.io/PATCH/.

AI.tldr: PATCH introduces a runtime monitor for robot manipulation that uses action-chunk-conditioned latent patch innovation to detect localized execution risks, enabling intervention and recovery under unexpected scene dynamics.
AI.motivation: Learning-based manipulation policies struggle in open workspaces due to unexpected local scene dynamics (e.g., moving objects, occlusions, disturbances), and existing runtime monitors cannot effectively distinguish task-relevant execution risk from benign visual variation.
AI.method: PATCH defines a projected execution corridor conditioned on the active action chunk, predicts latent patch evolution inside it, and accumulates persistent residuals unexplained by the robot's motion. PATCH-Router pauses execution, selects a recovery source, and resumes the policy when localized innovation subsides.
AI.result: Experiments on real robot rollout data show PATCH produces more stable and context-relevant triggers than competing runtime monitors. Real-robot deployment demonstrates successful monitor-driven intervention and policy resumption for disturbance-aware manipulation.
AI.conclusion: PATCH provides a localized, action-aware runtime monitoring framework that improves robustness of manipulation policies under dynamic disturbances, outperforming existing global anomaly-based monitors.

title: TimeVista: Exploring and Exploiting Vision-Language Models as Judges for Time Series Forecasting
summary: High-quality time series forecasting is pivotal for real-world decision-making. However, traditional point-wise metrics often fail to reveal complex temporal patterns and align poorly with human intuitive preferences. While the ''LLM-as-a-Judge'' paradigm has revolutionized text evaluation by providing flexible, human-aligned judgment, its application to time series remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we leverage Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as judges for time series forecasting, harnessing their ability to comprehend time series plots grounded in textual information. Specifically, we propose a novel framework integrating micro- and macro-level judgments informed by contextual information to evaluate time series forecasting. To this end, we introduce TimeVista, a comprehensive VLM-as-a-Judge benchmark comprising 5563 time series samples paired with detailed evaluation rubrics. Extensive meta-evaluations demonstrate that VLMs are highly reliable judges, achieving significantly higher consistency with human preferences than conventional metrics. Building upon our benchmark, we comprehensively assess recent Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) under the VLM-as-a-Judge paradigm. Our results demonstrate that VLMs serve as robust and interpretable judges, providing a comprehensive, human-aligned standard for evaluating time series models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as judges for evaluating time series forecasting, introducing the TimeVista benchmark of 5,563 samples. VLMs achieve higher consistency with human preferences than traditional point-wise metrics, offering a more human-aligned evaluation standard.
AI.motivation: Traditional point-wise metrics for time series forecasting fail to capture complex temporal patterns and align poorly with human intuitive preferences, while the "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm has been successful in text evaluation but remains unexplored for time series.
AI.method: The authors propose a VLM-as-a-Judge framework integrating micro- and macro-level judgments informed by contextual information. They introduce TimeVista, a benchmark of 5,563 time series samples with detailed evaluation rubrics, and use VLMs to evaluate Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs).
AI.result: VLMs achieve significantly higher consistency with human preferences compared to conventional point-wise metrics. Meta-evaluations confirm VLMs as highly reliable judges for time series forecasting.
AI.conclusion: VLMs serve as robust and interpretable judges, providing a comprehensive, human-aligned standard for evaluating time series models, outperforming traditional metrics in alignment with human judgment.

title: VENOM: Versatile Embodied Network for Omni-bodied Motion tracking
summary: Achieving expert-level expressive full-body motion tracking across multiple humanoids solely from demonstration data remains a challenging and relatively an underexplored problem in humanoid robot learning. Cross-embodiment motion tracking policies are mostly trained by decoupling the control problem into upper and lower body control. This work proposes VENOM, a cross-embodiment full-body motion tracking model for humanoids in simulation. VENOM is a GPT-based motion tracker trained on multiple humanoid data that can track the entire body without the requirement to split into upper and lower body control. We curate a multi-humanoid motion tracking dataset called the VENOM dataset that contains states, actions, and rewards and train VENOM and the baselines on this dataset. In this letter, we evaluate VENOM's performance against baselines and show that we can achieve a stable motion tracker across different humanoids more capable than an MLP trained on multiple humanoid data with supervised learning alone, and also show that despite lack of reward feedback, VENOM closely matches the tracking capability of experts that were trained using asymmetric-actor critic reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: VENOM is a GPT-based cross-embodiment full-body motion tracking model for humanoids that tracks entire body without splitting control, trained on a curated multi-humanoid dataset, matching expert-level tracking without reward feedback.
AI.motivation: Achieving expert-level expressive full-body motion tracking across multiple humanoids solely from demonstration data remains challenging and underexplored; existing methods decouple control into upper/lower body.
AI.method: VENOM uses a GPT-based architecture as a motion tracker trained on the curated VENOM dataset (containing states, actions, rewards) across multiple humanoid embodiments for full-body tracking without splitting upper/lower body control.
AI.result: VENOM achieves stable motion tracking across different humanoids, outperforms MLP trained with supervised learning on multi-humanoid data, and closely matches expert-level tracking capability of asymmetric-actor critic RL models despite lacking reward feedback.
AI.conclusion: A GPT-based cross-embodiment full-body motion tracker can achieve expert-level performance without reward feedback or decoupled control, offering a simpler training paradigm for multi-humanoid motion tracking.

title: PAL-Bench: Evidence-Grounded Profile Reconstruction from Longitudinal Personal Albums
summary: Longitudinal personal albums are weak-schema multimodal databases: noisy perceptual records whose key facts require joins across faces, text, timestamps, locations, and repeated events. Existing visual, video, document, and lifelog benchmarks test sub-problems, but not album-scale profile reconstruction with social identity binding and evidence citation. Benchmarking this task is difficult because the ground truth needed for evaluation--owner profiles, social graphs, face-name maps, and evidence provenance--is private state that real albums cannot safely release. We introduce PAL-Bench, a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded reconstruction under a public-record contract. Its Evidence Compiler builds latent private worlds, programs target-level evidence paths, renders album pixels, re-measures them through perception pipelines, and exports audited public/private views. Agents receive only perception-derived public records; targets, identifier maps, and evidence paths remain hidden. PAL-Bench contains 50 synthetic users, 36,659 public photo records, and 2,799 targets over owner facts, identities, and relations. A privacy-preserving audit with 10 participants confirms that PAL-Bench evidence structures match real private albums, though equivalent releases remain privacy-prohibitive. Across seven systems and two compute-matched diagnostics, a seven-metric protocol reveals a gap between plausible profile summarization and faithful social reconstruction: systems recover some owner facts but struggle with recurring identities and evidence citation. PAL-TRACE, a reference framework that freezes identity bindings before owner-fact mining, performs best but leaves hard identity resolution far from solved. PAL-Bench provides a testbed for perceptual entity resolution, multimodal data integration, temporal evidence aggregation, and provenance-aware structured prediction.

AI.tldr: PAL-Bench is a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded reconstruction of personal albums, addressing the challenge of evaluating profile reconstruction with social identity binding and evidence citation under privacy constraints. It includes 50 synthetic users, 36,659 public photo records, and 2,799 targets, revealing a gap between plausible summarization and faithful social reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks test sub-problems of personal album analysis but cannot handle album-scale profile reconstruction with social identity binding and evidence citation. Real albums cannot release private ground truth (owner profiles, social graphs, face-name maps, evidence provenance), motivating a controlled benchmark with a public-record contract.
AI.method: The Evidence Compiler builds latent private worlds, programs target-level evidence paths, renders album pixels, re-measures them through perception pipelines, and exports audited public/private views. Agents receive only perception-derived public records; targets, identifier maps, and evidence paths remain hidden. PAL-Bench contains 50 synthetic users, 36,659 public photos, and 2,799 targets over owner facts, identities, and relations.
AI.result: A privacy-preserving audit with 10 participants confirms PAL-Bench evidence structures match real private albums. Seven systems evaluated with a seven-metric protocol show a gap between plausible profile summarization and faithful social reconstruction. PAL-TRACE, which freezes identity bindings before owner-fact mining, performs best but hard identity resolution remains unsolved.
AI.conclusion: PAL-Bench provides a testbed for perceptual entity resolution, multimodal data integration, temporal evidence aggregation, and provenance-aware structured prediction. The benchmark reveals that while systems recover some owner facts, recurring identities and evidence citation remain challenging, and hard identity resolution is far from solved.

title: Pride and Prejudice: Toward an Information-Theoretic Framework for Mutually Communicative Driver Behavior Modeling
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for the IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems (T-ITS), June 2026
summary: Mixed autonomy driving becomes unsafe and inefficient when autonomous vehicles (AVs) and human-driven vehicles (HVs) misread each other's intentions. We study this problem as implicit mutual communication in lane changes. The proposed framework models how the ego vehicle both expresses its intent and probes the other driver's preference under epistemic uncertainty. It combines a level-k Bayesian persuasion game with virtual features for proactive signaling, information-theoretic rewards for mutual communication, and adaptive weights of communication affordances. We further introduce the Pride-Inquiry (P-I) and Pride-Prejudice (P-P) planes to analyze communication intensity and tendency. The model is calibrated with a Communication-Based Multi-Agent Inverse Reinforcement Learning algorithm (C-MIRL) on the naturalistic NGSIM dataset. Compared with the non-communicative baseline, the proposed model reduces the prediction error of mandatory lane changes by up to 20% while maintaining strong generalization. Driver-In-the-Loop questionnaire scores are positively correlated with the calibrated communication variables, supporting the subjective validity of the model. The learned rewards further show that inquiry and listening affordances contribute more than pride and expression alone, and that inquiry preference varies more strongly across drivers. These results support explicit modeling of mutual communication and epistemic uncertainty in interactive driving.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for proactive mutual communication between AVs and HVs during lane changes, using a level-k Bayesian persuasion game with virtual signaling features and information-theoretic rewards, achieving up to 20% reduction in lane change prediction error on NGSIM data.
AI.motivation: Mixed autonomy driving is unsafe and inefficient when AVs and HVs misread each other's intentions during lane changes, motivating the need to model implicit mutual communication under epistemic uncertainty.
AI.method: The framework combines a level-k Bayesian persuasion game with virtual features for proactive signaling, information-theoretic rewards for mutual communication, and adaptive weights of communication affordances. It introduces P-I and P-P planes to analyze communication intensity and tendency. The model is calibrated using C-MIRL on the NGSIM dataset.
AI.result: The model reduces prediction error of mandatory lane changes by up to 20% compared to non-communicative baselines, maintains strong generalization, and shows positive correlation between Driver-In-the-Loop questionnaire scores and calibrated communication variables. Inquiry and listening affordances contribute more than pride and expression alone; inquiry preference varies more strongly across drivers.
AI.conclusion: Explicit modeling of mutual communication and epistemic uncertainty is crucial for interactive driving, with inquiry/listening behaviors being more impactful and variable across drivers than expressive signaling.

title: Measuring Whether LLM Tutors Teach or Solve: A Diagnostic for Educational Impact
summary: Large language models are increasingly proposed as educational tutors, yet stronger task-solving ability does not necessarily imply stronger learning support. Motivated by recent calls to measure the social impact of NLP systems in practice, we study whether public LLM tutoring benchmarks distinguish learning-supportive behavior from mere answer production. We propose a lightweight diagnostic based on the gap between solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented benchmark performance. Using public MathTutorBench leaderboard results, we show that these dimensions are only partially aligned: across eight publicly reported models, the correlation between solving and pedagogy composites is 0.421, and several models shift meaningfully in rank when evaluation moves from solving to pedagogy. We then analyze the public TutorBench sample and show that agency-relevant behaviors are explicitly encoded in benchmark rubrics, especially in active-learning settings that reward guiding questions, calibrated hints, and non-disclosive scaffolding. Together, these findings suggest that educational-impact evaluation should not treat task success as a sufficient proxy for learning support. We argue that public tutoring benchmarks can better support positive-impact evaluation by reporting solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented scores separately and by making disclosure-sensitive, student-agency-preserving criteria more explicit.

AI.tldr: Public LLM tutoring benchmarks show only weak alignment (r=0.421) between solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented performance across eight models, suggesting task success is not a sufficient proxy for learning support. The paper advocates for separate reporting of these dimensions and more explicit disclosure-sensitive evaluation criteria.
AI.motivation: Despite increasing deployment of LLMs as educational tutors, stronger task-solving ability does not guarantee better learning support. The paper addresses the need for practical measurement of educational impact, responding to calls to evaluate the social impact of NLP systems.
AI.method: Proposes a lightweight diagnostic based on the gap between solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented benchmark performance. Uses public MathTutorBench leaderboard data to compute correlations and rank shifts across eight models, and analyzes the TutorBench sample rubric for agency-relevant behaviors.
AI.result: The correlation between solving and pedagogy composites is only 0.421 across eight models. Several models exhibit meaningful rank shifts when moving from solving to pedagogy evaluation. Active-learning rubric criteria reward guiding questions, calibrated hints, and non-disclosive scaffolding.
AI.conclusion: Educational-impact evaluation should not treat task success as a sufficient proxy for learning support. Public tutoring benchmarks should report solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented scores separately and make student-agency-preserving criteria more explicit.

title: DataLadder: A Simulation-Enabled Interconversion Toolchain for the Embodied Data Pyramid
summary: Generalist robot policies require trustworthy evaluation and robot-usable training data, but both are difficult to scale with physical robots alone. Real-robot trials and demonstrations remain the most faithful source of deployment signals, yet they are slow, costly, and hard to reproduce. We present DataLadder, a simulation-enabled interconversion toolchain for human-robot aligned model evaluation and data generation, denoted as Robot $\rightleftharpoons$ Simulation $\rightleftharpoons$ Human. On the one hand, the Robot $\rightarrow$ Simulation $\rightarrow$ Human pathway supports human-robot aligned model evaluation by reconstructing real-robot tabletop organization tasks as calibrated digital twins for scalable evaluation, while using human embodied feedback to inspect and refine the naturalness of simulated motions. On the other hand, the Human $\rightarrow$ Simulation $\rightarrow$ Robot pathway supports human-robot aligned data generation: it lifts ego-centric human demonstrations into simulation, checks them under robot physical constraints, and converts them into robot-centered trajectories, annotations, and visual observations. Together, these pathways use the JoySim simulator as both a scalable evaluation layer and a physical consistency filter for robot data generation. We further package the core reconstruction, simulation, rendering, and realism-augmentation modules as cloud services on JD Cloud, turning the system into reusable infrastructure for robot data generation and model evaluation.

AI.tldr: DataLadder is a simulation-enabled toolchain (Robot ⇌ Simulation ⇌ Human) that supports human-robot aligned model evaluation and data generation for generalist robot policies, using digital twins for scalable evaluation and simulated human demonstrations for training data.
AI.motivation: Real-robot trials and demonstrations are the most faithful source of deployment signals but are slow, costly, and hard to reproduce, creating a bottleneck for both trustworthy evaluation and scalable training data for generalist robot policies.
AI.method: The system has two pathways: (1) Robot→Simulation→Human reconstructs real-robot tabletop tasks as calibrated digital twins for evaluation, with human feedback refining motion naturalness; (2) Human→Simulation→Robot lifts ego-centric human demos into simulation, checks them under robot physical constraints, and converts them into robot-centered trajectories/annotations/visual observations. Both pathways use the JoySim simulator as an evaluation layer and physical consistency filter, packaged as cloud services on JD Cloud.
AI.result: A reusable infrastructure for robot data generation and model evaluation that interconverts between robot and human data via simulation, enabling scalable evaluation and training without exclusive reliance on physical robots.
AI.conclusion: DataLadder effectively bridges the gap between real-robot and simulation-based pipelines by providing a bidirectional toolchain that maintains physical consistency and human alignment, turning simulation into both a scalable evaluation layer and a data generation filter for generalist robot policies.

title: Sensor-Conditioned Representation Learning via Scene-Relevant Observation Quotients
summary: Learned representations in intelligent sensing systems are often evaluated by reconstruction fidelity or downstream prediction accuracy, but these criteria do not specify which latent distinctions are justified by the sensing process. In sensor-conditioned environments, nuisance factors can change measurements without changing the scene, while distinct scenes may be indistinguishable under limited sensing capability. This paper formulates sensor-conditioned representation correctness as preserving sensing-supported scene distinctions while suppressing nuisance-induced and sensor-unsupported variation. We introduce the scene-relevant observation quotient, a representation target induced by sensing-supported distinguishability after nuisance canonicalization, and develop Observation-Quotient Tucker-Structured Autoencoding (OQ-TSAE), a scene-nuisance factorized framework with diagnostics for false distinction, false merge, nuisance sensitivity, and latent ordering consistency. Experiments on a controlled benchmark show that quotient-consistent supervision improves representation-correctness diagnostics over reconstruction-oriented, metric-learning, and contrastive-learning baselines. Sensitivity, perturbation, and ablation studies show the importance of quotient-aligned supervision, reliable quotient relations, and quotient geometry. Complementary real-radar experiments show that a reconstruction-only OQ-TSAE variant retains competitive downstream utility, robustness under observation degradation, and low seed-to-seed variability. These results suggest that sensor-conditioned representations should be evaluated not only by predictive utility, but also by whether their latent geometry preserves sensing-justified scene distinctions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a sensor-conditioned representation learning framework (OQ-TSAE) that evaluates representations by whether they preserve sensing-supported scene distinctions while suppressing nuisance and sensor-unsupported variation, rather than by reconstruction fidelity or prediction accuracy alone.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation criteria (reconstruction fidelity, downstream prediction accuracy) do not specify which latent distinctions are justified by the sensing process, leading to representations that may conflate nuisance variation with scene-relevant information or fail to respect sensor limitations.
AI.method: Formulates sensor-conditioned representation correctness via the scene-relevant observation quotient (induced by sensing-supported distinguishability after nuisance canonicalization) and develops Observation-Quotient Tucker-Structured Autoencoding (OQ-TSAE), a scene-nuisance factorized framework with diagnostics for false distinction, false merge, nuisance sensitivity, and latent ordering consistency.
AI.result: Quotient-consistent supervision improves representation-correctness diagnostics over reconstruction, metric-learning, and contrastive-learning baselines on a controlled benchmark. Real-radar experiments show a reconstruction-only OQ-TSAE variant retains competitive downstream utility, robustness under observation degradation, and low seed-to-seed variability.
AI.conclusion: Sensor-conditioned representations should be evaluated not only by predictive utility but also by whether their latent geometry preserves sensing-justified scene distinctions.
