title: DIFF-IPPO: Diffusion-Based Informative Path Planning with Open-Vocabulary Belief Maps
summary: Exploration and object search require robots to perceive their environment, identify regions of interest, and plan trajectories that improve target-detection likelihood or maximize information gain. Many IPP methods, especially in continuous environmental monitoring, rely on Gaussian-process belief models, while object-search settings often produce complex, multimodal belief maps from semantic or open-vocabulary perception. Global trajectory generation directly conditioned on such non-Gaussian belief maps remains comparatively underexplored. Although diffusion-based planners offer strong capabilities for modeling such distributions, their use in informative path planning remains limited. In this work, we propose DIFF-IPPO, a pipeline that integrates an open-vocabulary belief map generator with a diffusion-based planner for global trajectory generation over belief maps. The method generates trajectories that concentrate sensor coverage over high-belief regions, achieving normalized detection scores between 81.49% and 86.55% across different dataset scenarios. We validate the system in a simulated search-and-rescue scenario where the planner searches candidate building regions to locate a burning building. In this setting, a team of five drones using batched belief-map-conditioned trajectory generation achieves first detections in 3.5 minutes.

AI.tldr: DIFF-IPPO integrates an open-vocabulary belief map generator with a diffusion-based planner for global trajectory generation in informative path planning, achieving normalized detection scores of 81.49%-86.55% and enabling a drone team to detect a burning building in 3.5 minutes in a simulated search-and-rescue scenario.
AI.motivation: Global trajectory generation directly conditioned on non-Gaussian, multimodal belief maps (e.g., from open-vocabulary perception) remains underexplored. Diffusion-based planners, despite their capability to model such distributions, are rarely used in informative path planning.
AI.method: DIFF-IPPO pipeline: (1) an open-vocabulary belief map generator to produce multimodal belief maps, (2) a diffusion-based planner that generates global trajectories conditioned on these belief maps, concentrating sensor coverage over high-belief regions.
AI.result: Normalized detection scores of 81.49%–86.55% across different dataset scenarios. In a simulated search-and-rescue task, a team of five drones using batched belief-map-conditioned trajectory generation achieves first detections in 3.5 minutes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed diffusion-based approach effectively handles non-Gaussian belief maps for informative path planning, outperforming in object-search and environmental monitoring tasks, with demonstrated real-world applicability in multi-drone search-and-rescue.

title: Latent Thought Flow: Efficient Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on intermediate reasoning, yet explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) suffers from a linguistic space bottleneck: each thought must be decoded into tokens, causing high inference overhead. Latent reasoning moves deliberation into continuous space, but existing methods mostly learn deterministic or reward-maximizing paths, lacking a principled way to allocate probability across trajectories with different correctness and costs. We propose Latent Thought Flow (LTF), which models reasoning as variable-length continuous trajectories and trains a sampler to match a reward-induced posterior over answer quality and computation cost. We instantiate this with a continuous GFlowNet using stochastic latent transitions. To handle sparse answer supervision, we introduce an Entropy-Weighted Subtrajectory Balance objective for intermediate rewards and a reference-prior regularizer to anchor exploration. Experiments under finetuning and transfer learning settings show that LTF outperforms explicit CoT and latent reasoning baselines, improving accuracy by 9.5% while reducing reasoning length by 27.2% on average compared with strong latent reasoning baselines.

AI.tldr: LTF models latent reasoning as variable-length continuous trajectories trained with GFlowNet to match a reward-induced posterior balancing accuracy and cost, outperforming CoT and latent reasoning baselines with 9.5% higher accuracy and 27.2% shorter reasoning.
AI.motivation: Explicit CoT suffers from linguistic space bottleneck (high inference overhead from token decoding), while existing latent reasoning methods learn deterministic or reward-maximizing paths without principled allocation of probability across trajectories with different correctness and costs.
AI.method: LTF models reasoning as variable-length continuous trajectories with a continuous GFlowNet using stochastic latent transitions. Introduces Entropy-Weighted Subtrajectory Balance objective for intermediate rewards and a reference-prior regularizer to anchor exploration.
AI.result: Outperforms explicit CoT and latent reasoning baselines under finetuning and transfer learning settings, improving accuracy by 9.5% while reducing reasoning length by 27.2% on average compared with strong latent reasoning baselines.
AI.conclusion: LTF provides a principled probabilistic framework for latent reasoning that jointly optimizes for correctness and computational cost, demonstrating superior efficiency and accuracy over existing reasoning paradigms.

title: SoK: Security and Privacy of Foundation-Model-Powered Robots
summary: Foundation models are reshaping robotics by enabling robots to interpret open-ended instructions, reason over multimodal contexts, and operate in complex, open-world environments. However, their integration also introduces security and privacy (S&P) risks that extend beyond the FMs themselves to embodied execution pipelines, supporting ecosystems, and broader governance impacts. Existing literature reviews provide valuable insights but often focus on specific FM types, risk categories, mitigation strategies, or trust boundaries. Consequently, the field lacks a unified structure for analyzing where risks originate, how they propagate across robotic systems, and where mitigations should intervene. To address this gap, we propose a progressive F-E-S-G structural boundary framework for analyzing the S&P of FM-powered robots. The framework comprises four layers: the Foundation model layer (F), Embodied system layer (E), Supporting ecosystem layer (S), and Governance impact layer (G). Building on this structure, we develop a multi-level taxonomy that organizes prior studies along three levels: F-E-S-G trust boundary, security-privacy concerns, and risk-mitigation perspectives. We further annotate each study using fine-grained coding attributes, including target, lifecycle stage, mechanism, system access, and effect. Guided by this framework and taxonomy, we systematize 96 papers. Our analysis uncovers multiple threat patterns, defense mismatches, and evaluation gaps that are difficult to identify from a single-boundary perspective. Based on these findings, we identify open challenges and future directions to provide a research agenda for developing secure, privacy-preserving, and responsibly governed FM-powered robotic systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a progressive F-E-S-G (Foundation model, Embodied system, Supporting ecosystem, Governance) structural boundary framework to systematically analyze security and privacy risks in foundation-model-powered robots, systematizing 96 papers to identify threat patterns, defense mismatches, and evaluation gaps.
AI.motivation: Existing literature reviews on security and privacy of FM-powered robots are fragmented, focusing on specific FM types, risk categories, or trust boundaries, lacking a unified structure to analyze where risks originate, how they propagate, and where mitigations should intervene.
AI.method: The authors propose a four-layer F-E-S-G framework (Foundation model, Embodied system, Supporting ecosystem, Governance) and develop a multi-level taxonomy with three levels: F-E-S-G trust boundary, security-privacy concerns, and risk-mitigation perspectives. They annotate 96 papers using fine-grained coding attributes (target, lifecycle stage, mechanism, system access, effect) and systematize them through this lens.
AI.result: The analysis uncovers multiple threat patterns, defense mismatches, and evaluation gaps that are difficult to identify from a single-boundary perspective, revealing systemic issues in how S&P risks propagate across the FM-powered robotic pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The authors identify open challenges and future directions, providing a research agenda for developing secure, privacy-preserving, and responsibly governed FM-powered robotic systems.

title: SpecAlign: Efficient Specification-Grounded Alignment of Large Language Models via Synthetic Data
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, alignment is no longer governed by a single universal notion of safety or helpfulness, but instead by provider- or application-specific model specifications. These specifications are typically long, structured, and frequently updated, yet existing alignment pipelines lack a systematic mechanism to operationalize them as training signals. In this paper, we propose specification-grounded alignment, a new alignment paradigm that treats provider-authored model specifications as the primary alignment target rather than abstract principles or static benchmarks. To instantiate this paradigm, we introduce SpecAlign, a framework that synthesizes alignment data directly from specification documents. SpecAlign combines structured rule annotation, controllable specification instantiation, and multi-agent adversarial data synthesis to generate fine-grained, boundary-aware preference pairs that capture both compliant behaviors and meaningful specification violations. Experiments across multiple model specifications and backbone models demonstrate that training with SpecAlign consistently improves rule compliance while preserving general capabilities and avoiding over-conservative behavior. These results suggest that grounding alignment in explicit model specifications enables rapid, precise, and scalable adaptation of LLM behavior to evolving policy requirements.

AI.tldr: SpecAlign is a framework for specification-grounded alignment that synthesizes fine-grained preference data directly from provider-authored model specification documents, enabling LLMs to comply with complex, evolving policy requirements without sacrificing general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing alignment pipelines lack a systematic mechanism to operationalize provider-specific, frequently updated model specifications as training signals, as alignment is no longer governed by a single universal notion of safety or helpfulness.
AI.method: SpecAlign combines three components: structured rule annotation, controllable specification instantiation, and multi-agent adversarial data synthesis to generate fine-grained, boundary-aware preference pairs covering both compliant behaviors and meaningful specification violations.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple model specifications and backbone models show that training with SpecAlign consistently improves rule compliance while preserving general capabilities and avoiding over-conservative behavior.
AI.conclusion: Grounding alignment in explicit model specifications enables rapid, precise, and scalable adaptation of LLM behavior to evolving policy requirements.

title: ATOM-Bench: A Real-World Benchmark for Atomic Skills and Compositional Generalization in Manipulation Policies
summary: Generalist manipulation policies are increasingly presented as foundation models for robotic control, but their real-world generalization remains difficult to diagnose. A policy may succeed on demonstrated tasks while still failing to execute fine-grained atomic skills or recombine learned skills in new task structures. We introduce \textbf{ATOM-Bench}, a real-world benchmark for evaluating both atomic skills and compositional generalization in manipulation policies. ATOM-Bench factorizes tabletop manipulation into motor atoms and instruction atoms, and contains 30 atomic tasks and 24 held-out compositional tasks across paired single-arm and dual-arm robot tracks. We collect 3,000 human demonstrations for atomic fine-tuning and release both the demonstration data and evaluation rollout data to support reproducible real-world evaluation. Policies are fine-tuned on atomic tasks and evaluated on both atomic skill acquisition and held-out compositional tasks. We further introduce Atomic Score (AS) and Compositional Failure Share (CFS) to distinguish failures caused by weak atomic skills from failures caused by limited compositional reuse. Through 2,700 physical rollouts on five representative manipulation policies, we find that current policies can acquire simple instruction-grounding skills, but still struggle with fine-grained motor atoms, counting, and logical filtering. More importantly, strong atomic performance does not reliably transfer to held-out compositional tasks. ATOM-Bench provides a diagnostic testbed for studying whether failures arise from weak motor execution, poor instruction grounding, or limited compositional reuse.

AI.tldr: ATOM-Bench is a real-world benchmark with 30 atomic tasks and 24 compositional tasks across single-arm and dual-arm tracks, used to evaluate manipulation policies' atomic skill acquisition and compositional generalization through 2,700 physical rollouts. It introduces Atomic Score (AS) and Compositional Failure Share (CFS) metrics to distinguish failure sources.
AI.motivation: Current generalist manipulation policies lack diagnostic evaluation methods to determine whether failures stem from weak atomic skill execution or limited compositional reuse of learned skills in novel task structures.
AI.method: ATOM-Bench factorizes tabletop manipulation into motor atoms and instruction atoms, comprising 30 atomic tasks and 24 held-out compositional tasks for single-arm and dual-arm robot tracks. It collects 3,000 human demonstrations for atomic fine-tuning, evaluates policies on atomic skill acquisition and compositional tasks, and uses AS and CFS metrics to diagnose failure sources.
AI.result: Through 2,700 physical rollouts on five manipulation policies, current policies can acquire simple instruction-grounding skills but struggle with fine-grained motor atoms, counting, and logical filtering. Strong atomic performance does not reliably transfer to held-out compositional tasks.
AI.conclusion: ATOM-Bench serves as a diagnostic testbed to identify whether manipulation policy failures arise from weak motor execution, poor instruction grounding, or limited compositional reuse, revealing critical gaps in current generalist robotic policies.

title: State-Grounded Multi-Agent Synthetic Data Generation for Tool-Augmented LLMs
summary: Training tool-augmented LLM agents requires large corpora of multi-turn, tool-grounded conversational data that is expensive to annotate, privacy-constrained in production settings, and largely absent from public datasets. We present StateGen, a synthetic data generation platform that produces scored, reasoning-trace-rich training conversations by orchestrating a four-role LLM loop: a persona-conditioned user simulator, an agent under test, a state-grounded tool simulator, and a multi-axis LLM judge. The key architectural contribution is an authoritative state manager that maintains a structured world-state object across turns, enforcing a backend-is-truth invariant that eliminates the dominant class of tool-call hallucinations by construction. StateGen extends naturally to hierarchical multi-agent settings by declaring sub-agents as tools, all sharing a single state object. We report results on 64,698 evaluated conversations across three production corpora: tool-call hallucination scores reach 9.66/10, the system supports persona-driven variation via a 23-dimensional trait vector, and a cleanly separated train and golden evaluation set split confirms the data is not memorization bait (per-criterion gap analysis). Comparison with eight external systems shows that no single publicly available platform combines multi-turn generation, state-grounded tool simulation, hierarchical multi-agent support, and built-in judge scoring.

AI.tldr: StateGen is a synthetic data generation platform that produces scored, reasoning-trace-rich training conversations for tool-augmented LLM agents using a four-role LLM loop with an authoritative state manager that eliminates tool-call hallucinations by enforcing a backend-is-truth invariant.
AI.motivation: Training tool-augmented LLM agents requires large corpora of multi-turn, tool-grounded conversational data that is expensive to annotate, privacy-constrained in production settings, and largely absent from public datasets.
AI.method: StateGen orchestrates a four-role LLM loop (persona-conditioned user simulator, agent under test, state-grounded tool simulator, multi-axis LLM judge) with an authoritative state manager maintaining a structured world-state object across turns, enforcing a backend-is-truth invariant. Extends to hierarchical multi-agent settings by declaring sub-agents as tools sharing a single state object.
AI.result: Evaluated on 64,698 conversations across three production corpora: tool-call hallucination scores of 9.66/10, persona-driven variation via a 23-dimensional trait vector, clean train/eval split confirming no memorization issues. Comparison shows no other public platform combines all four capabilities (multi-turn generation, state-grounded tool simulation, hierarchical multi-agent support, built-in judge scoring).
AI.conclusion: StateGen uniquely provides comprehensive synthetic data generation for tool-augmented LLM agents with strong hallucination elimination and persona variation capabilities, filling a gap in existing public platforms.

title: Video-Based Optimal Transport for Feedback-Efficient Offline Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Conveying complex objectives to reinforcement learning (RL) agents often requires meticulous reward engineering. Preference-based RL (PbRL) offers a promising alternative by learning reward functions from human feedback, but its scalability is hindered by high labeling costs. Inspired by advances in Video Foundation Models (ViFMs), we present Video-based Optimal Transport Preference (VOTP), a semi-supervised framework that learns effective reward functions from only a handful of labels. By leveraging optimal transport to align visual trajectories within the rich representation space of ViFMs, VOTP effectively generates high-fidelity pseudo-labels for large amounts of unlabeled data, substantially reducing human supervision. Extensive experiments across locomotion and manipulation benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of VOTP, which outperforms state-of-the-art offline PbRL methods under limited feedback budgets. We also showcase the robustness of VOTP in the presence of visual distractors and validate its utility on real robotic tasks, where it learns meaningful rewards with minimal human input.

AI.tldr: VOTP is a semi-supervised preference-based RL framework that uses Video Foundation Models and optimal transport to generate pseudo-labels, enabling effective reward learning from minimal human feedback, outperforming prior methods on locomotion, manipulation, and real robotic tasks.
AI.motivation: Preference-based RL reduces the need for reward engineering but suffers from high labeling costs; the authors aim to scale PbRL by drastically reducing human supervision requirements.
AI.method: VOTP leverages Video Foundation Models (ViFMs) for rich video representations and uses optimal transport to align visual trajectories, generating high-fidelity pseudo-labels for unlabeled data in a semi-supervised manner.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art offline PbRL methods under limited feedback budgets on locomotion and manipulation benchmarks; shows robustness to visual distractors and effectiveness on real robotic tasks with minimal human input.
AI.conclusion: Video-based optimal transport alignment with ViFMs enables scalable, label-efficient preference-based RL, reducing human annotation burden while maintaining reward quality.

title: Architectural Wisdom: A Framework for Governing Optimization in AI Systems
summary: Modern AI systems exhibit structural failures that capability scaling alone does not reliably fix: they optimize under-specified objectives with no architectural mechanism to question whether the objective should be optimized at all. Engagement maximization can amplify harmful pathways; tool-using agents can commit irreversible actions; preference-trained language models can become sycophantic. We argue that this failure is a wisdom problem, not an intelligence problem. We use "wisdom" in a deliberately architectural sense, not as a claim about virtue, consciousness, or moral omniscience. Intelligence accepts a goal and optimizes within it; wisdom interrogates whether the goal should be optimized at all. The two are separable architectural properties. We propose architectural wisdom as a corrigible objective-governance layer above the optimization substrate. The layer makes three structural commitments explicit and nondegenerate before any action: temporal horizon, relational boundary, and irreversibility. It is realized by four components (Structural Utility Transform, Moral Admissibility Interface, Arbitration and Escalation Controller, Value Revision Channel) that compute a six-coordinate wisdom tuple over horizon, relational coverage, irreversibility, admissibility, value revision, and auditability. We motivate the architecture by eight cases drawn from contemporary AI failures, secular wisdom traditions, and hard ethical situations, and defend the distinction against the intelligence-completeness thesis using goal-questioning over goal-taking, Bostrom's orthogonality, structural separation in our exemplar cases, and persistent failure modes despite capability scaling. The framework is the conceptual contract for a larger architecture whose formal specifications and empirical validation are developed in subsequent work.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that modern AI failures stem from a lack of architectural wisdom—a corrigible governance layer that interrogates whether goals should be optimized—rather than insufficient intelligence, and proposes a four-component framework producing a six-coordinate wisdom tuple (horizon, relational coverage, irreversibility, admissibility, value revision, auditability) as a separable layer above the optimization substrate.
AI.motivation: Modern AI systems exhibit structural failures (e.g., engagement amplification, irreversible tool-use actions, sycophancy) that capability scaling does not reliably fix, suggesting the problem is not insufficient intelligence but a lack of architectural mechanisms to question whether an objective should be optimized at all.
AI.method: The paper introduces architectural wisdom as a corrigible objective-governance layer above the optimization substrate, with three structural commitments (temporal horizon, relational boundary, irreversibility) realized by four components: Structural Utility Transform, Moral Admissibility Interface, Arbitration and Escalation Controller, and Value Revision Channel, which compute a six-coordinate wisdom tuple.
AI.result: The framework is conceptually motivated by eight cases from contemporary AI failures, secular wisdom traditions, and hard ethical situations. The intelligence-completeness thesis is challenged using goal-questioning vs. goal-taking, Bostrom's orthogonality thesis, structural separation in exemplar cases, and persistent failure modes despite capability scaling.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that intelligence and wisdom are separable architectural properties, and that a corrigible objective-governance layer is necessary to address structural AI failures. This framework serves as the conceptual contract for subsequent formal specification and empirical validation work.

title: ExoTraj: A General Lower-limb Exoskeleton Assistance Policy for Complex Environments
summary: Adaptive torque prediction in dynamic exoskeleton scenarios requires expensive motion capture systems, which are infeasible in complex outdoor environments. Trajectory prediction has emerged as one of the effective approaches to address such an issue. However, the core challenges of exoskeleton trajectory prediction are twofold: establishing the mapping from multi-modal features to trajectory information; constructing the mapping from trajectory to torque. For the former, most existing methods perform only single-step prediction and neglect inter-subject trajectory variability, thereby limiting the trajectory optimization space and prediction generalization. To address this, this paper proposes a fast flow matching method that enables accurate trajectory prediction and better generalization for real-time performance, where trajectory generation errors and encoded observations are used to guide the training direction. For the second challenge, due to the high dynamics of the human-robot system and the strong coupling between perception and control, simple control methods struggle to achieve efficient assistance based on the predicted trajectory. This paper utilizes model predictive control and designs a novel optimization objective to optimize torque, ensuring the exoskeleton achieves comfortable and robust assistance. By integrating the above two components, the unified policy, denoted as ExoTraj, is developed to enable adaptive assistance in complex outdoor scenarios without high data acquisition cost. Experimental results show that compared to traditional methods, ExoTraj reduces cross-subject prediction error by 14.0% during the online phase and maintains robustness against external noise. Relative to the zero torque condition, ExoTraj decreases metabolic rate by 11.5-24.4%, heart rate by 1.7-19.5%, and peak muscle activation levels by 10.9-41.3%, respectively.

AI.tldr: ExoTraj proposes a fast flow matching method for trajectory prediction and model predictive control with a novel optimization objective for torque prediction, enabling adaptive exoskeleton assistance in complex outdoor scenarios without expensive motion capture. It reduces cross-subject prediction error by 14.0%, metabolic rate by 11.5-24.4%, heart rate by 1.7-19.5%, and peak muscle activation by 10.9-41.3%.
AI.motivation: Adaptive torque prediction in dynamic exoskeleton scenarios requires expensive motion capture systems that are infeasible in complex outdoor environments. Existing trajectory prediction methods perform only single-step prediction and neglect inter-subject trajectory variability, limiting optimization space and generalization. Simple control methods struggle with high dynamics and strong coupling in human-robot systems.
AI.method: 1) Fast flow matching method for accurate trajectory prediction with better generalization, using trajectory generation errors and encoded observations to guide training. 2) Model predictive control with a novel optimization objective to optimize torque for comfortable and robust assistance. The unified policy is called ExoTraj.
AI.result: ExoTraj reduces cross-subject prediction error by 14.0% during online phase, maintains robustness against external noise, decreases metabolic rate by 11.5-24.4%, heart rate by 1.7-19.5%, and peak muscle activation levels by 10.9-41.3% relative to zero torque condition.
AI.conclusion: ExoTraj enables adaptive assistance in complex outdoor scenarios without high data acquisition cost, outperforming traditional methods in both prediction accuracy and biomechanical efficiency.

title: AdaSTORM: Scaling LLM Reasoning on Dynamic Graphs via Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable potential in dynamic graph reasoning, but suffer from a scaling bottleneck: current models can only handle graphs with tens of nodes, constrained by exponential reasoning overhead and finite context windows. While multi-agent systems (MAS) offer collective reasoning and topology-aware orchestration, capabilities naturally suited for graph-structured tasks, their application to dynamic graphs remains unexplored. This paper presents Scaling LLM Reasoning on Dynamic Graphs via Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Multi-Agent Collaboration (AdaSTORM), a framework that reformulates large-scale dynamic graph reasoning into two stages: (i) Adaptive Partitioning, partitioning large-scale dynamic graphs into subregions that match the model's reasoning capacity while minimizing inference cost; and (ii) Collaborative Reasoning, aligning graph partition topologies with a spatio-temporal decoupled multi-agent architecture. AdaSTORM is the first multi-agent framework tailored for dynamic graph reasoning. Extensive experiments show that AdaSTORM successfully breaks through the scaling bottleneck, scaling reasoning to thousand-node graphs with over 90% accuracy across several large-scale dynamic graph settings without external tools, significantly outperforms seven competitive baselines. Furthermore, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on existing benchmarks and generalizes robustly to real-world datasets. The source code is available at: https://github.com/irisorchid107/AdaSTORM/.

AI.tldr: AdaSTORM is a multi-agent framework that scales LLM reasoning on dynamic graphs to thousands of nodes via adaptive partitioning and spatio-temporal multi-agent collaboration, achieving >90% accuracy without external tools.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with dynamic graph reasoning due to exponential reasoning overhead and finite context windows, limiting them to graphs with only tens of nodes. Multi-agent systems have collective reasoning capabilities suited for graph tasks but have not been applied to dynamic graphs.
AI.method: AdaSTORM reformulates large-scale dynamic graph reasoning into two stages: (i) Adaptive Partitioning, which partitions large graphs into subregions matching model capacity while minimizing inference cost; and (ii) Collaborative Reasoning, which aligns partition topologies with a spatio-temporal decoupled multi-agent architecture.
AI.result: Scales reasoning to thousand-node graphs with over 90% accuracy across several large-scale dynamic graph settings without external tools; significantly outperforms seven competitive baselines; achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on existing benchmarks and robust generalization to real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: AdaSTORM is the first multi-agent framework tailored for dynamic graph reasoning, successfully breaking through the scaling bottleneck of LLMs on dynamic graphs.

title: SGM-SLAM: Scene Graph Matching for Data-Efficient Distributed SLAM
summary: We introduce a data-efficient distributed Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) framework designed for a team of robots equipped with LiDAR, cameras, and inertial sensors. Our framework uses scene graph matching to identify inter-robot measurement constraints. Unlike prior approaches that rely on feature-level matching, our framework is the first to perform scene graph matching using only object labels and centroids. Our approach constructs a scene graph by using fused RGB-LiDAR point clouds to generate both a semantically segmented point cloud layer, and a layer of discrete bounded objects, to accompany estimated robot trajectories. Scene graph matching is performed collaboratively through exchanging and matching object data with neighboring robots. To maximize communication efficiency, we utilize a multi-step data exchange and optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach using both simulation and real-world datasets collected by legged robots in indoor and outdoor environments.

AI.tldr: A data-efficient distributed SLAM framework for multi-robot systems that uses scene graph matching with only object labels and centroids (no feature-level matching) to identify inter-robot constraints, leveraging fused RGB-LiDAR point clouds for semantic segmentation and object layers.
AI.motivation: To enable data-efficient collaborative SLAM for teams of robots (legged robots with LiDAR, cameras, and inertial sensors) without relying on computationally expensive feature-level matching or sharing raw sensor data.
AI.method: Constructs scene graphs from fused RGB-LiDAR point clouds with two layers: a semantically segmented point cloud layer and a discrete bounded objects layer. Inter-robot constraints are identified via scene graph matching using only object labels and centroids, followed by a multi-step data exchange and optimization process for communication efficiency.
AI.result: Demonstrated effectiveness and efficiency in both simulation and real-world datasets collected by legged robots in indoor and outdoor environments.
AI.conclusion: Scene graph matching using only object labels and centroids is sufficient for data-efficient distributed SLAM, eliminating the need for feature-level matching while maintaining performance.

title: Exploiting Search in Symbolic Numeric Planning with Patterns
comment: Under Review at the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research
summary: In this paper, we present a procedure for numeric planning based on Symbolic Pattern Planning (SPP). Given a numeric planning problem $Π$, a pattern $\prec$ is a sequence of actions used to define a formula encoding the subsequences of $\prec$ executable from a starting state $S$. Cardellini, Giunchiglia, and Maratea (2024a) follow the Planning as Satisfiability approach by defining, at each step $n \ge 0$, a formula $Π^\prec_n$ in which $(i)$ the pattern $\prec$ is computed only for $n=0$ in the initial state $I$ of $Π$, and then exploited at each step $n$, $(ii)$ the starting state $S$ is set to $I$, and $(iii)$ the set $G$ of goals is required to hold in the last state that can be reached by one of the subsequences of $\prec$ concatenated $n$ times. The procedure begins with $n=0$, terminates as soon as $Π^\prec_n$ is satisfiable, and otherwise proceeds by incrementing $n$. In this paper, possibly at each step, $(i)$ we symbolically search for an intermediate state $P$ reachable from $I$, closer to a goal state, $(ii)$ dynamically recompute the pattern $\prec_h$ -- to be used in the next step -- in $P$, $(iii)$ refine the pattern $\prec_g$ used to reach $P$, and $(iv)$ start the new search from the state $S$ which can be either the initial state $I$ or the last computed intermediate state $P$, exploiting the computed patterns $\prec_g$ and $\prec_h$ to define the pattern $\prec$ to be used in the search. In particular, at each step, we define a formula $Π^{\prec}_{S,P}$ encoding the existence of a state $P'$ closer than $P$ to a goal state, with $P'$ reachable from the starting state $S$ when using the pattern $\prec$. We present different techniques for producing such formulas, each corresponding to a different strategy for exploring the search space. We prove their correctness and completeness, the latter under certain conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Symbolic Pattern Planning (SPP) for numeric planning by dynamically recomputing patterns during search, using intermediate states to iteratively refine both the pattern used to reach a state and the pattern for future search, resulting in multiple strategies for exploring the search space.
AI.motivation: Prior SPP work (Cardellini et al., 2024a) computes the pattern only once in the initial state and reuses it statically, which may be suboptimal when the pattern becomes less relevant as the search progresses. The authors aim to improve efficiency by allowing pattern recomputation based on intermediate states reached during search.
AI.method: At each step n, the procedure (i) symbolically searches for an intermediate state P reachable from I and closer to a goal; (ii) dynamically recomputes a new pattern \prec_h in P for the next step; (iii) refines the pattern \prec_g used to reach P; (iv) starts the next search from either I or P, combining \prec_g and \prec_h to form \prec. They define formulas Π^{≺}_{S,P} encoding existence of a state P' closer to goals than P, reachable from S using pattern \prec. Multiple formula variants correspond to different search strategies.
AI.result: The paper proves correctness of the proposed techniques, and completeness under certain conditions. It presents multiple strategies for exploring the search space, each corresponding to a different encoding of the formula Π^{≺}_{S,P}.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic pattern recomputation and intermediate state guidance improve the original SPP framework, with theoretical guarantees for correctness and conditional completeness.

title: LOPAL: Local Performance-Aware Active Learning from Imperfect Demonstrations
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RAL), 2026
summary: Learning from Demonstration (LfD) enables intuitive robot skill acquisition by allowing robots to learn directly from human task demonstrations. However, current methods often fail to address the fact that due to suboptimal and inconsistent human behavior, the quality of the demonstration can vary within each demonstration. Therefore, we introduce LOPAL (LOcal Performance-aware Active Learning), an active learning approach that leverages this local demonstration quality information. Our approach consists of two synergistic components. First, a local performance-driven LfD method uses a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to encode both the demonstrated trajectories and their associated local quality assessments. This enables the generation of trajectories that outperform the imperfect demonstrations by utilizing complementary local data of high performance. Second, active data acquisition allows to improve beyond the imperfect demonstrations by collecting additional informative samples. In areas missing good data, the user is actively requested to provide corrections through a shared autonomy (SA) mechanism, while the robot autonomously executes the learned behavior. The efficacy of LOPAL was validated in both a simulation and a real-world experiment. The results from a real-world pipe inspection task showed that the proposed approach can achieve up to 27.31 % improvement in task performance while also reducing the effort required to collect the demonstrations.

AI.tldr: LOPAL introduces a local performance-aware active learning approach for Learning from Demonstration that accounts for varying demonstration quality, using a GMM-based method to leverage high-quality local data and active data acquisition with shared autonomy for corrections, achieving up to 27.31% improvement in a real-world pipe inspection task.
AI.motivation: Existing LfD methods fail to address that human demonstrations contain locally varying quality due to suboptimal and inconsistent behavior, limiting robot performance when learning from imperfect demonstrations.
AI.method: Two synergistic components: (1) Local performance-driven LfD using GMM to encode trajectories with local quality assessments; (2) Active data acquisition requesting user corrections via shared autonomy where good data is missing, with autonomous execution of learned behavior.
AI.result: Up to 27.31% improvement in task performance on a real-world pipe inspection task, with reduced demonstration collection effort.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging local demonstration quality information through active learning can outperform imperfect demonstrations while reducing human effort in data collection.

title: Phase-Aware Guidance Injection for Recurrent MAPPO in Assembly-Line Disruption Recovery
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, accepted by the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (CASE 2026)
summary: Disruption recovery in industrial assembly lines requires timely decisions under machine faults, worker absence, and emergency orders. Existing methods either rely on rigid handcrafted recovery logic or learn adaptive policies that do not readily exploit heterogeneous external recovery knowledge at decision time to reduce abnormal recovery time (ART) and preserve on-time delivery (OTD). To address this gap, we propose a phase-aware guidance injection framework that augments a trained recurrent MAPPO (RMAPPO) scheduling policy through logit-level action bias during evaluation. The framework provides a unified decision-time interface for rule-based, replay-based, and online LLM-based guidance, while activating intervention only during abnormal and recovery phases. Experiments on a custom AssemblyLineEnv show that high-quality rule guidance yields the strongest gains, replay-based guidance degrades smoothly under imperfect availability, and online LLM guidance still provides useful intermediate improvements. These results show that decision-time guidance injection can exploit heterogeneous recovery hints without redesigning the actor.

AI.tldr: A phase-aware guidance injection framework augments RMAPPO scheduling policies with heterogeneous external knowledge (rules, replay, LLM) during assembly line disruption recovery, improving ART and OTD without policy redesign.
AI.motivation: Existing disruption recovery methods in industrial assembly lines rely on rigid handcrafted logic or adaptive policies that cannot exploit heterogeneous external recovery knowledge at decision time to reduce abnormal recovery time (ART) and preserve on-time delivery (OTD).
AI.method: A phase-aware guidance injection framework that augments a trained RMAPPO scheduling policy via logit-level action bias during evaluation, providing a unified decision-time interface for rule-based, replay-based, and online LLM-based guidance, with intervention activated only during abnormal and recovery phases.
AI.result: High-quality rule guidance yields strongest gains; replay-based guidance degrades smoothly under imperfect availability; online LLM guidance provides useful intermediate improvements on a custom AssemblyLineEnv.
AI.conclusion: Decision-time guidance injection can exploit heterogeneous recovery hints without redesigning the actor policy.

title: Binary Tracking for Spatial QA and Navigation with Open Vision-Language Models
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 15 tables. Project page: https://ndb796.github.io/BinaryTracking ; Code and dataset: https://github.com/ndb796/BinaryTracking
summary: This work addresses spatial question answering for service robots traversing long egocentric routes. Given a query such as "where can I find a dry cleaner on the way back home?", the system returns a metric coordinate that downstream navigation components can act on. Prior Spatial Question Answering approaches leverage retrieval-augmented agents built on closed-source models such as GPT-4o for path exploration. However, robots operating in the real world often cannot reliably depend on online closed-source models due to network instability, communication latency, and deployment cost. It creates a need for open-source based Spatial Question Answering approaches that can run onboard the robot, yet prior research in this direction remains limited. This work proposes BinTrack, a simple yet effective, fully open-source spatial-localization agent that leverages the temporal ordering of a robot's trajectory. BinTrack performs a binary search over the trajectory segments between two anchor landmarks identified from a query. It improves overall accuracy by up to 22.8% over other open-source implementations and even matches the reported closed-source model result on the global category of the SpaceLocQA benchmark, the most challenging setting that has so far required strong reasoning agents such as GPT-4o. Furthermore, its optimized inference strategy consistently yields more than a 1.5x inference speedup over previous approaches. Finally, this work releases GangnamLoop, a novel and practical multi-trip outdoor benchmark collected by deploying a real quadruped robot on public streets with the anonymization policy. It revisits the same locations under different outdoor conditions and pairs the robot's low viewpoint with the human owner's. The source codes and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/ndb796/BinaryTracking

AI.tldr: BinTrack is a fully open-source spatial question answering system for service robots that uses binary search over trajectory segments to answer location queries, achieving up to 22.8% accuracy improvement over other open-source methods and matching GPT-4o performance on the SpaceLocQA benchmark, with over 1.5x inference speedup. The paper also introduces GangnamLoop, a multi-trip outdoor benchmark collected using a real quadruped robot.
AI.motivation: Prior Spatial Question Answering approaches rely on closed-source models (e.g., GPT-4o) for path exploration, but real-world robots face network instability, communication latency, and deployment costs. This creates a need for open-source based approaches that can run onboard the robot, which has been limited in prior research.
AI.method: BinTrack performs a binary search over trajectory segments between two anchor landmarks identified from a query, leveraging the temporal ordering of a robot's trajectory for efficient spatial localization.
AI.result: BinTrack improves overall accuracy by up to 22.8% over other open-source implementations and matches GPT-4o's reported result on the global category of SpaceLocQA benchmark. It also achieves more than 1.5x inference speedup over previous approaches.
AI.conclusion: BinTrack demonstrates that fully open-source spatial question answering can match closed-source model performance while being deployable onboard robots. The release of GangnamLoop benchmark further supports practical multi-trip outdoor robot navigation research.

title: Medical Heuristic Learning: An LLM-Driven Framework for Interpretable and Auditable Clinical Decision Rules
summary: Predictive modeling for clinical tabular data is central to clinical decision support and therefore requires not only strong predictive performance but also transparent decision logic. Although deep learning and tree-based ensemble methods can achieve high accuracy, their black-box nature remains a major obstacle to clinical deployment. This challenge is further compounded by common characteristics of medical data, including limited sample sizes, severe class imbalance, and feature evolution arising from changes in diagnostic criteria and clinical documentation. To address these issues, we propose Medical Heuristic Learning (MHL), an instantiation of the learning-beyond-gradients paradigm for clinical tabular prediction. Instead of relying on neural network weight updates, MHL uses a large language model (LLM)-driven workflow that integrates statistical probes, medical knowledge probes, rule synthesis, and code-level iterative refinement to optimize a deterministic and executable decision system. The resulting model is expressed not as opaque parameters, but as versioned pure-Python decision rules that are explicitly interpretable, fully auditable, and clinically grounded. MHL also supports continual learning by starting from previously validated rules and iteratively revising them using updated feature information under data drift or feature evolution. Comprehensive experiments on medical datasets show that MHL achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining strong behavior in small-sample and highly imbalanced settings. The results further indicate that this explicit rule update mechanism can help alleviate catastrophic forgetting under feature evolution. Overall, these findings suggest that non-gradient-based heuristic systems offer a transparent and adaptable alternative for high-stakes clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: Medical Heuristic Learning (MHL) is a non-gradient-based, LLM-driven framework for clinical tabular prediction that produces fully interpretable Python decision rules, achieving performance comparable to SOTA methods while excelling in small-sample and imbalanced settings and supporting continual learning under feature evolution.
AI.motivation: Clinical predictive modeling requires both high accuracy and transparent decision logic, but deep learning and tree-based ensemble methods are black-box. This challenge is worsened by limited sample sizes, severe class imbalance, and feature evolution due to changes in diagnostic criteria and clinical documentation.
AI.method: MHL is an LLM-driven workflow that integrates statistical probes, medical knowledge probes, rule synthesis, and code-level iterative refinement to optimize a deterministic, executable decision system expressed as versioned pure-Python decision rules, without relying on neural network weight updates.
AI.result: MHL achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining strong behavior in small-sample and highly imbalanced settings. Its explicit rule update mechanism helps alleviate catastrophic forgetting under feature evolution.
AI.conclusion: Non-gradient-based heuristic systems like MHL offer a transparent, auditable, and adaptable alternative for high-stakes clinical decision support.

title: Unified Motion-Action Modeling for Heterogeneous Robot Learning
summary: We present Unified Motion-Action (UMA) Model, an approach that uses 3D object motion trajectories as a shared interface to bridge visuomotor control and dynamics modeling. UMA treats object motion and robot actions as co-evolving variables under a masked generative objective, in which the mask pattern determines both the supervision regime during pretraining and the inference mode at deployment. Using hindsight-relabeled motion contexts and a contrastive objective that disentangles task intent from scene geometry, UMA enables multi-task pretraining across heterogeneous data sources without requiring manually annotated task instructions. At deployment, the same pretrained parameters support motion-conditioned visuomotor control, motion-based dynamics modeling, and task adaptation from few-shot demonstrations. Pretrained on a mixture of robot demonstrations, human videos, and simulated data, UMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines specialized for each inference mode.

AI.tldr: UMA uses 3D object motion trajectories as a shared interface for visuomotor control and dynamics modeling, enabling multi-task pretraining across heterogeneous data sources without manual annotations, and outperforming specialized baselines across multiple inference modes.
AI.motivation: To bridge visuomotor control and dynamics modeling using a unified framework that leverages 3D object motion trajectories as a shared interface, eliminating the need for manually annotated task instructions and enabling pretraining across diverse data sources (robot demonstrations, human videos, simulated data).
AI.method: UMA treats object motion and robot actions as co-evolving variables under a masked generative objective, where mask patterns determine supervision regime during pretraining and inference mode at deployment. It uses hindsight-relabeled motion contexts and a contrastive objective to disentangle task intent from scene geometry.
AI.result: Pretrained on a mixture of robot demonstrations, human videos, and simulated data, UMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines specialized for each inference mode (motion-conditioned visuomotor control, motion-based dynamics modeling, and task adaptation from few-shot demonstrations).
AI.conclusion: The same pretrained parameters support multiple downstream tasks without task-specific fine-tuning, demonstrating that 3D object motion trajectories serve as an effective shared interface for unifying visuomotor control and dynamics modeling across heterogeneous data.

title: Whose hotel does the AI recommend? An algorithm audit of reputation signals in LLM-assisted hotel selection
summary: Travelers increasingly ask large language model (LLM) assistants which hotel to book, making these systems gatekeepers of property visibility -- yet what moves their recommendations is undocumented. We conduct a pre-specified algorithm audit using a randomized choice-based conjoint: across personas, prompt templates, and twelve open-weight and proprietary models, assistants choose among five hotels whose guest rating, review volume and recency, management response, chain affiliation, price, eco-certification, and list position are independently randomized. We estimate the average marginal component effect of each signal on the probability of recommendation. Guest rating and price dominate (a top rating raises selection by 31.6 percentage points; a high price lowers it by 30.0), reproducing human valence-and-price primacy but over-weighting eco-certification and ignoring management response. List position -- a content-free artifact -- shifts recommendations causally, worth about \$12 per night. Stated reasons track revealed weights imperfectly. The findings ground generative engine optimization and the accountability of AI infomediaries in causal evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a randomized conjoint audit of LLM hotel recommendations, finding that guest rating and price dominate decisions, eco-certification is overweighted, management response is ignored, and list position causally shifts recommendations with an effect equivalent to ~$12/night.
AI.motivation: LLM assistants increasingly serve as hotel booking gatekeepers, yet the signals driving their recommendations remain undocumented and unaccountable.
AI.method: Pre-specified algorithm audit using a randomized choice-based conjoint experiment across personas, prompt templates, and 12 open-weight and proprietary models, estimating average marginal component effects (AMCE) of eight hotel attributes on recommendation probability.
AI.result: Guest rating (+31.6 pp) and price (-30.0 pp) dominate; eco-certification is overweighted; management response is ignored; list position causes a causal shift equivalent to ~$12/night; stated reasons imperfectly track revealed weights.
AI.conclusion: The findings ground generative engine optimization and establish causal evidence for accountability of AI infomediaries in travel recommendations.

title: CrossMaps: Confidence-Aware Open-Vocabulary Semantic Mapping for Rover Navigation
comment: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2026: ROSE International Workshop on Robotics Software Engineering, June 01, 2026, Vienna, Austria
summary: Rovers rely on perception to maintain spatial maps that encode both objects and sensor quality (e.g., range reliability, lighting artifacts, data density), guiding data fusion, embedding updates, and navigation under partial observability. To study these coupled perception-navigation processes, we present CrossMaps, a real-time confidence-aware open-vocabulary semantic mapping pipeline that constructs language-queryable maps from RGB-D data. Building on VLMaps-style approaches, CrossMaps integrates multi-scale CLIP embeddings with confidence-aware fusion and a dual-memory architecture consisting of Short-Term Memory (STM) and Long-Term Memory (LTM). The STM aggregates noisy visual observations using geometric, semantic, and temporal confidence cues, while confident and coherent cells are promoted to the LTM as persistent semantic landmarks. Designed for deployment with a Jetson Orin-powered UGV alongside SLAM, CrossMaps runs in real time and produces semantic heatmaps that can be queried with natural language to guide rover navigation.

AI.tldr: CrossMaps is a real-time, confidence-aware open-vocabulary semantic mapping pipeline for rovers, integrating multi-scale CLIP embeddings with dual-memory (STM/LTM) architecture and confidence fusion to produce language-queryable maps from RGB-D data for navigation.
AI.motivation: To study coupled perception-navigation processes in rovers by enabling real-time semantic mapping that accounts for sensor quality (range reliability, lighting artifacts, data density) and supports natural-language-guided navigation under partial observability.
AI.method: CrossMaps builds on VLMaps-style approaches, integrating multi-scale CLIP embeddings with confidence-aware fusion and a dual-memory architecture: Short-Term Memory (STM) aggregates noisy observations using geometric, semantic, and temporal confidence cues, and confident coherent cells are promoted to Long-Term Memory (LTM) as persistent semantic landmarks. Deployed on a Jetson Orin-powered UGV with SLAM.
AI.result: Real-time operation on embedded hardware (Jetson Orin), producing semantic heatmaps queryable via natural language for rover navigation.
AI.conclusion: CrossMaps enables real-time, confidence-aware, open-vocabulary semantic mapping that bridges perception and navigation, allowing rovers to maintain spatial maps encoding both objects and sensor quality for guided navigation.

title: Looking Is Not Picking: An Attention-Segment Account of Tool-Selection Failures in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents mis-call tools, and the natural guess is that the model failed to see the right tool in a crowded harness. We show the opposite through a lens concurrent work sets aside -- the model's attention to labeled tool-definition segments. On real BFCL failures, by per-candidate attention argmax the model attends most to the correct tool 80% of the time (vs. 21% chance), and the gold is the under-attended segment on only 10%: it looks at the right tool and still picks wrong. This directly refutes the intuitive "crowded-harness / lost-in-the-middle" explanation: the failure is at the decision readout, not the harness, and we pin it there three ways. (1) Input vs. readout: repairing the prompt (reordering or duplicating the gold tool) recovers <=23% of failures, while readout-side interventions recover 59-91%. (2) Representation-invariance: two gold-pointed interventions in different representations -- an additive attention-logit bias and a residual-stream steering vector -- recover largely the same failures (per-task Jaccard 0.865 pooled, 0.79-0.91 per model), so the bottleneck is localized to the readout independent of which representation is poked. (3) A training-free, gold-free selector: per-segment attention closes most of the gold-free-vs-oracle gap on BFCL (+11.9 pts pooled function-name selection vs. +17.9-pt oracle headroom) and adds +14.9 pts on Seal-Tools; every model positive (exact McNemar p<=8e-4 each). Scopes differ: the causal attention-bias dose-response is bidirectional and monotonic on 10 mask-honoring models (3-32B), the full 0.5-32B span carrying only the correlational diagnostic; the deployable selector is evaluated on 5 single-turn models and does not yet transfer to a multi-turn loop.

AI.tldr: LLM agent tool-calling errors are not due to the model failing to see the correct tool in a crowded context (lost-in-the-middle). Instead, attention analysis shows the model attends to the correct tool 80% of the time but still selects incorrectly, pinpointing the failure at the decision readout stage rather than the input harness.
AI.motivation: To challenge the intuitive "crowded-harness" explanation for LLM agent tool-calling failures by investigating whether models actually attend to the correct tool definitions, and to precisely locate the failure mechanism.
AI.method: (1) Per-candidate attention argmax analysis on real BFCL failures to measure attention to correct vs. incorrect tools. (2) Three-way failure localization: comparing input-side repairs (reordering/duplication) vs. readout-side interventions; demonstrating representation-invariance via two different interventions (attention-logit bias and residual-stream steering) recovering the same failures; and building a training-free, gold-free per-segment attention selector.
AI.result: Models attend to the correct tool 80% of the time (vs. 21% chance), with gold under-attended in only 10% of failures. Input repairs recover ≤23% of failures, while readout interventions recover 59-91%. The two representation-different interventions show high per-task Jaccard similarity (0.865 pooled). The gold-free attention selector closes most of the gap to oracle performance (+11.9 pts on BFCL, +14.9 pts on Seal-Tools, all models significant at p≤8e-4).
AI.conclusion: Tool-calling failures in LLM agents are primarily decision readout errors rather than input encoding/harness problems. The bottleneck is localized to the readout stage, independent of the representation being manipulated. A simple per-segment attention-based selector can substantially recover performance without training or gold labels.

title: SidewalkBench: Benchmarking Visual Navigation on Urban Sidewalks
summary: Urban sidewalk navigation presents significant challenges due to complex structural layouts, dynamic pedestrian behaviors, and long distances. While recent visual navigation models offer a promising solution, the lack of a unified benchmark hinders quantitative and reproducible evaluation. To bridge this gap, we propose SidewalkBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed for visual navigation on urban sidewalks. Built upon NVIDIA Isaac Sim, SidewalkBench brings GPU-accelerated simulation of diverse, high-fidelity sidewalk environments, including both procedurally generated and real-world scanned scenes. We further populate the scenes with rich, reactive event-based pedestrian behaviors and flexible, efficient animation, enabling standardized model evaluation under realistic real-world settings. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 9 visual navigation models on 330 unit-test scenarios, 800 pedestrian-reactive scenarios, and 105 long-horizon scenarios. Our findings highlight that pedestrian interaction and long-horizon robustness remain critical bottlenecks for existing models, and scaling up sidewalk training with synthetic data emerges as a promising solution.

AI.tldr: SidewalkBench is a unified benchmark for visual navigation on urban sidewalks built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim, featuring GPU-accelerated simulation, diverse environments (procedural and real-scanned), and reactive pedestrian behaviors. Evaluations of 9 models across 1,235 scenarios reveal pedestrian interaction and long-horizon robustness as key bottlenecks, with synthetic data scaling showing promise.
AI.motivation: Urban sidewalk navigation faces challenges from complex layouts, dynamic pedestrian behaviors, and long distances. Existing visual navigation models lack a unified benchmark for quantitative and reproducible evaluation.
AI.method: SidewalkBench is built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim with GPU-accelerated simulation, procedurally generated and real-world scanned scenes, and event-based reactive pedestrian behaviors with flexible animation. It includes 330 unit-test, 800 pedestrian-reactive, and 105 long-horizon scenarios.
AI.result: Evaluation of 9 visual navigation models shows pedestrian interaction and long-horizon robustness remain critical bottlenecks. Scaling up sidewalk training with synthetic data emerges as a promising solution.
AI.conclusion: SidewalkBench provides a standardized evaluation framework, identifies key model limitations in pedestrian-reactive and long-horizon settings, and suggests synthetic data scaling as a viable path forward for sidewalk navigation.

title: Posterior Twins: Distributional Behavioral Simulation for Enterprise Decisions
summary: Enterprise behavioral simulation requires more than producing a plausible response. Many decisions depend on the shape of a population under a proposed action: which segments accept, defect, hesitate, or move into risk-sensitive states. This paper introduces Posterior Twins, a memory-grounded digital-twin approach that represents likely behavior as an updated distribution under a specific decision context. We evaluate a family of Twinning Labs behavioral-model operating points on a 226-example held-out behavioral-response benchmark and report both modal accuracy and Wasserstein-1 distance. The results show that modal accuracy and distributional fidelity identify different operating regimes. TL-Twin Alpha achieves the lowest observed Wasserstein-1 distance in the reported result set ($W_1 = 1.16$), while TL-Twin Delta and TL-Twin Gamma provide balanced operating points near the modal-accuracy frontier. The paper frames these results as a systems result: governed memory, behavioral model routing, scenario orchestration, distributional aggregation, and auditability are necessary for turning simulated behavior into reusable enterprise decision evidence.

AI.tldr: Posterior Twins is a memory-grounded digital-twin approach for enterprise behavioral simulation that captures population distributions (not just plausibility), evaluated on a 226-example benchmark using modal accuracy and Wasserstein-1 distance. TL-Twin Alpha achieves the best distributional fidelity (W₁=1.16), while other variants offer balanced trade-offs. The paper emphasizes that governed memory, model routing, scenario orchestration, distributional aggregation, and auditability are essential for reusable decision evidence.
AI.motivation: Enterprise behavioral simulation requires more than producing a plausible response—it needs to capture the shape of population distributions under proposed actions, including which segments accept, defect, hesitate, or enter risk-sensitive states.
AI.method: Posterior Twins, a memory-grounded digital-twin approach, represents likely behavior as an updated distribution under a specific decision context. A family of Twinning Labs behavioral-model operating points is evaluated on a 226-example held-out behavioral-response benchmark using both modal accuracy and Wasserstein-1 distance.
AI.result: Modal accuracy and distributional fidelity identify different operating regimes. TL-Twin Alpha achieves the lowest Wasserstein-1 distance (W₁=1.16). TL-Twin Delta and TL-Twin Gamma provide balanced operating points near the modal-accuracy frontier.
AI.conclusion: Governed memory, behavioral model routing, scenario orchestration, distributional aggregation, and auditability are necessary for turning simulated behavior into reusable enterprise decision evidence. The results are framed as a systems result.

title: When Should a Robot Replan? Regret-Guided Update Scheduling in Time-Varying MDPs
summary: Robots operating in non-stationary environments must continually adapt their policies as the dynamics drift, but onboard energy and compute budgets cap how often a full state estimation and re-planning step can be performed. This raises a question: \emph{when}, along a horizon, should a robot spend its limited budget? We formulate this problem in time-varying Markov decision processes (TVMDPs) with a known bound on the rate of transition drift. We model execution as a \emph{skip-update} scheme in which, at chosen update times, the agent estimates the transition kernel by maximum likelihood and computes a finite-horizon policy, and between updates reuses this policy under a propagated state estimate. We analyze the dynamic regret of this scheme and show how it grows during skip intervals in terms of the properties of the TVMDP and the skip lengths; the resulting bound answers the opening question via an online, regret-guided update rule that allocates the budget adaptively. We evaluate the rule in a simulated Mars-rover navigation task with time-varying slip dynamics and on a Crazyflie quadrotor in indoor obstacle fields. Adaptive allocation outperforms other budgeted baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses when, along a horizon, a robot with limited onboard budget should update its policy in non-stationary environments. It formulates the problem in time-varying MDPs with bounded drift, proposes a skip-update scheme with regret-guided adaptive budget allocation, and validates it in simulation and real quadrotor experiments.
AI.motivation: Robots operating in non-stationary environments must continually adapt to drifting dynamics, but onboard energy and compute budgets limit how often full state estimation and re-planning can be performed, raising the question of when along a horizon a robot should spend its limited budget.
AI.method: The problem is formulated in time-varying Markov decision processes (TVMDPs) with a known bound on transition drift rate. Execution follows a skip-update scheme: at chosen update times, the agent estimates the transition kernel via maximum likelihood and computes a finite-horizon policy; between updates, the policy is reused under a propagated state estimate. Dynamic regret is analyzed, yielding a regret-guided update rule that adaptively allocates the budget.
AI.result: The dynamic regret bound shows how regret grows during skip intervals in terms of TVMDP properties and skip lengths. The adaptive allocation rule outperforms other budgeted baselines in a simulated Mars-rover navigation task with time-varying slip dynamics and on a Crazyflie quadrotor in indoor obstacle fields.
AI.conclusion: The regret-guided adaptive budget allocation rule effectively answers when to update policies under limited budgets, achieving superior performance compared to baseline budgeted approaches in both simulation and real-world robotics experiments.

title: When Agent Automation Becomes Profitable: Quantifying and Insuring Autonomous AI Risk through Trace-Economic Underwriting
summary: AI agents can now take irreversible actions in operational systems, but agent-caused losses are still not clearly assigned, priced, or transferred. Providers often disclaim consequential damages, users are left with uncompensated losses, and default human review limits the efficiency gains of automation. We ask when autonomous AI deployment can become economically acceptable despite failure risk. Our answer is to quantify risk at the customer-task-trace episode level and transfer it through insurance. Automation is acceptable when its expected benefit exceeds the premium, control cost, and remaining risk. This requires a defined role with bounded permissions and comparable traces. We introduce trace-economic underwriting, which maps tool-use traces to customer exposure and claimable loss, then uses this representation for pricing, control, and risk transfer. It uses deterministic economic labels rather than an LLM judge. In our trace-to-loss testbed, trace-economic pricing reduces pricing MAE from $17.7K to $569 and removes regressive cross-subsidy. A 300-trace expert audit accepts 295 labels unchanged. On 1,000 real SWE-smith traces, trace-conditioned controls reduce CVaR95 by 72%. Theorem~1 gives a finite-sample scope condition. We release code, labels, and audit sheets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes trace-economic underwriting—a framework for insuring autonomous AI agents by quantifying risk at the episode level using deterministic economic labels on tool-use traces—enabling pricing, control, and risk transfer that reduces pricing error from $17.7K to $569, cuts CVaR95 by 72%, and passes expert audit, making automation economically acceptable when expected benefit exceeds premium, control cost, and residual risk.
AI.motivation: AI agents can now take irreversible actions in operational systems, but agent-caused losses are not clearly assigned, priced, or transferred; providers disclaim consequential damages, users bear uncompensated losses, and default human review undermines automation efficiency. The authors ask when autonomous AI deployment can become economically acceptable despite failure risk.
AI.method: The paper introduces trace-economic underwriting: mapping tool-use traces to customer exposure and claimable loss using deterministic economic labels (not an LLM judge) for pricing, control, and risk transfer. It formalizes a finite-sample scope condition (Theorem 1) and evaluates the approach on a trace-to-loss testbed and 1,000 real SWE-smith traces.
AI.result: Trace-economic pricing reduces pricing MAE from $17.7K to $569 and removes regressive cross-subsidy. A 300-trace expert audit accepts 295 labels unchanged. On 1,000 real SWE-smith traces, trace-conditioned controls reduce CVaR95 by 72%.
AI.conclusion: Automation is economically acceptable when its expected benefit exceeds the premium, control cost, and remaining risk, requiring a defined role with bounded permissions and comparable traces. The proposed insurance-based risk transfer mechanism makes autonomous AI deployment viable despite failure risk.

title: Task-Error Residual Learning for Real-Robot Five-Ball Juggling
comment: Submitted to the 2026 International Symposium on Robotics Research (ISRR)
summary: For residual learning that refines existing behavior, sample efficiency depends on two things: how much information each rollout returns, and how efficiently the learner uses that information. Reinforcement learning's standard scalar reward carries far less information than the directional task error that defines the task. Random exploration further discards whatever information each rollout returns. Through residual learning with directional task-error supervision and a task error model that drives sample selection, we achieve stable three-, four-, and five-ball juggling on anthropomorphic Barrett WAM arms. Despite planning and controlling through a simple, idealized stack, the system converges from the second attempt. The first attempt drops, after which task error decreases monotonically without further failures. In comparison, five-ball juggling typically takes humans years of practice. We compare residual learners across two ternary axes, the directional information in the learning feedback and the commitment of the analytic prior, spanning Newton-style Jacobian updates, Composite Bayesian Optimization, and stochastic search methods. Both axes prove necessary: neither directional feedback nor an informative prior suffices alone, and the simplest method that combines them, a fixed-Jacobian Newton update, is the most reliable. The learned residual tolerates substantial prior misalignment and degraded joint tracking, affecting mainly convergence speed. The bottleneck for residual learning on real robots is therefore the information content of the supervision signal and how the learner uses it, not the accuracy of the surrounding stack. Video documentation of all experiments is available at https://kai-ploeger.com/residual-juggling.

AI.tldr: Residual learning with directional task-error supervision enables stable 3-5 ball juggling on anthropomorphic robotic arms, converging from the second attempt, by using informative feedback (directional error vs. scalar reward) and a committed analytic prior (task error model for sample selection), outperforming methods lacking either component.
AI.motivation: Standard reinforcement learning uses scalar rewards and random exploration, which provide low information per rollout and inefficient learning. The paper aims to improve sample efficiency in residual learning for robotic control by using more informative supervision signals.
AI.method: The method uses directional task-error supervision (instead of scalar reward) and a task error model that drives sample selection. It compares residual learners across two axes: directional information in feedback and commitment of the analytic prior, spanning Newton-style Jacobian updates, Composite Bayesian Optimization, and stochastic search.
AI.result: Achieves stable 3-, 4-, and 5-ball juggling on anthropomorphic Barrett WAM arms. System converges from the second attempt; first attempt drops, then task error decreases monotonically without further failures. The fixed-Jacobian Newton update (combining both directional feedback and informative prior) was the most reliable method.
AI.conclusion: Both directional feedback and an informative prior are necessary for sample-efficient residual learning; neither alone suffices. The bottleneck for real-robot residual learning is the information content of the supervision signal and how the learner uses it, not the accuracy of the surrounding control stack.

title: Tensor-Coord: Algebraic Decomposition of Joint Plan Tensors for Conflict-Free Multi-Agent LLM Planning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain limited in multi-agent planning because independently generated plans can create coordination failures such as spatial collisions, resource contention, and temporal deadlocks. We introduce Tensor-Coord, a multilinear algebra framework that represents the joint plan of N agents as a third-order tensor \(T \in R^{N \times H \times A}\) over agents, timesteps, and actions. Canonical Polyadic (CP) and Tucker decompositions are used to identify latent coordination structure. The minimal epsilon-approximate CP rank R* defines a computable coordination complexity measure, with \(CC(Pi)=(R*-N)/N\). We prove that R*=N is necessary and sufficient for plan independence. The residual \(E=T-T_{R*}\) defines a conflict score over agent pairs, timesteps, and actions, localizing failures without domain-specific rules. Tucker factors provide interpretable agent roles, temporal phases, and action clusters that are converted into natural language constraints for iterative LLM replanning. Experiments on multi-robot delivery tasks across Easy (2 agents, 5x5 grid), Medium (3 agents, 5x5 grid), and Hard (4 agents, 5x5 grid) settings show convergence to conflict-free plans in 100% of 2-agent cases within 1.4 iterations on average, 80% of 3-agent cases within 3.2 iterations, and 60% of 4-agent cases within 4.0 iterations. CP rank scaled approximately linearly as \(R*(N) = 3.9N + 0.5\), supporting its use as a predictor of coordination complexity.

AI.tldr: Tensor-Coord uses multilinear algebra (CP/Tucker decompositions of a third-order agent×timestep×action tensor) to measure coordination complexity (CC) via CP rank, localize conflicts via residual tensor, and generate interpretable constraints for iterative LLM replanning, achieving conflict-free convergence in multi-agent planning tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with multi-agent planning due to coordination failures (collisions, resource contention, temporal deadlocks); existing methods lack a principled, domain-agnostic way to detect and resolve conflicts without hand-crafted rules.
AI.method: Represents N-agent joint plan as a third-order tensor T ∈ R^{N×H×A}; applies CP decomposition to compute minimal ε-approximate rank R* and coordination complexity CC = (R*-N)/N; uses residual tensor E = T - T_{R*} to localize conflicts across agent pairs, timesteps, and actions; Tucker decomposition yields interpretable factors converted to natural language constraints for iterative LLM replanning.
AI.result: 100% conflict-free convergence for 2 agents (avg 1.4 iterations), 80% for 3 agents (avg 3.2 iterations), 60% for 4 agents (avg 4.0 iterations). CP rank scales as R*(N) ≈ 3.9N + 0.5, confirming linear growth with agent count.
AI.conclusion: Tensor-Coord provides a formal, scalable coordination complexity measure and an interpretable conflict localization mechanism that enables iterative LLM replanning without domain-specific rules, with empirical validation on multi-robot delivery tasks.

title: ROVE: Unlocking Human Interventions for Humanoid Manipulation via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Human interventions provide crucial corrective signals for post-training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.
